title: Tempura
summary: Prawns and seasonal vegetables in the lightest batter in the world, mixed ice cold at the last second, barely stirred, fried in small batches and served at once with a dashi dipping sauce and grated daikon. After a whole fish in a wok, tempura asks the opposite: precision, control of gluten and a batch rhythm where every piece leaves the oil at its peak.
skills: an ice cold, barely mixed batter
equipment: Heavy pot at least 4 inches (10 cm) deep, or a wok, or an electric fryer
Deep fry thermometer
Long cooking chopsticks and a fine mesh skimmer
Wire rack over a tray lined with paper
Two mixing bowls, one sitting in a larger bowl of ice
Small saucepan for the dipping sauce
Fine grater for daikon and ginger
Small sharp knife and a cutting board
Sieve for sifting flour

ingredients.item: Kabocha squash or sweet potato, sliced 1/4 inch (5 mm) thick
Onion, cut in rings 1/3 inch (8 mm) thick, held with a toothpick

ingredients.note: optional; battered on one side only

ingredients.item: Cake flour or low protein plain flour, chilled

ingredients.note: with a few tablespoons of toasted sesame oil if you like

ingredients.item: Daikon radish, finely grated and squeezed lightly
Flaky salt mixed with a little matcha or lemon zest

mise: Prepare the prawns: twist off the heads, peel off the shells but leave the last tail segment on. Cut off the very tip of the tail and scrape out the water inside it with the knife, which stops it spitting. Remove the dark vein along the back.

Straighten the prawns: make 4 or 5 shallow cuts across the underside, then lay each prawn on its back and press down along its length until you feel small clicks; it should lie straight. For butterflied prawns, cut down the back almost through and open them flat.
Pat all prawns and vegetables completely dry with paper and arrange them on a tray in the order you will fry them: vegetables first, prawns last.
Make the tentsuyu: bring the dashi, mirin and soy to a boil in the small pan, take off the heat and keep warm.
Grate the daikon and ginger; shape the daikon into small mounds with a little ginger on top.
Chill the flour in the freezer for 15 minutes; set up the batter bowl inside the bowl of ice.

timeline.do: Prepare and dry the prawns and vegetables; chill the flour.
Make the tentsuyu and grate the daikon and ginger.
Heat the oil to 340°F (170°C).
Mix the first batch of batter; fry the vegetables.
Raise the oil to 355°F (180°C); fresh batter; fry the prawns and serve in waves.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 340°F (170°C). Lightly dust each vegetable and prawn in the 1/4 cup (30 g) flour and tap off the excess.
steps.look: A whisper of flour on every surface, so the batter will grip.
steps.mistake: Skipping the dusting, so the batter slides off and leaves bare patches.
steps.fix: Dust everything, shaking off thoroughly; it is a primer, not a coat.

steps.do: Make the batter only now: in the chilled bowl, beat the egg yolk into the ice water. Sift in the cold flour all at once and stir with chopsticks in a few quick strokes, about 10 seconds, stopping while there are still lumps and dry flour at the edges.
steps.look: A thin, lumpy batter with pockets of dry flour, like a badly made pancake batter; it runs off the chopsticks in streams.
steps.mistake: Whisking until smooth, which develops gluten and gives a heavy, bready crust.
steps.fix: Stop early. If it is smooth, it is overmixed: use it, but make the next batch with fewer strokes. Make the batter in small batches through the meal.

steps.do: Dip vegetable pieces into the batter one at a time, let the excess drip off for a second and slide them into the oil, frying 4 or 5 pieces at a time. Fry kabocha and sweet potato 2 to 3 minutes, mushrooms and beans 1 to 1 1/2 minutes, turning once.
steps.look: The batter puffs and spreads into lacy edges, bubbles steadily and sets pale gold, not brown.
steps.mistake: Frying too many pieces at once, so the oil drops below 320°F (160°C) and the tempura turns greasy.
steps.fix: Fry small batches and wait for the thermometer to recover each time. Skim floating bits of batter between batches so they do not burn.

steps.do: Lift each piece with chopsticks, hold it over the oil for 2 seconds, and stand it upright or on its edge on the rack. Season vegetables lightly with salt if not using the dipping sauce.
steps.look: A pale, crisp, lacy shell that rings when tapped with a chopstick; you can see the colour of the vegetable through the thinnest parts.
steps.mistake: Laying the pieces flat on paper in a pile, so they steam and go soft.
steps.fix: Stand them on a rack in a single layer and eat within minutes.

steps.do: Raise the oil to 355°F (180°C) for the prawns. Mix a fresh small batch of batter. Hold each prawn by the tail, dip it, let it drip, and lay it in the oil away from you, pulling it slightly through the oil as you let go so it stays straight. Fry 4 at a time for 1 1/2 to 2 minutes.
steps.look: The prawn floats straight under a crisp, spiky coat; the flesh shows pink through it.
steps.mistake: Dropping prawns in so they curl and stick together.
steps.fix: Lay them in one by one with a gentle pull; for extra crunch, drizzle a little batter over them from chopsticks as they fry so it catches as flakes.

steps.do: Drain the prawns on the rack and serve at once, in waves as they come out, with a small bowl of warm tentsuyu per person and a mound of grated daikon and ginger to stir into it.
steps.look: Prawns with a pale golden, crisp coat; when bitten the coat shatters and the prawn is juicy and just cooked.
steps.mistake: Holding the tempura in the kitchen until it is all done, by which time the first pieces are soft.
steps.fix: Serve each batch as it is fried, as tempura counters in Japan do; the cook eats last.

steps.do: When finished, turn off the heat and let the oil cool completely before straining it into a container.
steps.look: The oil is still clear, not dark, if the temperature was kept steady and the debris skimmed.
steps.mistake: Moving a pot of hot oil, risking a severe burn.
steps.fix: Leave it on a back burner to cool for several hours.

science: The crispness of tempura depends on keeping gluten from forming. Gluten develops when wheat proteins meet water and are mixed; ice cold water slows the process, low protein flour has less to form it, and minimal stirring gives it little chance. Lumps of dry flour are a sign of success, not failure. In the oil, the water in the thin batter flashes to steam and escapes quickly, leaving a fragile, porous starch shell. The egg yolk adds a little fat and protein for colour and tenderness. Oil kept at 340 to 355°F (170 to 180°C) is hot enough to drive off moisture fast and set the crust before oil can soak in; lower temperatures leave the batter wet and greasy. Grated daikon contains enzymes and a fresh bite that cut the richness.
plating: Line a basket or a flat plate with folded paper. Arrange the tempura leaning against each other in a small pile: tall vegetables at the back, prawns crossed at the front with their tails pointing up, a shiso leaf battered side out to one side. Set a small bowl of tentsuyu and a neat cone of daikon topped with ginger beside it, and a little mound of flavoured salt at the edge of the plate.

pairing.drink: Dry Champagne or a crisp sparkling wine: the bubbles and acidity scrub the oil from the palate, a classic match for tempura; a dry sake also works.
pairing.brennans: Brennan’s Essential by Piper-Heidsieck Extra Brut NV: the house Champagne on the Brennan's list, very dry and fresh, ideal with anything fried as lightly as tempura.

variations: Kakiage: mix thin strips of carrot, onion and small shrimp with a little batter and fry spoonfuls as lacy fritters.
Tendon: serve the tempura over rice and drizzle with tentsuyu reduced to a light syrup.
Vegetable only: use lotus root, aubergine fans, pepper strips and courgette alongside the squash and mushrooms.
safety: Keep the oil no more than half the depth of the pot and never leave it unattended. Keep a lid nearby.
Dry everything well and remove the water from the prawn tails: water in hot oil spits.
Prawns are cooked when opaque and pink through, about 120 to 145°F (49 to 63°C).

title: Fish and Chips
summary: Thick fillets of haddock or cod in a crisp beer batter, proper chips blanched and then fried, and mushy peas made from dried marrowfat peas. Coming straight after tempura, it shows how a heavier, leavened batter behaves and makes the double fried chip second nature.
skills: skinning and portioning haddock or cod
equipment: Large heavy pot at least 6 quarts (5.7 litres), or an electric deep fryer
Deep fry thermometer
Flexible filleting knife
Wire rack over a tray, and a second lined tray
Spider or wire basket and long tongs
Large bowl and a whisk
Medium saucepan for the peas, and a potato masher
Clean tea towels
Fire blanket or large lid

ingredients.item: Haddock or cod fillet, thick, skin on or off
ingredients.note: from the thick loin end; buy from sustainable stocks

ingredients.item: Floury potatoes (Maris Piper, King Edward or Russet)
Beef dripping or neutral oil for frying
ingredients.note: dripping is traditional in the north of England

ingredients.item: Lager or pale ale, ice cold
ingredients.note: straight from the fridge, opened at the last moment

ingredients.item: Plain flour, for dusting the fish

mise: The night before: put the marrowfat peas in a large bowl with the bicarbonate of soda and cover with 4 cups (950 ml) boiling water. Leave to soak overnight; they will double in size.

Skin the fish if needed: lay each fillet skin down, tail end towards you, cut down to the skin at the tail end, then grip the skin with a cloth and push the knife away from you, blade angled slightly down, wiggling the skin. Check for pin bones and remove them.
Portion the fish into even pieces of about 6 oz (170 g), trimming thin tail ends to fry separately. Pat dry and refrigerate on paper.
Peel the potatoes and cut into chips about 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) thick. Rinse in cold water until it runs clear, then soak for 30 minutes.
Put the beer in the freezer for 15 minutes and mix the dry batter ingredients in the bowl and chill them too.
Heat the oven to 200°F (95°C) to keep things warm.

timeline.do: Soak the marrowfat peas with bicarbonate of soda.
Skin and portion the fish; cut and soak the chips.
Simmer the peas; heat the fat to 265°F (130°C).
Blanch the chips in batches; cool on a rack.
Raise the fat to 350°F (177°C); mix the batter; fry the fish.
Raise the fat to 375°F (190°C); fry the chips the second time; serve.

steps.do: Mushy peas: drain and rinse the soaked peas, put them in the saucepan and cover with fresh cold water by 1 inch (2.5 cm). Bring to a boil, skim, then simmer gently, partly covered, for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring often near the end, until they collapse. Mash lightly with the butter and season with salt.
steps.look: Thick, soft and green, holding its shape on a spoon but soft enough to fall off slowly; some peas still whole.
steps.mistake: Letting them catch on the bottom as they thicken.
steps.fix: Stir regularly in the last 15 minutes and add a splash of water if they become too thick.

steps.do: Blanch the chips: drain and dry them very well in a tea towel. Heat the fat to 265°F (130°C) and fry the chips in two or three batches for 6 to 8 minutes each, until soft right through but still pale. Lift onto the rack and cool for at least 20 minutes.
steps.look: Gentle bubbling; the chips stay pale and become floppy and soft when pressed.
steps.mistake: Frying wet chips, which spits and boils over.
steps.fix: Dry them thoroughly and lower slowly; never fill the pot more than half full of fat.

steps.do: Heat the fat to 350°F (177°C). Just before frying, open the cold beer and pour it into the chilled dry ingredients, whisking only until mostly smooth; a few lumps are fine.
steps.look: A batter the thickness of double cream that coats the back of a spoon and drips off in a ribbon; it foams slightly from the beer.
steps.mistake: Making the batter in advance, so the bubbles go flat and it warms up, giving a heavy crust.
steps.fix: Mix it at the last minute and keep the bowl over ice if frying takes a while.

steps.do: Dust a piece of fish in flour, shake off the excess, then dip it in the batter, lift it by one end and let the excess drip for 3 seconds. Lower it into the fat away from you, holding it for a moment so the end sets before letting go, then lay it in. Fry two pieces at a time.
steps.look: The batter puffs immediately and the fish floats; bubbling is lively.
steps.mistake: Dropping the fish in so it sinks and sticks to the bottom of the pot or basket.
steps.fix: Lower it slowly, swaying it through the fat for a second before letting go, so the batter sets before it touches the bottom.

steps.do: Fry for 6 to 8 minutes, turning once halfway, until deep golden and crisp. The fish is done when it reads 145°F (63°C) at the thickest point. Lift onto the rack and keep warm in the oven, uncovered, while you fry the rest.
steps.look: Amber, rigid and crisp; it sounds hollow when tapped, and the bubbles around it slow down.
steps.mistake: Draining on flat paper or covering it, which steams the batter soft.
steps.fix: Always drain on a rack, uncovered. Spoon a little extra batter over the top while frying for craggy bits if you like.

steps.do: Raise the fat to 375°F (190°C). Fry the blanched chips in batches for 2 to 4 minutes until deep golden and crisp. Drain on the rack and salt immediately.
steps.look: Golden brown, crisp outside and fluffy inside; they rattle in the basket.
steps.mistake: Overcrowding the pot, which drops the temperature and gives greasy chips.
steps.fix: Fry smaller batches and let the fat recover to 375°F (190°C) each time.

steps.do: Serve the fish on a pile of chips with a dollop of mushy peas, lemon wedges, tartare sauce and malt vinegar and salt at the table.
steps.look: A golden, crunchy fillet, steaming white flakes inside when broken.
steps.mistake: Seasoning the fish too late, when salt will not stick to the batter.
steps.fix: Salt everything as soon as it comes out of the fat, while the surface is still glistening.

science: Beer batter is leavened twice: carbon dioxide from the beer and baking powder creates bubbles that expand in the hot fat, giving a light, airy crust. Cold beer slows gluten formation, and rice flour adds a crispness that stays longer because it lacks gluten and holds less moisture. A dusting of flour on the fish absorbs surface water and helps the batter cling. Chips are blanched at a low temperature to cook the potato starch through without browning; the starch gelatinises and the inside becomes fluffy. Resting allows the surface to dry and form a skin. The hot second fry then dehydrates and browns that skin rapidly into a crisp shell. Bicarbonate of soda in the pea soak softens the skins by breaking down pectin, so the peas collapse into a mash.
plating: For the chip shop look, line a plate or a tray with greaseproof paper. Pile the chips at one side, lay the fish across them at an angle, with the fattest end towards the guest. Put a neat quenelle of mushy peas beside the fish and a ramekin of tartare sauce, plus a fat lemon wedge. Bring the malt vinegar and salt to the table separately.

pairing.drink: A crisp English sparkling wine or a cold pale ale: bubbles and acidity cut through the fried batter, as does a dry Muscadet.
pairing.brennans: Ridgeview ‘Bloomsbury’ Brut Sussex NV: an English sparkling wine from the Brennan's list, fresh and bright, and a natural match for Britain's national dish.

variations: Gluten-free batter: use 1 cup (130 g) rice flour and 1/2 cup (60 g) cornflour with sparkling water instead of flour and beer.
Quick mushy peas: simmer 1 lb (450 g) frozen peas with a knob of butter and a little mint for 5 minutes, then mash coarsely.
Scampi: batter or crumb peeled langoustine tails and fry 2 to 3 minutes at 350°F (177°C).
safety: Never fill the pot more than half full of fat; lower food in slowly and away from you; keep a lid or fire blanket ready.
Never leave hot fat unattended, and never move the pot until it has cooled.
Fish is safely cooked at 145°F (63°C): the flesh is opaque and flakes easily.

title: Korean Fried Chicken
summary: Chicken wings jointed at home, coated in a thin potato starch batter and fried twice, first gently to cook and then hot to set a glassy shell, before a sticky gochujang, honey and garlic glaze goes on at the very last moment. It extends the fried chicken of the Chef de Partie dinners by showing how starch and a second fry keep a crust crisp even under sauce.
skills: a gochujang glaze applied at the last moment
equipment: Heavy pot at least 5 quarts (5 litres) or a wok, or an electric fryer
Deep fry thermometer and an instant read probe
Heavy chef's knife or poultry shears
Two large mixing bowls
Wire rack over a tray lined with paper
Spider or slotted spoon and tongs
Large wide pan or wok for tossing in the glaze
Small saucepan for the glaze

ingredients.note: or 2 lb (900 g) boneless thigh in 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) pieces
adjust for a thin, drippy batter

ingredients.item: Toasted sesame seeds and sliced spring onion

mise: Joint the wings: stretch each wing out on the board. Feel for the joint between drumette and flat and cut straight through it with the heavy knife, where the knife slips between the bones. Cut off the wing tips at the next joint and save them for stock.
Pat the pieces dry, toss with the salt, pepper and ginger and refrigerate uncovered on a rack for at least 1 hour, up to overnight.
Make the glaze: in the small saucepan, simmer the gochujang, honey, soy, vinegar, ketchup and garlic over low heat for 2 to 3 minutes until glossy; stir in the butter and set aside.
Mix the potato starch, flour and baking powder in a bowl.
Set up the fryer away from the edge of the hob with the rack, tray, spider and lid beside it.

timeline.do: Joint the wings and dry brine them in the fridge.
Make the glaze; heat the oil to 325°F (163°C).
Batter and give the first fry in batches.
Rest; raise the oil to 375°F (190°C).
Second fry in batches.
Warm the glaze, toss, garnish and serve.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 325°F (163°C). Whisk the ice water into the dry mix to make a thin batter that coats a finger like single cream and drips freely. Add the chicken and toss until every piece is coated.
steps.look: A thin, translucent coat through which you can still see the skin; excess runs off in a stream.
steps.mistake: Making a thick, pasty batter that fries into a bready, heavy shell.
steps.fix: Thin it with more ice water a tablespoon at a time; the coat should look sparse.

steps.do: Lift the pieces one at a time, let excess drip off and lower them into the oil away from you, 7 or 8 pieces at a time. Fry 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally so they do not stick, until pale golden and cooked through. Lift onto the rack.
steps.look: Steady, energetic bubbling; the coat turns firm and pale blond, not brown.
steps.mistake: Adding too many pieces, so the oil drops below 300°F (150°C) and the coating goes greasy.
steps.fix: Fry in batches and let the oil recover to 325°F (163°C) between them.

steps.do: Check the largest drumette: it should read at least 165°F (74°C) near the bone. Wings are nicer at 175 to 185°F (79 to 85°C), where the connective tissue softens. Let all the pieces rest on the rack for at least 5 minutes, up to 30.
steps.look: The coating dries and goes matt as steam escapes from inside.
steps.mistake: Going straight into the second fry with steaming hot chicken, so moisture keeps softening the crust.
steps.fix: Rest them: the moisture moving to the surface during the rest is driven off in the second fry.

steps.do: Raise the oil to 375°F (190°C). Fry the chicken again in batches for 3 to 4 minutes until deep golden and very crisp. Drain on the rack.
steps.look: The coat turns a deeper gold and develops a craggy, glassy surface; tapped with tongs, it sounds hard and hollow.
steps.mistake: Taking them out too soon, before the crust has properly hardened.
steps.fix: Wait for a deep gold and a rattle in the spider; a few extra seconds at this heat do not dry the meat.

steps.do: Warm the glaze in the wide pan over low heat until it bubbles. Off the heat, add the hot chicken and toss quickly with tongs or by shaking the pan until every piece is lightly coated.
steps.look: A thin, shiny, brick red lacquer on each piece; the crust still shows its texture under the glaze.
steps.mistake: Simmering the chicken in the glaze, which soaks the crust.
steps.fix: Toss off the heat for seconds, not minutes, or serve the glaze in a bowl on the side for dipping.

steps.do: Pile onto a platter, scatter with sesame seeds and spring onion and serve at once with pickled daikon.
steps.look: Glossy, crackly pieces; when bitten, the shell shatters and the meat is juicy.
steps.mistake: Covering the platter, which traps steam and softens the coat.
steps.fix: Serve uncovered and immediately.

science: Potato starch forms a lighter, glassier crust than wheat flour because it has no gluten and its large granules gelatinise and then dry into a brittle film. A small amount of baking powder releases gas in the hot oil and makes the coating finely porous, increasing the surface that can dry out and crisp. The first fry at a lower temperature cooks the chicken through and drives off part of the moisture; the rest lets moisture inside migrate outward; the second, hotter fry removes that moisture rapidly and sets the starch into a rigid shell. A crust that is drier holds up longer under a glaze because there is less water to soften it. Sugars in the honey and gochujang add shine, and the glaze is applied briefly so the crust does not absorb it.
plating: Pile the chicken on a wide platter or in a paper-lined basket in a loose mound so the pieces do not steam each other. Scatter sesame seeds and a little spring onion over the top. Serve pickled daikon cubes in a small bowl at the side and any extra glaze in a ramekin. Provide a bowl for bones and plenty of napkins.

pairing.drink: A cold lager is the Korean standard ('chimaek', chicken and beer); a dry rosé sparkling wine also cuts through the fried coat and handles the chilli.
pairing.brennans: Ferrari Rosé Brut NV: a dry Italian sparkling rosé on the Brennan's list whose bubbles and berry fruit suit fried chicken with a sweet chilli glaze.

variations: Soy garlic: replace the gochujang glaze with 3 tbsp (45 ml) soy, 2 tbsp (40 g) honey, 4 cloves garlic, 1 tsp (5 g) grated ginger and 1 tbsp (15 ml) rice vinegar, simmered until syrupy.
Huraideu (plain): serve the double fried chicken unglazed with salt and pepper and the glaze on the side.
Boneless: use thigh pieces, frying 5 to 6 minutes the first time and 2 to 3 minutes the second.
safety: Chicken must reach at least 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point near the bone.
Wash the board, knife and your hands after handling raw chicken; never rinse raw chicken in the sink.
Keep the oil no more than half the depth of the pot; never leave it unattended; keep a lid nearby.

title: Pollo a la Brasa with Ají Verde
summary: A whole chicken with its backbone cut out, flattened, marinated overnight in dark beer, soy, cumin, ají panca and huacatay, roasted hot until the skin is lacquered and the thighs are done, and served with a bright green chilli sauce. Spatchcocking is the first real piece of butchery in the course, and the dish asks you to read two thermometer readings on one bird.
skills: a dark beer, cumin and huacatay marinade
equipment: Sturdy poultry shears
Large chopping board with a damp cloth underneath
Blender
Large zip bag or non-reactive dish for marinating
Rimmed baking tray with a wire rack that fits inside
Instant read probe thermometer
Small food processor or the blender again for the sauce
Pastry brush

ingredients.note: or 1 tbsp (7 g) sweet paprika and 1 tsp (2 g) ancho powder
a stout or Peruvian dark lager
optional; or a small handful of mint with a few tarragon leaves
for the ají verde; seeds in for heat
shop bought, made with pasteurised egg

ingredients.item: Lime juice, for the ají verde

mise: Spatchcock the chicken: lay it breast down, tail towards you. Cut along one side of the backbone with the shears from tail to neck, then along the other side, and lift the backbone out (keep it for stock).
Open the bird out like a book, turn it breast up, and press firmly on the breastbone with the heel of your hand until you hear a crack and it lies flat. Tuck the wing tips behind the breast.
Blend the soy, ají panca, beer, lime juice, vinegar, garlic, cumin, oregano, huacatay, pepper, salt and oil to a smooth paste.
Loosen the skin over the breast and thighs with your fingers. Rub a third of the marinade under the skin, the rest over the outside, put the bird in the bag or dish, and refrigerate 12 to 24 hours.
Make the ají verde: blend the jalapeños, ají amarillo, coriander, mayonnaise, cheese, lime juice and garlic until smooth; season and refrigerate. It keeps 3 days.

timeline.do: Spatchcock, marinate and refrigerate the chicken; make the ají verde.
Chicken out of the fridge; heat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
Chicken into the oven on a rack.
Start probing; raise to 475°F (245°C) for the final blast if needed.
Rest; prepare fries and salad.
Cut into quarters and serve with ají verde.

steps.do: Take the chicken out of the marinade, let excess drip off and pat the skin lightly with paper so it is moist but not wet. Set it skin up on the rack, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the tray, legs spread out, the thighs towards the back of the oven where it is hottest.
steps.look: A dark, rust coloured bird lying flat and even, with no puddles of marinade on top.
steps.mistake: Leaving thick marinade on the skin, which burns before the bird is cooked.
steps.fix: Scrape off clumps with the back of a knife; the colour you need is already in the skin.

steps.do: Roast at 425°F (220°C) on the middle shelf for 40 minutes, turning the tray once halfway. Pour 1 cup (240 ml) of water into the tray beneath the rack so drippings do not burn.
steps.look: Steady sizzling, a smell of cumin and roasting chicken; the skin darkens to mahogany at the edges.
steps.mistake: Roasting directly in the tray without a rack, so the underside stews in the juices.
steps.fix: Always use the rack; if the skin darkens too quickly at the edges, lay small pieces of foil over them.

steps.do: Probe the thickest part of the thigh and the thickest part of the breast. The bird is done when the thigh reads 175°F (79°C) and the breast 160°F (71°C). If the skin is not yet deep brown and blistered, raise the oven to 475°F (245°C) for the final 5 to 10 minutes. Total time is usually 45 to 55 minutes.
steps.look: A lacquered, almost black edged skin, crackling and blistered; juices running clear from the thigh.
steps.mistake: Pulling the bird by colour alone, which can leave the thighs pink at the joint.
steps.fix: Trust the thermometer: both readings must be reached. If the breast is ready first, cover it with foil and continue until the thighs are done.

steps.do: Rest the chicken on a board, uncovered, for 10 to 15 minutes. The breast climbs to at least 165°F (74°C) during the rest.
steps.look: The skin stays crisp and the juices settle into the meat.
steps.mistake: Covering it tightly with foil, which steams the skin soft.
steps.fix: Rest it uncovered; it stays hot for 20 minutes.

steps.do: After the 10 to 15 minute rest, cut into quarters with the shears: cut along the breastbone to halve the bird, then cut each half between the thigh and the breast.
steps.look: Four neat pieces, each with crisp skin.
steps.mistake: Hacking through the bone with a knife so it splinters.
steps.fix: Cut through the soft cartilage and joints with shears; they follow the natural lines of the bird.

steps.do: Serve with fries, a simple salad of lettuce, tomato and red onion with lime, and plenty of ají verde, about 1/2 cup (120 ml) for every two people.
steps.look: Dark, glossy chicken next to bright green sauce.
steps.mistake: Serving the ají verde straight from the fridge, when it is too cold to taste.
steps.fix: Take it out 20 minutes before serving and stir it well.

science: Spatchcocking removes the backbone and flattens the bird, so the thighs and breast lie at an even height and depth in the oven. The thighs, which need a higher temperature to soften their connective tissue, sit nearer the heat, while the breast, which dries out above about 160°F (71°C), is less exposed. A flat bird also cooks faster and exposes more skin to dry heat. The marinade works mostly on the surface: salt and soy penetrate slowly into the meat over 12 to 24 hours and season it, while cumin, garlic and huacatay flavour the outer layer. Sugars in the soy and beer, together with the proteins, brown through the Maillard reaction and caramelise at high heat, giving the deep, almost black lacquer.
plating: Serve on a large wooden board or warm platter: the four quarters arranged skin up, the leg pieces overlapping the breasts. Pile hot fries at one side and a small bowl of salad at the other. Put the ají verde in a bowl in the centre with a spoon, and more on the table. For a plated version, a quarter of chicken leaning against a pile of fries, salad on the side and a generous spoon of ají verde.

pairing.drink: A juicy, light red such as Beaujolais (Gamay) or a cold Peruvian beer: both handle the spice and the green chilli sauce without drowning the chicken.
pairing.brennans: Jean Foillard ‘Côte du Py’ Morgon 2022: a Beaujolais cru from the Brennan's list, bright and savoury, very good with spiced roast chicken.

variations: On the grill: cook the spatchcocked chicken over indirect heat on a covered barbecue at 400°F (200°C) for 45 to 55 minutes, finishing skin side down over direct heat for 3 minutes.
Chicken legs: use 8 thighs and drumsticks, marinated the same way and roasted for 35 to 40 minutes.
Ají de huacatay: add a handful of huacatay or mint to the sauce for an even greener, herbal version.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C); take the thigh to 175°F (79°C) for the best texture.
Wash shears, board and hands after handling raw chicken, and discard the used marinade.
Use shop bought mayonnaise made with pasteurised eggs; keep the sauce refrigerated.

title: Tandoori Chicken with Naan
summary: Chicken legs slashed to the bone and marinated twice, first in lemon, salt and chilli and then in spiced hung yoghurt with mustard oil, roasted at the hottest heat your oven can give and charred under the overhead grill (broiler), with yoghurt naan cooked in seconds on a smoking hot pan. The dish asks you to manage extreme heat for both meat and bread, which is the closest a home kitchen comes to a tandoor.
skills: a yoghurt naan dough slapped onto a hot surface
equipment: Sharp knife and a board
Large non-reactive bowl
Muslin or a clean tea towel and a sieve for hanging yoghurt
Rimmed baking tray with a wire rack
Instant read probe thermometer
Heavy cast iron frying pan or tawa, ideally with a handle, at least 10 inches (25 cm)
Gas hob, or an overhead grill for finishing naan
Rolling pin, pastry brush and tongs
Large mixing bowl for the dough and a clean cloth

ingredients.item: Chicken legs, skin removed, cut into thighs and drumsticks

ingredients.note: hung to about 3/4 cup (200 g) thick yoghurt
equal parts ginger and garlic pounded
heated to smoking then cooled; or neutral oil

ingredients.item: Ghee or melted butter, for basting
Garlic, minced, and coriander, chopped, for the naan
Red onion rings, lime wedges and mint chutney

mise: The day before or that morning: put the yoghurt in muslin set in a sieve over a bowl and refrigerate for 2 hours or more to drain until thick.
Cut 3 deep slashes in each piece of chicken, across the grain and right down to the bone.
First marinade: rub the chicken with the lemon juice, salt and chilli powder, working into the slashes. Leave 20 to 30 minutes at room temperature, no longer.

Second marinade: mix the hung yoghurt with the ginger garlic paste, chilli, garam masala, cumin, turmeric, kasuri methi and cooled mustard oil. Coat the chicken thoroughly, pushing the marinade into the slashes, cover and refrigerate 6 to 24 hours.

Naan dough: mix the flour, yeast, sugar, baking powder and salt. Add the yoghurt, warm milk and oil and knead 6 to 8 minutes into a soft, slightly sticky dough. Cover and leave to rise 1 to 2 hours until doubled.

timeline.do: Hang the yoghurt; slash the chicken; first and second marinades.
Make the naan dough and leave it to rise.
Chicken out of the fridge; oven on at its maximum, at least 500°F (260°C).
Divide the dough into 8 balls and rest them.
Roast the chicken; baste; finish under the grill.
Cook the naan one by one while the chicken rests.

steps.do: Heat the oven to its maximum, at least 500°F (260°C), with a shelf near the top, for 30 minutes. Lift the chicken out of the marinade, keeping a thick coat on it, and arrange it on the rack over the foil-lined tray, pieces not touching.
steps.look: Every piece evenly coated in thick, orange red yoghurt, with space all round for heat to move.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pieces together, so they steam rather than char.
steps.fix: Use two trays if needed; air must flow around each piece.

steps.do: Roast 15 minutes, then turn each piece, baste with ghee and roast another 8 to 12 minutes until a probe in the thickest drumstick near the bone reads 165°F (74°C); 175°F (79°C) is better for legs.
steps.look: The marinade sets and darkens and the edges start to blacken in spots; fat sizzles on the tray.
steps.mistake: Pulling the chicken at the first sign of colour, while the meat at the bone is still pink.
steps.fix: Always probe the biggest piece at the bone.

steps.do: Switch to the overhead grill on high. Baste the chicken once more and grill 3 to 5 minutes, watching closely, until charred at the ridges of the slashes.
steps.look: Blackened ridges and edges with orange red between them; the kitchen smells of smoky spice.
steps.mistake: Walking away from the grill, so the char becomes burnt and bitter in under a minute.
steps.fix: Stay with it and pull the tray as soon as the edges are charred; remove any piece that is ready earlier.

steps.do: Rest the chicken 5 to 10 minutes while you cook the naan. Punch the risen dough down and divide into 8 balls; cover. Heat the cast iron pan over high heat for at least 5 minutes until smoking.
steps.look: The pan is so hot that a drop of water vanishes instantly.
steps.mistake: Cooking naan in a pan that is not hot enough, which gives a pale, dense flatbread.
steps.fix: Be patient: the pan needs to be as hot as possible.

steps.do: Roll a ball into a teardrop about 8 by 5 inches (20 by 13 cm) and 1/4 inch (5 mm) thick. Wet one side with your fingers. Slap the WET side down onto the hot pan, pressing it on.
steps.look: The dough sticks firmly to the pan and big bubbles appear on the dry upper surface within 30 seconds.
steps.mistake: Putting the dry side down, so the naan slides around and cannot be flipped over the flame.
steps.fix: Wet only the side that touches the pan, and press it down firmly.

steps.do: Cook 1 minute until the top is covered in bubbles, then, using an oven glove, turn the pan upside down over a high gas flame so the top of the naan faces the fire, moving it to char the bubbles for 30 to 60 seconds. Without gas, put the pan under the hot grill for 1 minute instead. Prise the naan off with a spatula.
steps.look: Puffy blistered bubbles with dark, charred spots; the underside golden and cooked.
steps.mistake: Dropping the naan into the flame because it was not stuck firmly.
steps.fix: If it starts to peel, flip it the right way up and finish it under the grill instead.

steps.do: Brush each naan with ghee, sprinkle with garlic and coriander, and stack them in a cloth to keep warm. Serve with the chicken, raw onion rings, lime wedges and mint chutney.
steps.look: Soft, chewy bread with charred spots, glistening with ghee.
steps.mistake: Leaving naan uncovered, so it goes hard.
steps.fix: Wrap them in a cloth or foil as they are done.

science: Slashing to the bone creates channels for marinade and heat, so the thick meat cooks closer to the speed of the surface and seasoning reaches deeper. The first marinade of salt and lemon starts seasoning before the yoghurt seals the surface. Yoghurt's lactic acid is mild, so it tenderises gently rather than turning the surface mushy, and its proteins and sugars brown and char quickly at high heat. A tandoor runs at 700°F (370°C) or more; at home the highest oven setting followed by the grill imitates the intense radiant heat that chars edges before the meat dries out. Naan cooks so fast because a very hot surface flashes water in the dough to steam, puffing it, while baking powder and yeast add more gas.
plating: Line a wide platter with lettuce leaves or a cloth. Pile the chicken on top in a loose heap, the charred edges facing out. Scatter red onion rings and chopped coriander over and tuck lime wedges around. Fold the naan in quarters and stack them in a basket under a cloth. Serve the mint chutney in a small bowl.

pairing.drink: A dry or just off dry Chenin Blanc or Riesling, or a cold lager: acidity and a touch of fruit meet the smoke and spice.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Huet ‘Le Haut-Lieu’ Vouvray Sec 2024: a dry Loire Chenin Blanc from the Brennan's list with the acidity and orchard fruit to stand up to spiced, charred chicken.

variations: Paneer tikka: marinate 1 lb (450 g) paneer cubes with peppers and onions in the second marinade only, then grill on skewers 8 to 10 minutes.
Garlic naan: press minced garlic and coriander into the top of the dough before cooking.
On the barbecue: grill the marinated chicken over hot coals, covered, 25 to 30 minutes, turning often.
safety: Chicken must reach at least 165°F (74°C) at the bone.
Discard leftover marinade; it has been in contact with raw chicken.
Turning a pan over an open flame is a high heat skill: use a dry, thick oven glove and keep the handle firmly gripped.

title: Tira de Asado with Chimichurri
summary: Short ribs cut across the bone, seasoned with coarse salt and nothing else, grilled slowly high above wood or charcoal embers, bone side down first and turned only once, with chimichurri made a day ahead. The asado teaches fire as an instrument: building it, reading it with your hand and waiting.
skills: building and reading a wood or charcoal fire
equipment: Charcoal kettle grill or a parrilla, ideally with an adjustable grate height
Lump hardwood charcoal or dry hardwood logs
Chimney starter
Long tongs and heat resistant gloves
Small shovel or poker for moving embers
Instant read probe thermometer
Sharp knife and a wooden board
Glass jar with a lid for the chimichurri

ingredients.item: Beef short ribs, cut across the bones (flanken cut, tira de asado), 1 1/4 inches (3 cm) thick
ingredients.note: ask the butcher for strips with 3 or 4 bones each

ingredients.item: Coarse salt (sal parrillera or coarse sea salt)
ingredients.note: the only seasoning on the meat

ingredients.item: Flat leaf parsley, finely chopped by hand
Olive oil or a mix with sunflower oil

ingredients.note: with a pinch of salt, for the chimichurri

ingredients.item: Fine salt and black pepper, for the chimichurri
Tomatoes, onion and red pepper, for salsa criolla
ingredients.note: diced with vinegar and oil; optional

mise: The day before: make the chimichurri. Dissolve the salt in the hot water in the jar, add the garlic, oregano and pepper flakes and leave 5 minutes to soften the oregano. Add the parsley, vinegar, black pepper and oil, stir, close and refrigerate overnight.
Take the ribs out of the fridge 45 minutes before grilling and pat them dry.

Light the charcoal or wood an hour before cooking: half fill the chimney starter, light it and, when the top coals are ashed over, tip them into a pile on one side of the grill and add more fuel to build a bed.
Make the salsa criolla, if serving: dice the tomatoes, onion and pepper and dress with vinegar, oil and salt.
Bring the chimichurri to room temperature an hour before serving.

timeline.do: Make the chimichurri.
Light the fire; ribs out of the fridge.
Embers ready; spread them; test the heat with your hand.
Salt the ribs; on the grill bone side down for 25 to 30 minutes.
Turn once; meat side 15 to 20 minutes.
Rest, cut between the bones and serve.

steps.do: When the fuel has burned down to glowing embers coated in grey ash, with no flames, rake a layer of embers about 2 inches (5 cm) deep under where the meat will sit, keeping a reserve pile at one side to top up. Set the grate high, about 6 inches (15 cm) above the coals.
steps.look: Red glowing coals under a thin layer of grey ash; no tall flames; a steady radiant heat.
steps.mistake: Cooking over flames or freshly lit coals, which blacken the outside and leave smoke flavour that tastes acrid.
steps.fix: Wait. An asador spends as long building the fire as cooking the meat.

steps.do: Test the heat: hold your palm flat at grate height. You should be able to hold it there for 7 to 8 seconds before it is too hot; that is medium low heat, around 300 to 350°F (150 to 175°C).
steps.look: Strong but bearable heat; you count to seven before you must pull away.
steps.mistake: Grilling over heat so fierce that you can bear it for only 2 seconds, which chars the ribs before the fat renders.
steps.fix: Raise the grate or spread the coals thinner. If it is too cool, push in more embers from the reserve pile.

steps.do: Season the ribs generously with the coarse salt on both sides just before they go on. Lay them bone side DOWN on the grate.
steps.look: A gentle sizzle, not a violent flare up; the bones sit between the meat and the fire.
steps.mistake: Seasoning with pepper, garlic or marinade, which burns in the long cook and masks the beef.
steps.fix: Salt only; the flavour comes from the fat, the fire and the chimichurri.

steps.do: Leave them for 25 to 30 minutes without turning. Feed small embers from the reserve under the meat if the heat drops. Move pieces away from any flare ups.
steps.look: Fat starts to render and drip, the meat on top turns from red to grey around the edges and beads of juice appear on the surface; the smell of roasting beef fat.
steps.mistake: Turning the ribs repeatedly, which never lets either side brown properly.
steps.fix: Turn once only: when juices pool on the top surface, the first side is ready.

steps.do: Turn the ribs once and grill the meat side for 15 to 20 minutes until deeply browned. Check with a probe between bones: 140 to 150°F (60 to 66°C) gives juicy, slightly pink meat; asado is traditionally cooked further, and short ribs stay tender to 160°F (71°C) because of their fat.
steps.look: A deep bronze crust on the meat side; the fat crisp and golden; the meat yields when pressed.
steps.mistake: Rushing the meat side over hot coals so it burns.
steps.fix: Keep the heat steady and the grate high; patience gives a crust and soft fat.

steps.do: Rest the ribs on the board for 5 minutes, then cut between the bones into small pieces, each with a bone. Serve at once with chimichurri spooned over or on the side, and salsa criolla.
steps.look: Juicy meat with a crust and rendered fat; the chimichurri bright green and sharp.
steps.mistake: Drowning the meat in chimichurri, which overwhelms it.
steps.fix: Spoon it on lightly; the meat should taste of beef and fire first.

science: Short ribs are full of intramuscular fat and connective tissue. Slow cooking over moderate radiant heat lets the fat render and baste the meat from inside while the surface browns slowly, rather than charring before the fat melts. Cooking bone side down first uses the bones as a heat shield and a rack: they absorb and spread heat, protecting the meat while the fat renders. Embers give a steady, even radiant heat with little smoke, while flames deposit soot and cause flare ups as fat drips. The hand test is a rough measure of radiant heat at grate height. Salt alone draws out a little surface moisture that dissolves it, which then seasons the meat. Chimichurri improves overnight as the vinegar draws flavour from the garlic and dried oregano.
plating: Serve on a wooden board, as at an asado. Arrange the cut ribs in a row, overlapping, bones pointing the same way, with the crust facing up. Set the chimichurri in a small bowl with a spoon at one end of the board and the salsa criolla in another. Add crusty bread on the side. On a plate: four or five pieces at an angle with a spoon of chimichurri over the middle and a small heap of salsa criolla beside.

pairing.drink: An Argentine Malbec or a Cabernet blend: dark fruit, soft tannin and spice to match grilled beef fat and garlic.
pairing.brennans: Penfolds ‘Bin 389’ Cabernet Shiraz 2019: a rich, full Australian red from the Brennan's list with the structure and dark fruit for grilled short ribs.

variations: Gas grill: set one side to medium low and grill the ribs over it with the lid open for the same times; you lose the smoke but not the method.
Provoleta: grill a thick round of provolone cheese in a small cast iron pan on the grill until bubbling, topped with oregano and chilli.
Vacío or skirt steak: use the same fire and salt only, cooking 8 to 10 minutes a side for skirt.
safety: Light charcoal only outdoors, in an open space, away from buildings; never use a charcoal grill indoors or in a garage.
Keep children and pets away from the fire; wear gloves when moving embers; keep water or sand nearby for stray embers, not for the grill itself.
Beef whole cuts are safe at 145°F (63°C) with a short rest.

title: Andesteg (Danish Roast Duck with Red Cabbage)
summary: A whole duck, stuffed with apple and prune, its skin pricked all over and salted overnight, roasted slowly so the fat renders out and the skin crisps, served with a cream gravy and sweet and sour braised red cabbage. You learn to prepare and roast a whole duck and to treat its rendered fat as treasure.
equipment: Large, deep roasting tin with a wire rack
Sharp skewer, needle or the tip of a paring knife
Kitchen scissors and a sharp boning knife
Instant read probe thermometer
Large heavy casserole with a lid, for the cabbage
Heatproof jar or jug for collecting fat, and a fine sieve
Medium saucepan for stock and gravy, and a whisk
Carving board and carving knife

ingredients.note: giblets and neck removed and kept

ingredients.item: Red cabbage, cored and finely shredded
Butter or duck fat, for the cabbage
Red wine vinegar or cider vinegar
Cinnamon stick, 3 cloves and 1 bay leaf
Small waxy potatoes, boiled, to serve

mise: The day before: pull out any loose fat from inside the cavity and keep it for rendering. Cut off the wing tips at the first joint with scissors and keep them with the neck and giblets (not the liver) for stock.

Prick the skin all over, especially over the breast, thighs and the fatty area near the tail, holding the skewer almost flat to the skin so it goes through the fat but NOT into the meat. Make 50 or more holes.
Pat the duck dry and rub it all over and inside with the coarse salt. Set it breast up on a rack over a tray in the fridge, uncovered, overnight.

Red cabbage: melt the butter in the casserole, add the cabbage and stir for 5 minutes. Add the vinegar, sugar, juice, cinnamon, cloves, bay and a pinch of salt, cover and braise over low heat for 1 1/2 hours, stirring occasionally, until very soft and glossy. It is better made a day ahead.
Stock: brown the neck, wing tips and giblets in a little oil in the saucepan, add the onion, carrot, water, bay and peppercorns, simmer gently 1 1/2 hours, strain and keep.

timeline.do: Prick and salt the duck; braise the red cabbage; make the stock.
Duck out of the fridge; oven on to 325°F (160°C).
Stuff and roast the duck, breast up on the rack.
Pour off the rendered fat into a jar.
Raise the oven to 425°F (220°C) for the skin.
Duck out to rest; make the gravy; reheat the cabbage; boil the potatoes.
Carve and serve.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C). Stuff the cavity loosely with the apples, prunes and thyme, and close it with a skewer. Season the outside with pepper. Set the duck breast up on the rack in the roasting tin.
steps.look: A dry, slightly taut skin covered with small holes; the stuffing fills the cavity without bulging.
steps.mistake: Packing the cavity tightly, which slows the heat reaching the inside and the meat near the bone.
steps.fix: Fill loosely; extra apple can roast in the tin.

steps.do: Roast for 2 1/2 to 3 hours in total. Every 30 to 40 minutes, take the tin out, carefully tilt it and spoon or pour off the rendered fat into the jar through a sieve; prick any areas of skin that look puffy again.
steps.look: Clear, golden fat collecting in the tin, a cup or more over the roast; the skin slowly turns golden and drier.
steps.mistake: Leaving the fat in the tin, where it can smoke, spit and even catch fire at the higher heat later.
steps.fix: Pour off regularly; keep the strained fat in the fridge for roasting potatoes.

steps.do: For the last 25 to 30 minutes, raise the oven to 425°F (220°C) to crisp and brown the skin. The duck is done when a probe in the thickest part of the thigh reads at least 165°F (74°C), and the leg moves loosely in its socket.
steps.look: Deep golden brown, crackling skin; the legs pulling away from the body; juices running clear.
steps.mistake: Taking a whole duck out with the breast pink but the legs underdone and chewy.
steps.fix: A whole roast duck is cooked through in the Danish way; the slow roast keeps it moist. Check the thigh, not the breast.

steps.do: Lift the duck onto the board, tipping the juices from the cavity into the tin. Rest uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes.
steps.look: The skin stays crisp; the meat settles.
steps.mistake: Covering it tightly, which softens the skin.
steps.fix: Rest it uncovered in a warm place.

steps.do: Gravy: pour off all but 2 tbsp (30 ml) of fat from the tin, set it on the hob over medium heat and stir in the flour. Cook 1 minute, then whisk in 2 cups (480 ml) of the hot stock gradually, scraping up the browned bits. Simmer 5 minutes, then stir in the cream and redcurrant jelly. Season with salt and pepper and strain into a warm jug.
steps.look: A smooth, light brown, glossy gravy that coats the back of a spoon; it tastes savoury with a faint sweetness.
steps.mistake: Leaving it greasy, with a layer of fat on top.
steps.fix: Let it stand 1 minute and skim the surface fat with a wide spoon, or blot it with paper.

steps.do: Carve: cut through the skin between the leg and the body, pull the leg away and cut through the joint, then separate thigh and drumstick. Cut down along one side of the breastbone and lift each breast off the carcass in one piece, then slice it on the diagonal.
steps.look: Each person gets some leg and some sliced breast, every piece with crisp skin.
steps.mistake: Carving the breast while it is still on the bone, so slices are uneven and the skin tears.
steps.fix: Lift the whole breast off first, lay it skin up and slice.

steps.do: Serve with the hot red cabbage, the prunes and apple from the cavity, boiled potatoes and the gravy.
steps.look: Crisp, dark golden duck, deep purple cabbage, pale potatoes, a jug of gravy.
steps.mistake: Serving the cabbage dull and watery.
steps.fix: Reheat it uncovered for the last 10 minutes so the liquid reduces to a glaze; adjust with sugar or vinegar.

science: A duck carries a thick layer of fat under its skin to keep it afloat and warm in cold water. Pricking the skin, without piercing the meat, creates escape routes for that fat as it melts. A low oven melts the fat slowly, so it runs out of the holes rather than being trapped under a skin that has already hardened. Salting overnight draws moisture out of the skin and dries it, so it browns and crisps rather than steaming. Once most of the fat has rendered, a hot oven finishes the skin, crisping it like crackling. The leg meat has more connective tissue and benefits from the long cook. Red cabbage turns from blue-purple to bright red-purple in the acid of vinegar, because its anthocyanin pigments change colour with acidity.
plating: On a warmed plate, a spoon of red cabbage in a neat mound to one side, a few slices of breast fanned against it skin up, and a piece of leg leaning beside. Add three small potatoes and a prune and apple quarter from the stuffing. Pour the gravy over the potatoes and around, never over the skin. For a family table, arrange the carved duck on a platter over the cabbage and bring the gravy in a jug.

pairing.drink: A Pinot Noir with bright acidity, or an Alsace Pinot Gris: fruit and acidity cut the rich duck and meet the sweet and sour cabbage.
pairing.brennans: Roasted Rohan Duck Breast: on the Brennan's tasting menu the duck comes with cane syrup glazed peaches, the same pairing of rich duck with fruit and sweetness that the prunes and red cabbage give here.

variations: Brunede kartofler: caramelise boiled small potatoes in melted sugar and butter for the traditional Danish Christmas side.
Duck legs: roast 4 duck legs, pricked and salted, at 325°F (160°C) for 1 1/2 hours, then 425°F (220°C) for 15 minutes.
Goose: the same method works for a goose of 9 to 10 lb (4 to 4.5 kg), roasting about 3 1/2 to 4 hours.
safety: Whole duck is cooked through to at least 165°F (74°C) in the thigh.
Hot duck fat is dangerous: tilt the tin away from you and use oven gloves when pouring it off. Never pour fat down the sink.
Cool the rendered fat, store it in a clean jar in the fridge and use within a few months.
The apple and prune stuffing cooks inside the bird: check that its centre also reaches 165°F (74°C), and if in doubt roast the stuffing in the tin beside the duck instead.

title: Home-Cured Corned Beef and Cabbage
summary: A beef brisket cured at home for a week in a spiced brine with curing salt, then simmered gently for hours with carrots, potatoes and wedges of cabbage, sliced against the grain and served with a parsley sauce. It takes the cure you learnt for pastrami and asks for patience twice: a week in the fridge and a simmer that never boils.
skills: a spiced wet cure of brisket with curing salt over a week
equipment: Digital kitchen scale that reads to 1 g
Large stockpot of at least 8 quarts (7.5 litres)
Food safe container or large zip bag, big enough to hold the brisket covered in brine, that fits in the fridge
Plate or bag of brine to weigh the meat down
Instant read probe thermometer
Long carving knife and a board
Medium saucepan and a whisk for the sauce
Slotted spoon and a large warm platter

ingredients.item: Beef brisket, flat cut, fat trimmed to 1/4 inch (6 mm)
Pink curing salt No. 1 (6.25 percent sodium nitrite)
ingredients.note: weigh it exactly; not the same as Himalayan pink salt
mustard seed, coriander seed, peppercorns, allspice, bay, cloves, chilli

ingredients.item: Carrots, peeled, in 3 inch (7.5 cm) pieces
Green or Savoy cabbage, cut in 6 wedges through the core

mise: Make the brine: bring 2 cups (480 ml) of the water to a boil with the salt, sugar, curing salt, pickling spice and garlic, stirring until dissolved. Take off the heat, add the remaining water cold and chill the brine completely, below 40°F (4°C), before using.
Put the brisket in the container, pour over the cold brine and weigh it down so it is fully submerged. Refrigerate for 5 to 7 days, turning and stirring once a day.
Label the container with the date and keep the curing salt packet labelled and out of reach; it is not table salt.
On cooking day: lift the brisket out, discard the brine and rinse the meat well under cold water. Soak it in fresh cold water for 1 hour to draw out excess surface salt.
Prepare the vegetables; chop the parsley; measure the sauce ingredients.

timeline.do: Make and chill the brine; start the cure in the fridge.
Turn the brisket in the brine.
Rinse and soak the brisket.
Simmer the brisket gently with onion and spices.
Add potatoes and carrots; then cabbage.
Rest the beef; make the parsley sauce.
Slice against the grain and serve.

steps.do: Put the rinsed brisket in the stockpot with the onion and 1 tbsp (6 g) pickling spice. Cover with cold water by 2 inches (5 cm). Bring slowly to a simmer over medium heat, skimming off the grey foam that rises.
steps.look: The meat is a uniform rosy pink on the outside from the cure; foam rises as the water heats.
steps.mistake: Bringing it to a hard boil, which tightens the meat and makes it stringy.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down the moment the first bubbles appear and skim.

steps.do: Reduce the heat so the water barely trembles, at 180 to 190°F (82 to 88°C), with only an occasional bubble breaking the surface. Partly cover and cook 2 1/2 to 3 1/2 hours, topping up with hot water to keep the meat covered.
steps.look: A lazy surface with a bubble every few seconds; the kitchen smells of spice and beef.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil while you are not looking, which gives dry, tough meat even after hours.
steps.fix: Check every 30 minutes; use a thermometer in the liquid until you know your hob.

steps.do: Test for doneness: a long skewer or fork slides into the thickest part with little resistance, and the internal temperature is about 195 to 205°F (90 to 96°C).
steps.look: The meat yields to a fork like soft butter but still holds together when lifted.
steps.mistake: Taking it out because it reached a number, while it is still tough.
steps.fix: Tenderness is the test; give it another 30 minutes and test again.

steps.do: Lift the beef onto a board and cover loosely with foil to rest. Add the potatoes and carrots to the simmering liquid and cook 10 minutes, then lay the cabbage wedges on top and cook 12 to 15 minutes more until all are tender.
steps.look: Potatoes pierce easily; cabbage is tender at the core but still bright green.
steps.mistake: Boiling the cabbage for 45 minutes until grey and sulphurous.
steps.fix: Cabbage needs only 12 to 15 minutes; test with a knife at the core.

steps.do: Parsley sauce: melt the butter in the saucepan, stir in the flour and cook 1 minute without colouring. Gradually whisk in the milk and 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the cooking liquid, bring to a simmer and cook 5 minutes, whisking. Stir in the parsley and mustard; taste before adding any salt, as the liquid is salty.
steps.look: A smooth, creamy, pale green sauce that coats the back of a spoon.
steps.mistake: Adding the liquid all at once, so the roux forms lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk constantly as you add; if lumps form, pass the sauce through a sieve before adding the parsley.

steps.do: Look at the brisket to find the direction of the muscle fibres, then slice ACROSS them at a slight angle into slices about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.look: Each slice shows short, fine fibres in cross section and holds together; tender, pink and moist.
steps.mistake: Slicing along the grain, which gives long, stringy, chewy slices.
steps.fix: Turn the meat 90 degrees and slice the other way.

steps.do: Arrange the slices on the warm platter with the vegetables, moisten with a ladle of the cooking liquid and serve the parsley sauce and mustard alongside.
steps.look: Glossy pink slices, bright vegetables, green flecked sauce.
steps.mistake: Letting the sliced beef dry out while you plate.
steps.fix: Spoon a little hot cooking liquid over the slices as soon as they are cut.

science: Curing salt contains sodium nitrite, which reacts with myoglobin in the meat to form a stable pink pigment, gives cured meat its distinctive flavour, and inhibits the growth of Clostridium botulinum during the long cure. It is used at a precise, small dose, which is why it is weighed. Salt dissolves some muscle proteins and slowly diffuses through the meat over days, seasoning it throughout. Brisket is a heavily worked muscle full of collagen. Holding it at a bare simmer, around 180 to 190°F (82 to 88°C), for hours converts that collagen into gelatin, making the meat tender and moist, while a hard boil squeezes the muscle fibres and dries them out. Slicing across the grain shortens the fibres so each bite is tender.
plating: On a warm platter, overlap the slices of beef in a long row down the centre. Arrange the cabbage wedges at one end, cut side up, and the carrots and potatoes along the other side. Spoon a little hot cooking liquid over everything so it glistens. Serve the parsley sauce in a warm jug and English mustard in a small bowl. On a plate: three slices fanned, a cabbage wedge, potatoes and carrots, sauce poured over the potatoes.

pairing.drink: A dry Irish stout or a red ale: roast malt suits the cured beef and cuts the creamy sauce; a soft, fruity red such as a Merlot also works.
pairing.brennans: Brennan’s Irish Coffee: after an Irish dinner, the Brennan's version, built with chicory coffee, brown sugar and Irish whiskey under floated cream, is the natural close.

variations: Quick version: buy a ready cured corned beef brisket and start from the simmer.
Corned beef hash: dice leftovers with boiled potato and onion and fry in a hot pan until crusty; top with a fried egg.
Pastrami: dry the cured brisket, coat with cracked pepper and coriander and smoke it at 225°F (107°C) until it reaches 200°F (93°C) inside.
safety: Pink curing salt is toxic in large amounts: weigh it accurately, never guess with spoons only, label it clearly and store it out of reach.
Cure only in the fridge, below 40°F (4°C), with the meat fully submerged in brine that was chilled before the meat went in.
Cooked brisket should be held hot above 140°F (60°C) or cooled and refrigerated within two hours.

title: Sauerbraten
summary: A joint of beef marinated for three days in a spiced red wine and vinegar bath, seared hard, braised slowly in that marinade and served in a sweet and sour sauce thickened with crushed gingerbread biscuits. It teaches what acid does to meat over time and how to balance a sauce with sugar against vinegar.
skills: a three day vinegar and wine marinade
a sweet and sour gingerbread sauce
equipment: Medium saucepan for the marinade
Non-reactive container or large zip bag that fits the beef snugly
Heavy casserole (Dutch oven) with a lid, about 5 quarts (5 litres)
Tongs and a large plate
Fine sieve and a jug
Whisk
Instant read probe thermometer
Carving knife and board

ingredients.item: Beef rump, topside or bottom round, in one piece
ingredients.note: tied with string into an even shape

ingredients.item: Red cabbage and potato dumplings or spätzle

mise: Three days ahead: put the wine, vinegar, water, onions, carrot, celeriac, bay, cloves, juniper, peppercorns, allspice, mustard seeds and salt in the saucepan, bring to a boil, simmer 5 minutes and cool COMPLETELY.
Put the beef in the container, pour over the cold marinade so it covers the meat, seal and refrigerate for 3 days (up to 5), turning the meat once a day.
On the day, lift the beef out and pat it very dry with paper. Strain the marinade, keeping the liquid and the vegetables separately.
Crush the gingersnaps finely in a bag with a rolling pin.
Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C).

timeline.do: Make and cool the marinade; marinate the beef in the fridge.
Turn the beef.
Drain and dry the beef; strain the marinade; oven on.
Sear the beef and vegetables; start the braise.
Beef out to rest; make the gingerbread sauce; cook sides.
Slice and serve in the sauce.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the casserole over medium high heat until it shimmers. Sear the dried beef on all sides, 3 to 4 minutes per side, until deeply browned. Lift onto a plate.
steps.look: A dark brown crust on every surface; the pan smells of roasting meat; fond builds on the bottom.
steps.mistake: Searing wet beef straight from the marinade, which steams and turns grey.
steps.fix: Dry it thoroughly with paper; if it still steams, wait for the moisture to cook off before turning.

steps.do: Turn the heat to medium, add the drained marinade vegetables and cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until they soften and brown at the edges. Stir in the tomato purée and cook 1 minute.
steps.look: Browned onions and a darker, brick coloured fond on the base of the pan.
steps.mistake: Burning the fond so the sauce turns bitter.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of the marinade to loosen the base if it darkens too quickly.

steps.do: Pour in 2 cups (480 ml) of the strained marinade and scrape the bottom to lift the fond. Return the beef with its juices. The liquid should come about a third of the way up the meat. Bring to a simmer, cover and put in the oven.
steps.look: A gentle simmer at the edge of the pot; the sharp smell of vinegar cooking off.
steps.mistake: Covering the meat entirely with liquid, which boils it rather than braising.
steps.fix: Pour off excess liquid; a third of the way up is enough.

steps.do: Braise at 300°F (150°C) for 2 1/2 to 3 hours, turning the beef every 45 minutes, until a fork slides in easily and the meat reads about 195 to 200°F (90 to 93°C).
steps.look: The beef shrinks a little, turns a deep mahogany and yields to a fork; the liquid reduces and darkens.
steps.mistake: Taking it out because the clock says so, while it is still firm.
steps.fix: Tenderness decides; give it another 30 minutes and test again.

steps.do: Lift the beef onto a board and cover loosely. Strain the braising liquid into a jug, pressing the vegetables, and skim off the fat. You should have about 2 cups (480 ml); add marinade or water if less.
steps.look: A dark, aromatic liquid, glossy with gelatin.
steps.mistake: Leaving all the fat in, which makes a greasy sauce.
steps.fix: Let it settle a minute and spoon off the fat, or use a fat separator.

steps.do: Return the liquid to the casserole and bring it to a simmer. Whisk in the crushed gingersnaps a spoonful at a time and simmer 5 minutes, whisking, until they melt and thicken the sauce. Add the raisins. Taste: it should be clearly sour and gently sweet. Balance with brown sugar or a splash of vinegar.
steps.look: A smooth, thick, glossy brown sauce that coats a spoon, smelling of spice and wine.
steps.mistake: Adding all the gingersnaps at once, so they clump into lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk in gradually; if lumps form, blend or sieve the sauce.

steps.do: Cut away the string and slice the beef against the grain into slices about 3/8 inch (1 cm) thick. Return them to the sauce for a minute to heat, then serve with red cabbage and dumplings or spätzle.
steps.look: Tender slices that hold together, napped with glossy sauce.
steps.mistake: Slicing with the grain, which gives chewy, stringy slices.
steps.fix: Look for the fibres and cut across them.

science: Acid in a marinade works slowly and mainly near the surface. Over three days the vinegar and wine penetrate the outer part of the meat, partially breaking down proteins and seasoning it with their sour, spiced flavour. Contrary to legend, acid does not tenderise the centre of a large joint much; the tenderness comes from the long, gentle braise that converts collagen to gelatin. Cooling the marinade before it meets the meat keeps the meat out of the danger zone. Searing builds flavour through Maillard browning that a braise alone cannot give. Gingerbread biscuits are made of flour, sugar and spices: the flour thickens the sauce, the sugar balances the vinegar and the spices echo the marinade, all in one addition.
plating: Warm wide plates. Lay three slices of beef overlapping slightly in the centre, spoon plenty of sauce over them so it pools, and place a mound of red cabbage on one side and two potato dumplings or a pile of spätzle on the other. Scatter a few raisins from the sauce over the meat. Serve extra sauce in a jug.

pairing.drink: A spicy, medium bodied red such as a Grenache based southern Rhône or a German Spätburgunder: fruit and spice for the sauce, enough acidity for the vinegar.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Saint Damien ‘La Louisianne’ Gigondas 2023: a Grenache led Rhône red from the Brennan's list with the warmth, spice and acidity to sit beside a sweet and sour braise.

variations: Short rib sauerbraten: marinate 4 lb (1.8 kg) bone-in short ribs the same way and braise for 3 hours.
Without gingersnaps: thicken with 2 tbsp (16 g) flour cooked in butter and sweeten with 2 tbsp (25 g) brown sugar and a pinch of ground ginger and cloves.
Pork shoulder: marinate and braise a 3 lb (1.4 kg) boneless pork shoulder the same way, for about 2 1/2 hours, until a fork slides in easily.
safety: Cool the boiled marinade completely before it touches raw beef, and marinate only in the fridge.
Discard any marinade not used in the braise; it has been in contact with raw meat.
Use a non-reactive container: vinegar reacts with aluminium and some metals.

title: Texas Smoked Brisket
summary: Brisket trimmed by hand, seasoned with salt and coarse pepper only, smoked low over oak for most of a day, wrapped in butcher paper through the stall, cooked until a probe slides in like butter and rested for hours. It is the longest cook in the course and the purest test of fire control, patience and judgement by feel.
equipment: Offset smoker, kettle grill set up for indirect cooking, or a pellet smoker
Oak or hickory splits or chunks, and lump charcoal
Two probe thermometers: one for the meat, one for the air at grate level
Pink butcher paper, unwaxed, in a roll at least 18 inches (45 cm) wide
Long sharp boning knife and a long slicing knife
Large chopping board with a groove
Dry cool box and old towels for resting
Heat resistant gloves
Spray bottle with water or beef stock (optional)

ingredients.item: Beef brisket, a whole packer of 12 to 14 lb (5.5 to 6.4 kg) for a crowd, or for 4 with leftovers a 6 to 7 lb (2.7 to 3.2 kg) piece with point and flat attached
ingredients.note: choose one that bends easily when held in the middle, with a thick, even flat
about 1 tbsp (12 g) per 3 lb (1.4 kg) of trimmed meat

ingredients.item: Beef tallow or the rendered trimmings
ingredients.note: optional, spread on the paper before wrapping
post oak is the Central Texas wood

mise: The night before, trim the brisket cold from the fridge: turn it fat side down and remove the hard, waxy fat and any silverskin from the meat side. Turn it over and trim the fat cap to an even 1/4 inch (6 mm).

Find the thick, hard seam of fat (the deckle) between point and flat and trim away any large lumps you can reach without separating them. Round off thin edges and corners that would burn: an aerodynamic shape cooks evenly.
Mix the salt and pepper and season all over evenly, more heavily on the thick parts; it should look like a light, even coat with the meat visible underneath. Refrigerate uncovered overnight.
Next morning, light the smoker and bring it to 250°F (121°C) at grate level, burning down to a small, clean fire.
Lay out the butcher paper: two overlapping sheets about four times the length of the brisket.

timeline.do: Trim and season the brisket; refrigerate uncovered.
Light the smoker; stabilise at 250°F (121°C) with clean smoke.
Brisket on, fat side towards the heat source.
Stall at about 150 to 170°F (65 to 77°C) internal; bark set and dark: wrap in paper.
Probe tender at about 200 to 203°F (93 to 95°C): off and into the cool box to rest.
Slice the flat and the point and serve.

steps.do: Bring the smoker to a steady 250°F (121°C) at grate level. Add wood so it burns cleanly with a small flame and the smoke coming out of the chimney is thin and pale blue, almost invisible.
steps.look: Thin blue smoke, a sweet smell of burning oak, and an air temperature that holds within 15°F (8°C) for 30 minutes.
steps.mistake: Smoking under thick, white, billowing smoke from smouldering wood, which coats the meat in bitter creosote.
steps.fix: Open the intake vents to give the fire more air, use dry, seasoned wood and keep a small, hot, clean fire rather than a big, smouldering one.

steps.do: Put the brisket on the grate with the thicker point end towards the fire and the fat cap facing the heat source (down in most offsets, up in a pellet smoker). Insert the meat probe into the thickest part of the flat, from the side. Close the lid.
steps.look: The seasoned surface starts to sweat and darken within the first hour.
steps.mistake: Opening the lid constantly to look, which loses heat and smoke and lengthens the cook.
steps.fix: Leave it closed for at least 3 hours; watch the thermometers, not the meat.

steps.do: Feed the fire with a split or a chunk every 45 to 60 minutes to keep 250 to 275°F (121 to 135°C). After 3 hours, if the surface looks dry in spots, spritz it lightly with water or stock every hour.
steps.look: The bark turns from red brown to mahogany to nearly black; the pepper crust firms and does not rub off when touched.
steps.mistake: Letting the temperature swing between 200 and 350°F (93 and 177°C), which gives uneven, dry meat.
steps.fix: Make small, frequent adjustments; add fuel before the fire runs low.

steps.do: The STALL: at around 150 to 170°F (65 to 77°C) internal, the temperature stops rising and may stay flat for 2 to 5 hours. Do not raise the heat. Wait until the bark is dark and set and does not smear when you rub it with a gloved finger, usually 165 to 170°F (74 to 77°C).
steps.look: A dark, dry, firm bark; the internal temperature crawling or stuck.
steps.mistake: Panicking and turning up the fire, which dries and toughens the outside while the inside lags.
steps.fix: The stall is evaporation cooling the surface; it ends by itself. Wrapping (next step) shortens it.

steps.do: Wrap: spread tallow down the centre of the paper if using, set the brisket on it fat side up, fold the bottom edge over tightly, fold in the sides, then roll the brisket over and over until it is wrapped in several snug layers, seam side down. Return it to the smoker fat side up.
steps.look: A tight, neat parcel with no air pockets; the paper soon goes translucent with fat but does not tear.
steps.mistake: Wrapping loosely, so steam collects and softens the bark, or using foil, which braises the meat.
steps.fix: Wrap tightly in butcher paper, which breathes; if the paper tears, add another layer.

steps.do: Continue cooking at 250 to 275°F (121 to 135°C) until the internal temperature is about 200 to 203°F (93 to 95°C) and, most importantly, the probe slides into the flat in several places with almost no resistance, like pushing into soft butter. This may take 3 to 5 hours more.
steps.look: The parcel feels loose and wobbly when lifted at one end; the probe glides in.
steps.mistake: Taking it off at a number while it still feels tight, which gives tough slices.
steps.fix: Probe for feel; give it another 30 to 60 minutes if it resists in any spot.

steps.do: Lift the wrapped brisket into a dry cool box lined with towels, cover with more towels and close. Rest at least 1 1/2 hours, up to 4 hours; it should stay above 140°F (60°C) the whole time.
steps.look: When opened, the paper is warm and the meat still steaming; juices have settled.
steps.mistake: Slicing straight off the smoker, so the juices run out onto the board and the meat dries.
steps.fix: The rest is part of the cook: plan it into the timeline.

steps.do: Unwrap and pour the juices into a bowl. Separate the point from the flat along the fat seam. Slice the flat across the grain into slices the thickness of a pencil, about 1/4 inch (6 mm). Turn the point 90 degrees, because its grain runs another way, and slice slightly thicker or cut into cubes.
steps.look: A dark bark, a pink smoke ring under it, and slices that bend over a finger without breaking but pull apart with a gentle tug.
steps.mistake: Slicing the whole brisket in one direction, so the point's slices are stringy.
steps.fix: Check the grain of each muscle separately before cutting.

steps.do: Dip the slices in the saved juices and serve on butcher paper with white bread, pickles and raw onion.
steps.look: Glistening slices with a peppery crust; they taste of beef, smoke, salt and pepper.
steps.mistake: Smothering it in barbecue sauce before tasting.
steps.fix: Taste first; Central Texas serves it without sauce.

science: Brisket is two muscles with a great deal of collagen. Held for many hours between about 160 and 205°F (71 and 96°C) internal, that collagen dissolves into gelatin, which is what makes brisket tender and juicy. The stall happens because the moist surface cools by evaporation, like sweat, balancing the heat coming in; wrapping traps that moisture so the temperature rises again. Butcher paper lets some steam escape, protecting the bark, while foil holds it all and softens the crust. Smoke compounds dissolve in the moist surface; nitrogen dioxide from burning wood reacts with myoglobin to form the pink smoke ring. Clean, thin blue smoke carries pleasant flavour compounds, while smouldering wood produces bitter, sooty ones. The long rest lets the temperature even out and the juices thicken and redistribute.
plating: Serve it as Texas does, on a tray lined with pink butcher paper. Lay a row of flat slices slightly overlapping, bark side up, and a pile of point slices or cubes beside them. Add a stack of white bread, a few pickle slices, some raw onion rings and pickled jalapeños. Keep a small bowl of the resting juices to spoon over. For a plate, three slices of flat and two of point fanned out, the smoke ring showing.

pairing.drink: A ripe, peppery Syrah or a Zinfandel, or a cold Texas lager: dark fruit and pepper for the bark, enough acidity for the fat.
pairing.brennans: Piedrasassi ‘Bien Nacido Vineyard’ Santa Maria Valley Syrah 2021: a peppery, savoury Californian Syrah from the Brennan's list that matches a black pepper bark and smoked beef.

variations: Point only: smoke a 5 lb (2.3 kg) point end; it is fattier and more forgiving, about 8 to 10 hours.
Burnt ends: cube the cooked point, toss with a little sauce and rub, and return to the smoker in a pan for 1 to 2 hours until caramelised.
Oven finish: smoke for the first 5 to 6 hours, then wrap and finish in a 275°F (135°C) oven to the same tenderness.
safety: Keep raw brisket in the fridge until it goes on the smoker; trim cold.
During the rest the meat must stay above 140°F (60°C); if holding longer than 4 hours, keep it in a 150 to 170°F (65 to 77°C) oven.
Smokers and charcoal are outdoor appliances only; keep them away from buildings and never leave a fire unattended.
Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and reheat to 165°F (74°C).
