title: Osso Buco with Risotto alla Milanese
summary: Thick slices of veal shank, tied, dredged and seared, braised in white wine and stock until the meat loosens around the marrow bone, finished with gremolata and served with a saffron risotto stirred until it flows. It joins the braise to the risotto method, two techniques that must finish at the same moment.
skills: a saffron risotto stirred to all'onda
equipment: Heavy ovenproof casserole with a lid, wide enough to hold the shanks in one layer, about 12 inches (30 cm)
Butcher's twine and scissors
Shallow tray for the flour
Tongs
Wide heavy saucepan for the risotto, about 10 inches (25 cm)
Small saucepan to keep the stock simmering, and a ladle
Wooden spoon
Microplane for lemon zest

ingredients.item: Veal hind shank, cut across in slices 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) thick
ingredients.note: ask for the hind shank, which is meatier

ingredients.item: Onion, carrot and celery, in 1/4 inch (5 mm) dice

ingredients.note: steeped in 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot stock

ingredients.item: Shallot or small onion, very finely chopped

ingredients.note: half to start, half cold to finish
traditional; scooped from a marrow bone

ingredients.item: Dry white wine, for the risotto

mise: Tie each shank slice: wrap a length of twine snugly around the circumference and knot it; this holds the meat to the bone as it softens.
Pat the shanks dry; season both sides with salt and pepper.
Dice the vegetables; measure the wine and stock.
Make the gremolata: mix the lemon zest, parsley and garlic; cover and keep cold.
Steep the saffron in 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot stock; chop the shallot; grate the cheese; cube and chill half the risotto butter.
Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C).

timeline.do: Tie, season, dredge and sear the shanks; build the braise.
Into the oven for 2 hours, turning once.
Bring the risotto stock to a simmer; start the soffritto.
Toast the rice, add wine, then stock by the ladle for 17 to 18 minutes.
Shanks out of the oven, resting in their sauce.
Mantecatura: rest, beat in cold butter and cheese; scatter gremolata on the shanks; serve.

steps.do: Dredge each shank in flour, tapping off the excess. Heat the oil in the casserole over medium high heat and brown the shanks in one layer, 4 to 5 minutes per side, until both cut faces have a deep golden crust. Lift them out.
steps.look: A deep brown crust on the meat; the marrow bones sizzle; brown fond on the pan base.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan so the shanks steam and stay pale.
steps.fix: Brown in two batches if needed, and do not move them until the crust releases.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium, add the butter and the diced vegetables and cook 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent but not brown.
steps.look: Soft, glossy vegetables; a sweet smell.
steps.mistake: Burning the fond while the vegetables cook.
steps.fix: Keep the heat moderate; a splash of wine loosens a darkening base.

steps.do: Pour in the wine, scrape up the fond and simmer 2 to 3 minutes until reduced by half and the smell of alcohol has gone. Return the shanks in one layer, add stock to come two thirds of the way up them, bring to a simmer, cover and transfer to the oven.
steps.look: The marrow bones upright, the meat partly submerged, a gentle simmer.
steps.mistake: Covering the shanks completely, which boils them and gives a thin sauce.
steps.fix: Two thirds of the way up is right; the top steams under the lid.

steps.do: Braise for 2 hours, turning the shanks once halfway and basting. They are done when the meat is very tender, comes away from the bone with a fork, but still holds inside its string.
steps.look: A glossy, reduced sauce; meat pulling back from the bone; marrow soft and wobbling.
steps.mistake: Letting the sauce reduce too much and catch.
steps.fix: Add a splash of stock if it looks dry; if it is thin at the end, reduce it on the hob after lifting out the shanks.

steps.do: Risotto: in the wide saucepan, melt 2 tbsp (28 g) butter with the bone marrow (if using) over medium heat and cook the shallot 3 to 4 minutes until translucent. Add the rice and stir 2 minutes until the grains are hot and their edges turn translucent.
steps.look: Grains that look pearly with a white dot at the centre; they make a light clicking sound against the spoon.
steps.mistake: Browning the shallot or the rice.
steps.fix: Keep the heat moderate; this step is about heating the grain, not colouring it.

steps.do: Pour in the wine and stir until it is absorbed. Add a ladle of hot stock and stir until almost absorbed, then add another. Continue, adding the saffron and its liquid halfway, stirring often, for 16 to 18 minutes.
steps.look: The rice turns golden yellow and creamy as starch is released; each grain is soft outside with a tiny firm core.
steps.mistake: Adding all the stock at once or using cold stock, which gives soupy, unevenly cooked rice.
steps.fix: Add hot stock a ladle at a time and keep stirring; taste a grain from the 15 minute mark.

steps.do: When the rice is just al dente, take it off the heat, add a final splash of stock, and rest it 1 minute. Then add the cold cubed butter and the Parmigiano and beat vigorously with the spoon for 30 seconds (the mantecatura). Season with salt.
steps.look: All'onda: the risotto flows in a slow wave when the pan is tilted and spreads gently on a plate; it is glossy and creamy.
steps.mistake: Serving a stiff risotto that holds its shape like a mound.
steps.fix: Beat in another splash of hot stock until it flows.

steps.do: Cut the string off the shanks. Scatter the gremolata over the shanks in the pan just before serving, then plate each shank on a pool of risotto with sauce spooned over.
steps.look: Bright green and yellow flecks on dark meat; a strong smell of lemon and garlic as it hits the heat.
steps.mistake: Stirring the gremolata into the hot sauce, which cooks off its fresh aroma.
steps.fix: Add it at the last moment, on top.

science: Veal shank is full of collagen. In a covered, moist braise at oven heat, the collagen slowly turns to gelatin, which makes the meat tender and gives the sauce body. As it softens, the muscle tends to slump away from the bone, which is why each slice is tied. Flour on the shanks browns quickly and later thickens the sauce slightly. Risotto works because Carnaroli and Arborio rice have plenty of amylopectin starch on the surface; stirring and gradual addition of hot liquid rub that starch off into the liquid, creating a creamy sauce without cream. Resting and beating in cold butter and cheese emulsifies fat into that starchy liquid. Lemon zest's aroma lives in volatile oils that cook away quickly, so gremolata goes on last.
plating: Use warm, wide bowls. Spoon the risotto into the centre and tap the base of the bowl so it spreads in a flat, even pool. Set a shank in the middle, marrow bone upright, spoon the braising sauce over the meat (not over all the risotto) and scatter gremolata on top. Give a small spoon for the marrow.

pairing.drink: A Nebbiolo from Piedmont or a Lombard red: firm acidity and tannin for the rich marrow and veal, and an aroma that suits the saffron.
pairing.brennans: Produttori del Barbaresco Barbaresco 2020: a classic Nebbiolo from the Brennan's list, with the acidity and structure Milanese veal braises call for.

variations: With tomato: add 1 cup (240 g) chopped tinned tomatoes with the stock for a redder, sweeter braise, and finish with gremolata as here.
Pork or lamb shanks: tie and braise 2 1/2 to 3 hours in the same way.
Risotto al salto: shape leftover saffron risotto into patties and fry in butter until crusted.
safety: Veal is safely cooked at 145°F (63°C); braised shank goes far beyond that and is safe and tender at about 195°F (90°C).
Cool leftovers within 2 hours and reheat the braise to boiling.

title: Chiles Rellenos
summary: Poblano chillies charred over a flame, peeled whole without tearing, stuffed with melting cheese, wrapped in an egg white batter whipped like a meringue and fried until puffed, then served in a light tomato broth. Fine hands are the lesson: peeling and seeding a chilli whole and frying a batter that is half soufflé.
equipment: Gas hob with long metal tongs, or an overhead grill (broiler), or a barbecue
Large bowl and a plate or a plastic bag for sweating the chillies
Small sharp knife and a small spoon
Toothpicks
Stand mixer or hand mixer, and a clean, grease free bowl
Large rubber spatula
12 inch (30 cm) heavy, deep frying pan
Deep fry thermometer
Two spatulas or a spatula and a large spoon
Blender and a medium saucepan for the caldillo
Wire rack over a tray lined with paper

ingredients.item: Poblano chillies, large, straight and smooth
Queso Oaxaca or Monterey Jack, cut into fingers
Eggs, large, separated, at room temperature

ingredients.note: 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep in the pan
or a 28 oz (794 g) tin of whole tomatoes

ingredients.item: Thinly sliced white onion, for the caldillo
Warm corn tortillas or white rice

mise: Char the chillies: set them directly on the gas flame on high, turning with tongs every 30 seconds to 1 minute, until blistered and blackened all over, 5 to 8 minutes. Work quickly so the flesh does not cook soft. Under a grill, turn every 2 minutes.
Put the hot chillies in the bowl, cover with a plate (or seal in a bag) and leave 10 minutes to steam, which loosens the skin.
Peel: rub the skins off with your fingers or a paper towel, under a trickle of water only if needed. Leave the stems on.

Make a lengthwise slit about 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) long down one side, from just below the stem. Carefully cut out the seed pod under the stem with scissors or a knife and scrape out loose seeds with a small spoon.
Caldillo: blend the tomatoes, chopped onion and garlic until smooth.
Separate the eggs carefully: not a trace of yolk must get into the whites.

timeline.do: Char, sweat, peel and seed the chillies.
Make the caldillo and keep it warm.
Stuff the chillies; heat the oil to 360°F (182°C).
Whip the batter; dust and coat; fry 2 at a time.
Plate the chillies in the warm caldillo.

steps.do: Make the caldillo: heat the oil in the saucepan over medium high heat, pour in the tomato purée (it will splutter) and fry, stirring, 5 minutes until it darkens slightly and thickens. Add the stock, oregano, bay leaf and sliced onion, simmer 15 minutes, and season with salt. It should be thin, like a light soup.
steps.look: A brick red, brothy sauce with soft onion slices; it smells of sweet tomato and oregano.
steps.mistake: Reducing it to a thick salsa, which is too heavy for the light batter.
steps.fix: Thin it with stock; caldillo means little broth.

steps.do: Stuff each chilli through the slit with cheese fingers until full but not bulging, then pull the edges together and secure with one or two toothpicks threaded along the slit.
steps.look: Plump, closed chillies with the cheese hidden inside; no tears.
steps.mistake: Overstuffing, so the slit gapes and cheese leaks into the oil.
steps.fix: Fill to three quarters. If a chilli has torn, patch it from inside with a piece of cheese and close it with a toothpick.

steps.do: Heat the oil, 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep in the frying pan, to 360°F (182°C). Pat the chillies dry and dust them thoroughly in flour, tapping off the excess.
steps.look: A dry, dusty coat over each chilli with no wet patches.
steps.mistake: Skipping the flour, so the batter slides off the smooth chilli skin in the oil.
steps.fix: Flour every surface; it is the primer the batter grips.

steps.do: Make the capeado: whip the whites with a pinch of salt on medium high until they hold firm peaks that stand up with just the tip curling, 2 to 3 minutes. Add the yolks one at a time, beating only until each is incorporated, about 5 seconds each.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, pale yellow foam with the texture of shaving cream; it holds its shape on the beaters.
steps.mistake: Beating too long after the yolks, so the foam collapses and turns runny.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as the yolks are in. A runny batter can be saved by gently folding in another stiffly whipped white.

steps.do: Holding a chilli by its stem, lay it in the batter and use a spatula to cover it completely. Lift it out on the spatula and slide it into the oil, stem towards you. Fry two at a time.
steps.look: The batter puffs immediately and sets into a golden, cloud-like coat.
steps.mistake: Letting the batter stand for minutes, so it deflates.
steps.fix: Use the batter within 10 minutes of whipping; for more than 4 chillies, whip in two batches.

steps.do: Fry 2 to 3 minutes, spooning hot oil over the top constantly to set the batter there, until the underside is golden. Turn carefully with two spatulas, rolling it away from you, and fry the other side 2 minutes.
steps.look: A puffed, evenly golden coat; you can see the cheese starting to melt at the ends.
steps.mistake: Turning before the top has set, which squashes the batter and splashes oil.
steps.fix: Baste first until the top is pale gold and firm, then roll it gently away from you.

steps.do: Lift onto the rack to drain for 1 minute, then pull out the toothpicks. Ladle the warm caldillo into shallow bowls, set a chilli on top and serve at once with warm tortillas or rice.
steps.look: A golden, airy jacket sitting in a pool of red broth, the cheese molten inside.
steps.mistake: Pouring the sauce over the top, which softens the batter immediately.
steps.fix: Put the sauce underneath and around, not on top.

science: Charring over a flame heats the skin so fast that a layer of steam forms between skin and flesh, separating them; sweating in a covered bowl continues the process so the skin slips off. Charring briefly and hot keeps the flesh firm enough to hold its shape. The capeado batter is a foam: egg white proteins unfold when whipped and trap air bubbles in a stable network. The yolks add fat and flavour but weaken the foam, which is why they are folded in briefly at the end. In hot oil, the air in the bubbles expands and steam forms, puffing the batter like a soufflé while the proteins set it in place. A dusting of flour absorbs moisture on the chilli's waxy skin, giving the batter something to cling to.
plating: Use a warm, wide, shallow bowl. Ladle in the caldillo so it covers the base generously with a few onion slices showing. Set the chilli in the middle, stem pointing to two o'clock, golden and dry on top. Add a few leaves of fresh coriander or a crumble of queso fresco at one end. Serve tortillas wrapped in a cloth on the side.

pairing.drink: A dry rosé or a light, fruity red with little tannin: refreshing against the fried batter and gentle with the chilli and tomato. A Mexican lager works too.
pairing.brennans: Minuty ‘Prestige’ Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024: a dry Provence rosé from the Brennan's list, crisp and savoury, very good with fried, cheese filled chillies in tomato.

variations: Picadillo filling: stuff with pork picadillo cooked with tomato, raisins, almonds and spices instead of cheese.
Baked rellenos: skip the batter, stuff the roasted chillies and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15 minutes under a little cheese, then serve in the caldillo.
Chiles en nogada: the September dish of Puebla, stuffed with picadillo and served under walnut cream and pomegranate.
safety: Wear gloves or wash your hands well after handling chillies, and avoid touching your eyes.
Keep the oil no deeper than a third of the pan; lower the battered chillies in away from you; never leave the oil unattended.
The batter's eggs are fully cooked in the hot oil.

title: Maqluba
summary: Chicken braised with warm spices to make its own stock, aubergine and cauliflower fried until deep gold, and rice layered over them in one pot, cooked in that stock and then turned upside down onto a platter in a single, nerve-testing movement. It teaches layering for even cooking and the confidence to invert a full pot.
equipment: Heavy, straight sided non-stick or well seasoned pot, about 9 to 10 inches (23 to 25 cm) across and 5 inches (13 cm) deep
Second large pot for braising the chicken
Large frying pan or a wok for frying the vegetables, and a deep fry thermometer
Colander and a large bowl for salting the aubergine
Slotted spoon, tongs and a tray lined with paper
Large flat serving platter wider than the pot
Sieve and a jug for the stock
Oven gloves

ingredients.item: Chicken thighs, bone in, skin on
ingredients.note: or 1 1/2 lb (680 g) lamb shoulder in chunks

ingredients.us: 2 tsp, plus more for the aubergine

ingredients.item: Aubergine, sliced in rounds 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) thick
Basmati or Egyptian medium grain rice
Baharat (seven spice) or a mix of allspice, cinnamon and black pepper

ingredients.note: for the base of the pot

ingredients.item: Pine nuts or flaked almonds, toasted in butter

mise: Put the chicken, onion, cardamom, cinnamon, bay, peppercorns, allspice, 1 tsp (5 g) salt and the water in the large pot. Bring to a boil, skim, then simmer gently, partly covered, for 30 to 35 minutes until the chicken is just cooked. Lift the chicken out, strain the stock and keep 3 1/2 cups (840 ml) of it hot.
Salt the aubergine slices on both sides and stand them in the colander for 30 minutes; rinse briefly and pat completely dry.
Rinse the rice in several changes of cold water until it runs nearly clear, then soak in cold water for 30 minutes and drain well.
Pat the cauliflower dry; slice the tomatoes; toast the nuts in a little butter until golden.
Heat the frying oil to 350°F (177°C) in the frying pan or wok, no more than a third full.

timeline.do: Braise the chicken to make the stock; salt the aubergine.
Soak the rice; fry the aubergine and cauliflower in batches.
Brown the chicken pieces; layer the pot.
Pour on the stock; cook 35 to 40 minutes on low.
Rest off the heat 15 to 20 minutes.
Invert onto the platter; garnish and serve.

steps.do: Fry the aubergine slices in batches in the oil at 350°F (177°C) for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden brown on both sides. Lift onto the paper lined tray. Fry the cauliflower florets the same way, 5 to 6 minutes, until browned at the edges.
steps.look: Aubergine glossy and deep gold, soft through; cauliflower nutty brown with charred tips. Both smell sweet and toasty.
steps.mistake: Frying wet aubergine or crowding the pan, which makes the oil spit and the slices soak up oil and stay pale.
steps.fix: Dry thoroughly and fry in small batches; let the oil return to 350°F (177°C) before each batch.

steps.do: Pat the chicken dry, season with half the baharat and brown it skin side down in 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the frying oil in the maqluba pot over medium high heat, 4 to 5 minutes, until the skin is golden. Lift out. Pour off the fat and wipe the pot.
steps.look: Crisp golden skin; brown spots of fond in the pot.
steps.mistake: Skipping this step, so the chicken skin is pale and flabby in the finished dish.
steps.fix: Browning takes 5 minutes and pays for itself in colour and flavour.

steps.do: Rub the base and sides of the pot with the butter. Lay the tomato slices over the base in a single layer, then the chicken pieces skin side down, then the garlic cloves. Arrange the fried aubergine and cauliflower over and around the chicken in an even layer, pressing gently.
steps.look: A neat, tightly packed base: red tomato, golden chicken, then the browned vegetables filling all the gaps.
steps.mistake: Leaving gaps, so the layers slump when the pot is turned out.
steps.fix: Pack firmly; this base becomes the top of the dish, so arrange it with care.

steps.do: Toss the drained rice with the remaining baharat, the turmeric and 1 tsp (5 g) salt, and spread it evenly over the vegetables. Press it down lightly with the back of a spoon to level it.
steps.look: A flat, even layer of yellow flecked rice covering everything to the edges.
steps.mistake: Piling the rice in a dome, so the top cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Level it with a spoon; the pot should be no more than three quarters full.

steps.do: Place a small heatproof plate upside down on the rice to stop it moving. Pour the hot stock slowly over the plate until it covers the rice by about 1/2 inch (1.2 cm). Remove the plate, bring to a boil over medium high heat, then cover tightly and cook over the lowest heat for 35 to 40 minutes.
steps.look: The stock bubbles up through the rice at first; after 30 minutes, small steam holes appear on the surface and no liquid remains.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid repeatedly, which lets steam escape and leaves the rice hard.
steps.fix: Check once at 35 minutes: if the rice is still firm and dry, sprinkle 1/4 cup (60 ml) of hot stock over it and cover for 10 minutes more.

steps.do: Turn off the heat and leave the pot covered for 15 to 20 minutes. Then remove the lid and run a thin spatula carefully round the inside edge to loosen it.
steps.look: The rice is tender and separate; the edges come away from the sides of the pot.
steps.mistake: Inverting immediately, so the hot, loose layers collapse.
steps.fix: The rest lets the rice firm and the layers settle; do not skip it.

steps.do: Put the serving platter upside down on top of the pot. Wearing oven gloves, hold the platter and the pot handles firmly together and flip them over in one quick, confident movement. Set the platter down and leave the pot in place for 2 minutes, then tap the base and lift it straight up slowly.
steps.look: A golden cake of rice that stands on its own, topped with the tomatoes, chicken and fried vegetables.
steps.mistake: Hesitating halfway through the flip, so the contents slide and spill.
steps.fix: Flip decisively. If some vegetables stick in the pot, lift them out and place them back on top; nobody will know.

steps.do: Scatter the toasted nuts and parsley over the top and serve at once with yoghurt and cucumber salad.
steps.look: A domed rice cake crowned with chicken and browned vegetables, studded with golden nuts.
steps.mistake: Cutting into it with a knife, which crushes the layers.
steps.fix: Serve with a large spoon, cutting down through all the layers.

science: Rinsing and soaking the rice washes away surface starch, which would make the grains gummy, and lets them absorb some water first so they cook evenly in the shorter time. Salting aubergine draws out some of its water by osmosis and collapses its spongy cells, so it absorbs less oil when fried and browns better. Frying the vegetables first gives deep Maillard flavour and firms them so they hold their shape as the base. The rice cooks by absorption: the stock is measured to be taken up completely, and the tight lid traps steam to finish the grains. The rest allows steam to redistribute and starch to set slightly, which is what lets the whole pot stand up when turned out.
plating: Bring the inverted maqluba to the table on its platter, still steaming. Garnish only the top: a heavy scattering of golden pine nuts, then a little chopped parsley around the rim of the rice. Serve the yoghurt and cucumber salad in a bowl beside it. Each person gets a wedge cut from top to bottom, with chicken, vegetables and rice in every portion.

pairing.drink: A spicy, medium bodied red from the eastern Mediterranean, or a dry rosé: warm spice and fruit match baharat and fried aubergine without overpowering the chicken.
pairing.brennans: Château Musar Bekaa Valley 2003: a Lebanese red from the Brennan's list, savoury and spiced, from the same Levantine kitchen tradition as maqluba.

variations: Lamb maqluba: braise 1 1/2 lb (680 g) lamb shoulder for 1 1/2 hours for the stock and use it in place of the chicken.
Vegetarian: use vegetable stock and add fried potatoes and peppers to the aubergine and cauliflower layer.
Oven roasted vegetables: brush the aubergine and cauliflower with oil and roast at 425°F (220°C) for 25 to 30 minutes instead of frying.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C); after braising and the rice cook it is well beyond that.
Keep the frying oil no more than a third of the pan's depth and dry the vegetables well before they go in.
Inverting a heavy, hot pot can scald: use dry oven gloves, a stable platter and a clear space.

title: Fesenjan
summary: Walnuts toasted and ground to an oily paste, cooked slowly in water until the oil rises and the sauce turns the colour of milk chocolate, then simmered with chicken and pomegranate molasses until dark, glossy and balanced between sour and sweet. It teaches a long, low cook judged by colour, and seasoning by taste rather than by numbers.
skills: a pomegranate molasses braise until the oil rises
equipment: Large dry frying pan for toasting
Food processor or a strong blender
Heavy, wide casserole of about 5 quarts (5 litres)
Flat-ended wooden spoon or spatula for scraping the base
Mortar and pestle for the saffron
Medium saucepan with a tight lid for the rice
Tongs

ingredients.note: fresh; taste one: stale walnuts are bitter

ingredients.item: Chicken thighs, bone in, skin removed

ingredients.note: brands vary in sourness; taste yours
ground and steeped in 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot water

mise: Taste a walnut: it should be sweet and creamy. Discard any batch that tastes rancid or bitter.
Grind the saffron in the mortar with a pinch of sugar, add the 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot water and leave to steep.
Chop the onion; pat the chicken dry and season it with the salt and pepper.
Rinse the rice in several changes of water until it runs nearly clear and soak it for 30 minutes.

timeline.do: Toast and grind the walnuts; brown the onion and chicken.
Cook the walnut paste in water on the lowest heat, scraping often, 45 to 60 minutes.
Add molasses, sugar, saffron and chicken; simmer 40 to 50 minutes.
Cook the rice.
Balance the sauce; let it rest; garnish and serve.

steps.do: Toast the walnuts in the dry frying pan over medium heat, stirring and tossing constantly, for 5 to 7 minutes until they smell nutty and are lightly golden in places but still mostly pale. Tip them out immediately onto a plate to cool for 5 minutes.
steps.look: A warm, rich nut oil smell; a faint sheen on the surface; only light gold, not brown.
steps.mistake: Walking away, so the walnuts burn in seconds and turn bitter.
steps.fix: Stay at the pan; if a few blacken, pick them out. If the whole batch smells burnt, start again: no sugar will hide it.

steps.do: Grind the cooled walnuts in the food processor for 2 to 4 minutes, scraping down the sides, until they pass through a coarse crumb and become a fine, damp, oily paste.
steps.look: A thick, glossy paste that holds together like wet sand and leaves an oily film on the bowl.
steps.mistake: Stopping at a coarse crumb, which gives a gritty sauce.
steps.fix: Keep processing; the oil is released only once the nuts are fine.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the casserole over medium heat and cook the onion 8 to 10 minutes until golden brown. Push it aside, add the chicken and brown it 3 minutes per side. Lift the chicken out onto a plate.
steps.look: Golden onions and lightly browned chicken; a sweet, savoury smell.
steps.mistake: Rushing the onions, which leaves them raw tasting in the sauce.
steps.fix: Give them their full 10 minutes on moderate heat.

steps.do: Add the walnut paste and the water to the onions and stir until smooth. Bring to a gentle simmer, then turn the heat to the lowest setting. Cook uncovered for 45 to 60 minutes, scraping the base with the flat spoon every 3 to 5 minutes.
steps.look: The sauce darkens slowly from grey beige to tan to milk chocolate brown, thickens, and a slick of walnut oil rises and pools on the surface.
steps.mistake: Leaving it unattended, so the heavy paste sinks, catches and burns on the base.
steps.fix: Scrape the whole base often; if it starts to catch, move to a clean pot without scraping up the burnt layer and lower the heat.

steps.do: Stir in the pomegranate molasses, sugar, saffron and its water, and the cinnamon. Return the chicken with its juices, nestling the pieces into the sauce. Simmer uncovered on low heat for 40 to 50 minutes, stirring and scraping every 10 minutes.
steps.look: The sauce turns a deep, glossy mahogany, thick enough to coat a spoon, with oil beading on the surface; the chicken is tender at the bone.
steps.mistake: Adding the molasses at the start, which can stop the walnuts from darkening and releasing their oil.
steps.fix: Wait until the colour and oil have developed before adding the acid.

steps.do: Taste and balance: fesenjan should taste sour first, then sweet, with a rich nuttiness behind. Add 1 tbsp (20 g) more molasses if it is flat or too sweet, or 1 tsp (4 g) more sugar if it is harsh. Add salt if needed. Simmer 5 minutes after each change and taste again.
steps.look: A glossy, dark sauce whose flavour starts tart and finishes rounded and sweet.
steps.mistake: Seasoning by the recipe alone, when pomegranate molasses varies widely in sourness.
steps.fix: Adjust in small steps and taste between each one.

steps.do: Rest the stew off the heat for 10 minutes while you finish the rice, then serve in a warm dish, scattered with pomegranate seeds, with the rice alongside.
steps.look: Deep brown, almost black sauce with ruby seeds on top.
steps.mistake: Serving it straight from a boil, when the flavours are still sharp.
steps.fix: A short rest softens and rounds the sauce; it is even better the next day.

science: Walnuts are about 65 percent oil. Ground fine and held at a bare simmer for an hour, the paste breaks down: the oil separates and rises, and the walnut solids slowly brown in it through Maillard reactions, which is why the sauce darkens and deepens in flavour with no flour, cream or roux. The starch and protein in the walnut solids thicken the sauce as they cook. Pomegranate molasses is concentrated juice, rich in acids and sugars; its acidity balances the fatty nuts and the sugar rounds the acid. Adding acid early can slow browning, which works best in a less acidic environment. Toasting the walnuts first develops flavour quickly, but over-toasting or burning creates bitter compounds that cannot be masked.
plating: Spoon the fesenjan into a warmed shallow serving bowl so the chicken sits half submerged in the glossy sauce. Scatter pomegranate seeds over the top and a few toasted walnut halves. Serve the rice on a separate platter, fluffed and topped with a few grains of saffron rice. On a plate: a mound of rice on one side, chicken and sauce spooned beside it, so the sauce runs into the rice at the edge.

pairing.drink: A red with bright acidity and gentle tannin, such as Sangiovese or Pinot Noir: the acidity echoes the pomegranate and the fruit sits well beside the walnuts.
pairing.brennans: Fattoria di Fèlsina Chianti Classico 2022: a Sangiovese from the Brennan's list with the sour cherry acidity that suits a pomegranate and walnut sauce.

variations: Duck fesenjan: use 4 duck legs, browned well and their fat poured off, simmered 1 1/2 hours in the sauce.
Meatball fesenjan: roll 1 lb (450 g) minced lamb or beef with grated onion into small balls and simmer 30 minutes in the sauce.
Vegetarian: use roasted squash or aubergine cubes added for the last 20 minutes in place of chicken.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C); it will be well past that when tender at the bone.
Walnuts spoil quickly at room temperature; store them in the fridge or freezer.

title: Couscous with Seven Vegetables and Lamb
summary: A spiced lamb and vegetable broth cooked in the base of a couscoussier while the couscous above it is steamed three times, raked by hand with water, oil and butter between each steaming until every grain is separate and light, and finished with tfaya, a sweet onion and raisin topping. It teaches steaming grain by hand, the Moroccan art behind the Friday couscous.
skills: steaming couscous three times over the stew
equipment: Couscoussier, or a large stockpot with a colander or steamer basket that fits snugly on top
Strip of damp cloth or foil to seal the gap between pot and steamer
Very large, wide shallow bowl or a gasaa (wooden couscous bowl) for raking
Medium frying pan for the tfaya
Ladle and a slotted spoon
Measuring jug

ingredients.item: Lamb shoulder or neck, in 2 inch (5 cm) chunks, some bone in
Coriander and parsley, tied in a bundle
Pumpkin or butternut squash, in 2 inch (5 cm) pieces, skin on

ingredients.note: with 1 tsp (5 g) salt in the second lot

ingredients.item: Onions, thinly sliced, for the tfaya
Raisins, soaked 15 minutes in warm water
Honey and ground cinnamon, for the tfaya

mise: Cut all the vegetables in large pieces so they stay whole in the broth; keep the soft ones (squash and courgette) separate from the hard ones (carrot, turnip, cabbage).
Grate the tomatoes and one onion; tie the herb bundle.

Spread the dry couscous in the wide bowl, sprinkle with 1 cup (240 ml) water and work it with your fingers until evenly damp. Leave 10 minutes, then rub in the 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil, raking with spread fingers and rubbing between your palms to break every lump.
Slice the onions for the tfaya; soak and drain the raisins.
Make a seal: a strip of damp cloth or a rope of foil to wrap where the steamer meets the pot.

timeline.do: Start the lamb broth; wet and oil the couscous.
First steaming of the couscous over the broth, 15 minutes after steam rises.
Rake, water and salt; add the hard vegetables to the broth; start the tfaya.
Second steaming; rake again.
Add the soft vegetables and chickpeas; third steaming.
Butter the couscous; mound it; arrange meat, vegetables and tfaya.

steps.do: Broth: in the base of the couscoussier, combine the lamb, quartered and grated onion, grated tomato, olive oil, smen, ginger, turmeric, pepper, saffron, cinnamon, herb bundle and 2 tsp (10 g) salt. Stir over medium heat for 5 minutes until the meat is coated and fragrant, then add the water. Bring to a boil and skim.
steps.look: A golden yellow, fragrant broth with the lamb barely colouring; the smell of ginger and saffron.
steps.mistake: Boiling the broth hard throughout, which clouds it and toughens the lamb.
steps.fix: Bring it to a boil once, skim, then keep a lively simmer.

steps.do: First steaming: set the steamer on the pot, seal the join with the damp cloth, and tip in the oiled couscous gently, without packing it. When steam rises through the surface of the grain, steam for 15 minutes, uncovered.
steps.look: Wisps of steam rising evenly through the whole surface of the couscous.
steps.mistake: Pressing the couscous down or covering it, so steam cannot pass and it turns to paste at the bottom.
steps.fix: Pour it in loosely and leave it uncovered. If steam escapes round the edge, tighten the seal.

steps.do: Tip the couscous back into the wide bowl and spread it out. When cool enough to handle, sprinkle with 1 cup (240 ml) water mixed with 1 tsp (5 g) salt, a little at a time, raking and rubbing between your palms to break up every clump. Leave 10 minutes. Meanwhile add the carrots, turnips and cabbage to the broth.
steps.look: The grains swell and separate; no lumps when you run your fingers through it.
steps.mistake: Adding all the water in one go, which makes the couscous wet and clumpy.
steps.fix: Sprinkle and rake in stages; it should feel damp, never soggy.

steps.do: Tfaya: melt the butter in the frying pan over medium low heat, add the sliced onions and a pinch of salt, cover and cook 15 minutes until soft. Uncover, add the raisins, honey, cinnamon and 1/2 cup (120 ml) broth, and cook 20 to 25 minutes, stirring, until deep amber and jammy.
steps.look: Soft, sticky, caramel brown onions with plump raisins; it smells of honey and cinnamon.
steps.mistake: Rushing it over high heat, so the onions burn before they soften.
steps.fix: Low heat and patience; add a splash of broth if it catches.

steps.do: Second steaming: return the couscous to the steamer and steam another 15 minutes from when steam rises through it. Tip back into the bowl, sprinkle with the remaining 1/2 cup (120 ml) water, rake and rub again, and rest 10 minutes.
steps.look: The grains are larger, lighter and more separate than after the first steaming.
steps.mistake: Letting the couscous dry out in the bowl between steamings.
steps.fix: Keep it covered with a cloth while it rests.

steps.do: Add the squash, courgettes and chickpeas to the broth, and taste the broth for salt. Third steaming: steam the couscous a final 15 minutes. Check the lamb is tender and the vegetables just cooked through.
steps.look: Vegetables tender but holding their shape; lamb soft enough to pull apart with a spoon; couscous fluffy and hot.
steps.mistake: Adding the soft vegetables at the start, so they disintegrate into the broth.
steps.fix: Add them only for the final 20 to 25 minutes.

steps.do: Tip the couscous into the wide bowl and rub in the 3 tbsp (42 g) butter, cut in pieces, raking until every grain glistens. Taste for salt.
steps.look: Light, fluffy, separate grains with a gentle sheen and no lumps.
steps.mistake: Stirring with a spoon, which crushes the grains.
steps.fix: Use your fingers or a fork, lifting and letting the grains fall.

steps.do: Mound the couscous on a large platter and make a crater in the top. Put the lamb in the crater, arrange the vegetables around and up the sides in stripes, and spoon tfaya over the top. Moisten with a few ladles of broth and serve more broth and the harissa on the side.
steps.look: A volcano of pale gold couscous, crowned with meat and amber tfaya, vegetables standing up its sides.
steps.mistake: Drowning the couscous in broth so it turns soggy.
steps.fix: Moisten the top lightly; each person adds more broth to taste.

science: Dried couscous is tiny pellets of semolina already partly cooked. Steaming hydrates and gelatinises the starch gently with steam rather than boiling water, so each grain swells without the surface turning sticky. Wetting and raking between steamings lets water soak evenly into every grain, and the oil and butter coat them so they do not stick together. Three short steamings build volume gradually, giving larger, lighter grains than a single soak in boiling water. Steaming over the broth also perfumes the grain with the aromatic vapour of saffron and ginger. Hard vegetables need longer for their cell walls to soften, while courgette and squash break down quickly, which is why they are added in stages.
plating: Use the widest platter you have. Mound the couscous into a broad cone and press a crater into the top with the back of a ladle. Pile the lamb in the crater, then lean the vegetables up the slopes in coloured groups: carrots, turnips, courgettes, squash, cabbage wedges. Spoon the tfaya over the meat so it drips down, scatter the chickpeas round the base, and bring the broth to the table in a jug with harissa in a small bowl.

pairing.drink: A warm, spicy southern French red or a dry rosé: Grenache's red fruit and spice suit the saffron broth and sweet tfaya; mint tea is the classic finish.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de Durban Beaumes-de-Venise Rouge 2024: a Grenache based red from the Brennan's list with the warm spice and soft fruit for lamb, squash and sweet onions.

variations: Chicken couscous: use 2 lb (900 g) chicken pieces, simmered 40 minutes in the broth.
Vegetarian couscous: leave out the lamb and use 1 tbsp (15 g) more smen and a handful of broad beans.
Quick version: pour boiling broth over instant couscous, cover 5 minutes, then fluff with butter; it is not the same, but it is a weeknight version.
safety: Steam burns: lift the steamer off with oven gloves, tilting it away from you.
Lamb is safely cooked at 145°F (63°C); braised until tender it is well beyond that.

title: Thieboudienne
summary: Fish steaks stuffed with a pounded parsley, garlic and chilli paste, browned and simmered in a tomato broth with vegetables added in the right order, then lifted out while broken rice cooks in that red broth until it drinks it all and forms a crust on the base of the pot. One pot, three timings: it teaches sequencing and cooking rice by absorption in a flavoured broth.
skills: stuffing fish with rof herb paste
rice cooked in the broth with its crust
equipment: Large heavy pot of at least 7 quarts (6.5 litres) with a lid
Mortar and pestle
Small sharp knife
Slotted spoon and a large plate or tray
Fine sieve for washing rice
Large serving platter
Foil or a clean cloth for covering

ingredients.item: Thick white fish steaks, bone in (grouper, snapper, sea bass or hake)
Flat leaf parsley, leaves and tender stems

ingredients.note: for the rof; keep another whole for the broth

ingredients.item: Black pepper and fine salt, for the rof
Dried smoked fish (guedj) or dried shrimp, rinsed
Fish or vegetable stock, or water
Broken jasmine rice (riz brisé) or jasmine rice, pulsed briefly

mise: Make the rof: pound the parsley, spring onions, garlic, the half Scotch bonnet, pepper and salt in the mortar to a coarse, wet green paste.
Pat the fish steaks dry. Make two deep slits on each side of each steak, down to the bone, and pack the rof into the slits with a small spoon or your fingers. Rub any leftover rof over the outside.
Peel and cut all the vegetables into large pieces, grouping them by cooking time: cassava and carrots longest, then sweet potato and cabbage, then aubergine and okra.
Wash the rice in the sieve under cold water, rubbing it, until the water runs nearly clear; leave it to drain for 20 minutes.
Chop the onions; grate the tomatoes.

timeline.do: Make the rof; stuff the fish; prepare vegetables; wash the rice.
Brown the fish; fry the onions and tomato purée.
Build the broth; add vegetables in order; fish in for 15 minutes.
Lift out the fish and vegetables; measure the broth; add the rice.
Rice covered on low; let the crust form at the end.
Platter: rice, fish, vegetables, crust and lime.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the big pot over medium high heat. Brown the stuffed fish steaks 2 minutes per side, just to colour the outside, not to cook them. Lift them onto a plate.
steps.look: A light golden crust on each side; the green paste visible in the slits.
steps.mistake: Moving the fish too soon so it sticks and breaks.
steps.fix: Leave it until it releases on its own; turn with a wide spatula.

steps.do: Add the onions to the same oil and cook over medium heat 8 to 10 minutes until golden. Stir in the tomato purée and fry, stirring constantly, for 5 to 7 minutes until it turns from bright red to deep brick red and the oil separates. Add the grated tomatoes and the dried fish and cook 5 minutes more.
steps.look: A thick, dark red paste with a glossy layer of red oil around it; the sharp, tinny smell of tomato purée gone.
steps.mistake: Adding the liquid before the purée is properly fried, so the broth tastes raw and sour.
steps.fix: Keep frying until the colour darkens and the oil separates; lower the heat if it starts to catch.

steps.do: Pour in the stock, add the bay leaf and the whole Scotch bonnet and bring to a boil. Add the cassava and carrots and simmer 10 minutes, then add the sweet potato and cabbage and simmer 5 minutes.
steps.look: A bright red broth with vegetables bobbing; it smells rich and savoury.
steps.mistake: Adding all the vegetables at once, so the soft ones fall apart before the hard ones are cooked.
steps.fix: Add in order of hardness and test each with a knife.

steps.do: Slide the fish steaks into the broth with the aubergine and okra. Simmer gently 12 to 15 minutes until the fish is opaque at the bone (145°F, 63°C) and all the vegetables are tender. Taste and season the broth well: it should be slightly over salted, because the rice will absorb it.
steps.look: Fish flakes when nudged near the bone; vegetables pierce easily.
steps.mistake: Boiling the fish hard, which breaks it apart in the broth.
steps.fix: Keep a gentle simmer once the fish is in.

steps.do: Lift out the fish and all the vegetables with the slotted spoon onto a tray, cover with foil and keep warm. Remove the Scotch bonnet. Measure the broth: you need about 3 1/2 cups (840 ml) for the rice; set the rest aside to serve.
steps.look: A deep red, flavourful broth in the pot.
steps.mistake: Leaving too much broth, which gives soupy rice, or too little, which leaves it hard.
steps.fix: Measure: roughly 1 3/4 times the volume of rice. Keep the extra hot to add if needed.

steps.do: Bring the measured broth to a boil, stir in the drained rice and spread it evenly. When it boils again, cover tightly, turn the heat to low and cook 20 to 25 minutes without stirring. If it looks dry and the rice is still hard at 15 minutes, sprinkle on 1/4 cup (60 ml) hot broth.
steps.look: The rice absorbs all the liquid and turns an even orange red; steam holes appear on the surface.
steps.mistake: Stirring the rice as it cooks, which breaks the grains and makes it gummy.
steps.fix: Leave it alone; spread and cover, then trust the steam.

steps.do: For the crust (xoon), turn the heat up to medium for the last 3 to 5 minutes, listening for a gentle crackle from the base, then turn off and rest 5 minutes covered.
steps.look: A golden brown, crisp layer of rice on the base of the pot that smells toasty, not burnt.
steps.mistake: Leaving it too long on high heat, so the crust burns black and bitter.
steps.fix: Listen and smell; stop when it crackles and smells toasty.

steps.do: Spoon the rice onto the large platter in a broad, even layer. Arrange the fish in the centre and the vegetables around it. Scrape up the crust in pieces and lay it at one side. Serve with lime wedges or tamarind and the extra broth.
steps.look: A wide red bed of rice, fish in the centre, vegetables in colourful groups, crisp golden crust to one side.
steps.mistake: Piling everything in a heap, which hides each element.
steps.fix: Arrange the vegetables in groups so everyone can see and choose.

science: Pounding the rof crushes the cell walls of the parsley, garlic and chilli, releasing their aromatic oils so they flavour the fish from inside the slits as it cooks. Frying tomato purée in oil caramelises its sugars and develops deeper, sweeter flavours, while removing the raw, metallic taste; the oil also dissolves the fat soluble red pigments, colouring the broth. Vegetables cook at different rates because of their structure: dense cassava and carrot need far longer for their cell walls to soften than aubergine or okra. Broken rice absorbs broth quickly because its broken surfaces expose more starch. As the last of the liquid boils away, the rice in contact with the hot base dries and browns through Maillard reactions, forming the prized crust.
plating: Serve family style on a large round platter, as in Senegal. Spread the rice in an even layer almost to the rim. Set the four fish steaks in the centre, stuffed sides up, and arrange the vegetables around them in wedges like a clock: cassava, carrot, sweet potato, cabbage, aubergine, okra. Break the crust into shards and lay them on one side. Put lime halves around the rim and broth in a jug.

pairing.drink: A dry rosé or a crisp, full white such as a Provençal rosé or a Chenin Blanc: fresh acidity for the tomato and fish, enough body for the rice and vegetables. Bissap (hibiscus drink) is the Senegalese choice.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Tempier Bandol Rosé 2024: a serious, savoury rosé from the Brennan's list with the weight and freshness for a tomato and fish rice.

variations: Thiebou yapp: make it with lamb or beef in place of fish, browned and simmered 1 hour.
Thiebou dieune bu weex (white): leave out the tomato for a white broth version flavoured with onion and herbs.
Fillets: use 1 1/2 lb (680 g) thick fillets in large pieces, simmered only 8 to 10 minutes.
safety: Fish is safely cooked at 145°F (63°C), opaque and flaking at the bone.
Scotch bonnets are very hot: wear gloves to seed them and keep them away from your eyes.
Pick out bones carefully when serving; steaks carry a central bone and small pin bones.

title: Beef Rendang
summary: Beef simmered for hours in coconut milk and a pounded paste of shallot, chilli, galangal, ginger, turmeric and lemongrass, cooked on past the stage of a curry until the coconut oil splits out and the beef fries in its own dark, clinging sauce. It closes the Sous Chef dinners because it is the fullest lesson in a paste and in reading a sauce as it passes through its stages.
skills: simmering beef in coconut milk for hours
cooking on until it fries in its own oil
equipment: Large mortar and pestle, or a food processor or blender
Wide, heavy pot or wok, about 12 inches (30 cm), not narrow and deep
Wooden spoon or a flat spatula
Small dry frying pan for the kerisik
Sharp knife and board

ingredients.item: Beef chuck or shin, in 2 inch (5 cm) cubes
Fresh red chillies, long, seeded for less heat
Dried red chillies, soaked in hot water 20 minutes
Lemongrass, tender lower third only, sliced
Turmeric leaf, tied in a knot
Cinnamon stick, star anise and cloves
Desiccated unsweetened coconut, for the kerisik

mise: Make the kerisik: toast the coconut in the dry pan over medium low heat, stirring constantly, 6 to 8 minutes until evenly deep golden brown. Pound it hot in the mortar (or grind in a spice grinder) until it becomes an oily, dark paste.

Make the paste: drain the dried chillies. Pound or blend the shallots, garlic, fresh and dried chillies, galangal, ginger, turmeric and sliced lemongrass to a fine, smooth paste. If blending, add up to 3 tbsp (45 ml) of the coconut milk to help the blades turn.
Pat the beef dry and cut it into even cubes so they cook at the same rate.
Bruise the whole lemongrass stalk with the back of a knife; tear the lime leaves.

timeline.do: Make the kerisik and the spice paste; cube the beef.
Combine everything in the wide pot; bring to a simmer.
Simmer uncovered, stirring every 15 minutes: soup, then stew.
The oil splits; stir more often; add the kerisik.
Stir constantly as the beef fries in its own oil until dark and dry.
Rest; cook the rice; serve.

steps.do: Put the beef, spice paste, coconut milk, water, lime leaves, turmeric leaf, whole lemongrass, cinnamon, star anise, cloves, tamarind, sugar and salt in the wide pot. Stir well and bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring.
steps.look: A loose, orange, soupy mixture with the beef submerged; it smells of lemongrass and coconut.
steps.mistake: Using a narrow, deep pot, so the liquid takes many more hours to reduce.
steps.fix: Use the widest heavy pot you have; the surface area is what drives the reduction.

steps.do: Turn the heat to medium low so it simmers steadily, uncovered. Cook for about 2 hours, stirring every 15 minutes and scraping the base. It passes from a thin soup (gulai) to a thicker stew (kalio).
steps.look: The level drops by half, the sauce thickens and darkens to brick orange, and the beef begins to soften.
steps.mistake: Covering the pot, which stops the reduction.
steps.fix: Keep it uncovered and simmering, not boiling hard.

steps.do: When the sauce is thick and you see beads of orange oil separating and pooling on the surface, the coconut milk is splitting. Stir in the kerisik. From now on, stir every 5 minutes, scraping the base thoroughly.
steps.look: A thick, dark orange sauce with a visible layer of clear, red-gold oil; it starts to sizzle rather than bubble.
steps.mistake: Panicking that the sauce has split. In rendang, splitting is the point.
steps.fix: Keep going; the split oil is what will fry the paste and the beef.

steps.do: Turn the heat down a little and stir almost constantly for the final 30 to 60 minutes as the remaining moisture cooks away and the beef and paste fry in the oil.
steps.look: The sauce turns from orange to deep brown, almost black at the edges, and clings to each piece of beef as a thick, dry, crumbly paste; the pot sizzles and the smell is intensely toasty and spiced.
steps.mistake: Stepping away in this final stage, when the paste can scorch in a minute.
steps.fix: Stay at the pot, stir and scrape constantly, and lower the heat if it catches. A few dark spots are flavour; black, acrid patches are not.

steps.do: Check the beef: a piece should be tender enough to break with the side of a spoon. Taste the sauce and adjust with salt or a pinch of sugar. Remove the whole spices, lemongrass stalk and turmeric leaf if you can find them.
steps.look: Dark, glossy beef coated in a thick, clinging paste, with a little oil pooling around.
steps.mistake: Stopping while the sauce is still wet and orange, which gives kalio rather than rendang.
steps.fix: Keep cooking until the colour is deep brown and the sauce clings; if the beef is tender before the sauce is dry, raise the heat and stir hard.

steps.do: Rest the rendang off the heat for 10 minutes and serve with steamed jasmine rice. It improves overnight in the fridge and reheats well in a pan over low heat.
steps.look: Deep brown, almost dry pieces of beef that glisten with oil.
steps.mistake: Serving it with lots of oil pooled on the plate.
steps.fix: Tilt the pot and spoon off excess oil before serving if you like.

science: Rendang reduces coconut milk until its emulsion breaks. Coconut milk is an emulsion of fat droplets in water held by proteins; as water evaporates and the proteins are heated for hours, they can no longer hold the droplets apart, and the fat separates out as clear oil. Once most of the water has gone, the temperature in the pot is no longer limited to the boiling point, so the paste and beef begin to fry in that oil, browning through Maillard reactions and caramelisation into deep, savoury flavours. The long simmer converts the collagen in chuck or shin to gelatin, making it tender. Kerisik adds toasted coconut flavour and body. Fresh aromatics pounded to a paste release their oils into the coconut fat.
plating: Spoon a neat dome of jasmine rice on one side of a warm plate. Arrange four or five pieces of rendang beside it, piled slightly, spooning the dark paste over them. Add a few thin slices of fresh red chilli and a shred of lime leaf on top, and perhaps a few slices of cucumber at the side for freshness. For a feast, serve in a shallow bowl with the rice separately.

pairing.drink: A rich, aromatic white with low tannin such as an Alsace Pinot Gris or an off dry Gewürztraminer: body and spice to meet the coconut and chilli without clashing.
pairing.brennans: F.E. Trimbach Pinot Gris ‘Réserve Personnelle’ 2007: a rich, mature Alsace Pinot Gris from the Brennan's list with the weight and spice for a dry coconut braise.

variations: Malaysian style: fry the paste in 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil for 10 minutes before adding the beef and coconut milk, for a slightly sweeter rendang.
Chicken rendang: use 2 lb (900 g) bone-in chicken pieces and cook for 1 1/2 hours in total.
Jackfruit rendang: use young green jackfruit chunks for a vegetarian version with the same paste.
safety: Beef is safe at 145°F (63°C); braised for hours it is far beyond that.
The final stage spits hot oil: stir with a long spoon and keep your forearms covered.
Cool leftovers within 2 hours; rendang keeps 4 days in the fridge.

title: Semifreddo al Caffè
summary: A frozen coffee mousse made from a yolk and espresso base cooked over water, an Italian meringue whipped with sugar syrup boiled to soft ball, and whipped cream, folded together and frozen in a loaf tin with crushed amaretti. It opens the Sous Chef desserts with the cooked meringue every pastry cook must know and the fold that keeps the air in.
skills: an Italian meringue with sugar syrup at soft ball
equipment: Stand mixer with whisk attachment (a hand mixer works with a helper for the syrup)
Small heavy saucepan for the syrup
Sugar or digital probe thermometer
Heatproof bowl that sits over a saucepan of simmering water
Balloon whisk
Second clean, grease free bowl for the cream
Large flexible spatula
Loaf tin of about 6 cups (1.5 litres), roughly 8 1/2 by 4 1/2 inches (22 by 11 cm)
Cling film, and a pastry brush with a cup of water

ingredients.item: Espresso or very strong coffee, cooled

ingredients.note: dissolved in the coffee for depth

ingredients.item: Egg whites, large, at room temperature
Double or heavy cream, very cold

ingredients.note: half folded in, half to finish

mise: Line the loaf tin with cling film, leaving plenty overhanging on all sides; a light brush of water inside the tin first helps it stick.
Brew the espresso, dissolve the espresso powder in it and cool completely; add the rum.
Separate the eggs; wipe the mixer bowl and whisk with a little lemon juice or vinegar on paper to remove any grease.
Make sure the cream is very cold; put its bowl and whisk in the freezer for 10 minutes.
Clear space in the freezer for the tin to sit level.

timeline.do: Line the tin; brew and cool the coffee.
Cook the yolk base to 160°F (71°C) and whip it cool.
Boil the syrup to 240°F (116°C); make the Italian meringue.
Whip the cream; fold the three together; fill the tin.
Freeze, covered, at least 6 hours.
Turn out, slice with a warm knife and finish.

steps.do: Yolk base: whisk the yolks, the 1/4 cup (50 g) sugar and the coffee in the heatproof bowl. Set it over a pan of barely simmering water and whisk constantly for 4 to 6 minutes until the mixture reaches 160°F (71°C) and has thickened and doubled in volume.
steps.look: Pale coffee coloured foam that holds a ribbon on its surface for 3 seconds; it smells of coffee and warm custard, never scrambled egg.
steps.mistake: Letting the bowl touch the water or the water boil, so the yolks curdle into grains at the edges.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and lift the bowl off for a few seconds if it heats too fast; strain through a sieve if a few specks form.

steps.do: Take the bowl off the heat and whisk (or whip with the mixer) for 5 to 6 minutes until completely cool and thick. Set aside.
steps.look: A thick, mousse-like base at room temperature that falls from the whisk in a heavy ribbon.
steps.mistake: Folding warm base into cream, which melts the cream and deflates everything.
steps.fix: Whip until cool to the touch; set the bowl over iced water to speed it up.

steps.do: Syrup: put the 1/2 cup (100 g) sugar and 2 tbsp (30 ml) water in the small saucepan, stir once to wet the sugar, then heat over medium heat without stirring. Brush the inside of the pan with water to wash down any crystals. Clip on the thermometer.
steps.look: Clear, bubbling syrup with no undissolved sugar on the pan walls.
steps.mistake: Stirring the boiling syrup, which can make it crystallise and turn cloudy and grainy.
steps.fix: Swirl the pan instead of stirring; if it crystallises, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water, dissolve and start again.

steps.do: When the syrup reaches 230°F (110°C), start whipping the whites with the salt on medium speed until they form soft peaks. Keep heating the syrup to 240°F (116°C), the soft ball stage.
steps.look: Large, slow bubbles in the syrup; a drop in cold water forms a soft ball that flattens when pressed. The whites are foamy and hold soft, drooping peaks.
steps.mistake: Whipping the whites too early, so they are dry and grainy before the syrup is ready.
steps.fix: Start the whites when the syrup is at about 230°F (110°C); if they are ready first, turn the mixer to its lowest speed to keep them moving.

steps.do: With the mixer on medium, pour the hot syrup in a thin, steady stream down the inside wall of the bowl, between the side and the whisk. Then turn to high and whip 6 to 8 minutes until the meringue is thick, glossy and the bowl feels only just warm.
steps.look: A shiny, dense, satiny meringue that holds stiff peaks with a slight curl; it no longer feels hot.
steps.mistake: Pouring the syrup onto the whisk, so it is flung against the bowl and sets in hard threads.
steps.fix: Aim for the narrow gap between the bowl and the whisk; a few threads of sugar can be picked out.

steps.do: Whip the cold cream in the chilled bowl to soft peaks that just hold their shape and fall over at the tip.
steps.look: Thick, billowy cream that mounds softly on the whisk.
steps.mistake: Whipping the cream to stiff, grainy peaks, which makes folding harder and the texture heavy.
steps.fix: Stop at soft peaks. If over whipped, gently fold in 1 to 2 tbsp (15 to 30 ml) of liquid cream.

steps.do: Fold: stir a quarter of the meringue into the coffee base to loosen it. Add the rest of the meringue and fold gently: cut down through the centre with the spatula, sweep along the bottom and up the side, turning the bowl a quarter turn each time. Then fold in the cream the same way, and half the amaretti, stopping as soon as no streaks remain.
steps.look: A light, airy, even pale coffee mousse with a few amaretti pieces; it holds soft mounds.
steps.mistake: Stirring or beating, which knocks out the air and makes an icy, dense block.
steps.fix: Fold with large, slow movements and stop as soon as it is even; a few small streaks are better than overmixing.

steps.do: Pour into the lined tin, smooth the top, cover with the overhanging film and freeze for at least 6 hours, or overnight. To serve, lift out by the film, peel it away, scatter with the remaining amaretti and chocolate, and slice with a knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry.
steps.look: A firm but sliceable block that cuts cleanly and shows a smooth, fine texture with tiny bubbles.
steps.mistake: Serving it rock hard straight from a very cold freezer.
steps.fix: Leave it at room temperature for 5 minutes before slicing; it is meant to be half frozen.

science: Semifreddo is never churned, so its smooth texture depends on air and sugar rather than an ice cream machine. The yolk base is cooked to 160°F (71°C), which thickens it as the proteins set slightly and makes it safe. An Italian meringue is made by pouring sugar syrup at 240°F (116°C) into whipping whites: the hot syrup partly cooks the egg white proteins and coats the air bubbles with a thick sugar solution, creating a very stable foam that resists collapse when folded and frozen. Whipped cream adds more air and fat. The air bubbles interrupt ice crystal growth, and the high sugar content lowers the freezing point, so the semifreddo stays soft enough to slice straight from the freezer. A spoonful of alcohol lowers the freezing point further.
plating: Chill the plates. Cut a slice about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick with a warm knife and lay it flat in the centre of the plate, slightly off centre. Scatter crushed amaretti along one edge of the slice and a few chocolate shavings over the top. A small pool of cold espresso syrup or a spoon of softly whipped cream beside it finishes the plate. Serve at once, before it softens.

pairing.drink: A coffee cocktail, a vin santo or a sweet Marsala: coffee echoes coffee, and nutty, caramel wines suit the amaretti and cream.
pairing.brennans: Ralph’s Coffee: the Brennan's coffee cocktail of chicory coffee with Frangelico and Nocello under whipped cream, whose hazelnut and walnut notes match the amaretti in this semifreddo.

variations: Semifreddo al torroncino: replace the coffee with 1/4 cup (60 ml) milk and fold in 3 oz (85 g) chopped nougat.
Pistachio semifreddo: whisk 3 tbsp (45 g) pistachio paste into the cooled yolk base and leave out the coffee.
Single bowl version: make only the yolk base (step 1), fold in the cream and amaretti and freeze; denser, but simpler.
safety: The yolk base is cooked to 160°F (71°C). The Italian meringue whites are heated by the syrup but may not reach that, so use pasteurised egg whites for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or unwell.
Boiling sugar syrup causes severe burns: keep children away, use a heavy pan and pour carefully.
Keep frozen at 0°F (minus 18°C) and eat within 2 weeks.

title: Quindim
summary: Small, glossy golden custards made almost entirely of egg yolks, sugar and grated coconut, baked gently in a water bath so the coconut rises to form a chewy base while the yolks set into a clear, shining top. It builds on crème brûlée by asking for an even gentler bake and a perfect unmoulding.
skills: a very high yolk custard with coconut
equipment: Eight small metal moulds or ramekins of about 1/3 cup (80 ml), or a muffin tin
Roasting tin deep enough for the moulds to sit in water halfway up
Mixing bowl and a silicone spatula (not a whisk)
Fine sieve
Kettle
Small thin knife or a palette knife
Pastry brush

ingredients.note: freeze the whites for a pavlova or meringues
or desiccated coconut soaked 10 minutes in the coconut milk

ingredients.item: Soft butter and caster sugar, for the moulds

mise: Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C) with a shelf in the middle. Boil a kettle of water.
Brush the moulds generously with soft butter, then coat with caster sugar, tapping out the excess. Every part must be coated or the custard will stick.
Separate the eggs carefully; strain the yolks through the sieve to remove the threads (chalazae), which can leave white specks.
If using desiccated coconut, soak it in the coconut milk for 10 minutes.

timeline.do: Oven on; prepare the moulds; strain the yolks.
Stir the custard; rest it 15 minutes; skim.
Fill and bake in the water bath, 30 to 40 minutes.
Cool in the moulds, then chill at least 3 hours.
Loosen and unmould.

steps.do: Put the strained yolks and the 3/4 cup plus 2 tbsp (170 g) sugar in the bowl. Stir slowly with the spatula, not a whisk, for 2 to 3 minutes until the sugar has mostly dissolved and the mixture is smooth and glossy.
steps.look: A thick, bright orange, glossy liquid with no foam on top; it feels only slightly gritty between your fingers.
steps.mistake: Whisking hard, which whips in air bubbles that bake into holes and spoil the glassy top.
steps.fix: Stir gently; if foam has formed, let it rest longer and skim it off.

steps.do: Stir in the melted butter, coconut milk, salt and grated coconut. Rest the mixture for 15 minutes, then skim any bubbles from the surface with a spoon.
steps.look: Coconut flakes suspended in a thick yolk mixture; the surface clear of foam.
steps.mistake: Adding hot butter, which can start to cook the yolks.
steps.fix: Let the melted butter cool to warm before adding.

steps.do: Stir once to redistribute the coconut, then fill the moulds to 1/4 inch (5 mm) below the rim, sharing the coconut evenly. Set them in the roasting tin and pour boiling water into the tin to come halfway up the sides of the moulds.
steps.look: Evenly filled moulds sitting level in a hot water bath.
steps.mistake: Splashing water into the moulds while pouring.
steps.fix: Put the tin on the oven shelf first, then pour the water in from the kettle at one corner.

steps.do: Bake at 325°F (160°C) for 30 to 40 minutes, until the tops are set, glossy and deep golden, and a toothpick pushed into the middle comes out clean while the centre still trembles slightly when the tin is nudged.
steps.look: A shiny, amber, smooth surface; the custard has pulled very slightly from the sides; a gentle wobble in the middle.
steps.mistake: Baking at a higher heat to save time, which makes the custard bubble, crack and turn grainy.
steps.fix: Keep the oven at 325°F (160°C) and the water bath topped up; if the tops are colouring too fast, lay a sheet of foil loosely over them.

steps.do: Lift the moulds out of the water and cool on a rack to room temperature, about 45 minutes, then refrigerate at least 3 hours.
steps.look: Firm, glossy custards that have settled slightly.
steps.mistake: Unmoulding while warm, when they are too soft and break.
steps.fix: Be patient; chilled quindim release far more cleanly.

steps.do: To unmould, run a thin knife around the inside edge of each mould, pressing against the mould rather than the custard. Dip the base of each mould in hot water for 10 seconds, put a plate on top and invert in one movement, then lift the mould away.
steps.look: A small golden dome with a shiny, glass-like top and a chewy coconut layer at the base, now on top as it stands.
steps.mistake: Prising it out with a knife, which tears the glossy surface.
steps.fix: If one sticks, dip it in hot water for 10 seconds more and try again.

science: Egg yolks contain proteins and emulsifiers that set into a smooth, dense gel when heated gently; their fat gives richness. Sugar dissolves into the water in the yolks and raises the temperature at which the proteins set, which is why such a sweet custard can bake for so long without curdling. In the oven, the lighter grated coconut floats up while the heavier yolk custard sinks, so after unmoulding the shiny yolk layer is on top and the coconut forms the base. The water bath keeps the temperature around the moulds close to 212°F (100°C), well below the oven temperature, so the custard heats slowly and evenly. Too much heat makes the proteins tighten and squeeze out water, giving holes and a grainy texture.
plating: Set two quindins on a small white plate, a little apart, so the golden tops catch the light. Add a few shavings of toasted coconut or a single slice of fresh mango or passion fruit pulp beside them for colour and acidity. Wipe any syrup from the plate edge. They can also be served on a platter in small paper cases, as at a Brazilian party.

pairing.drink: A sweet white with good acidity, such as a Coteaux du Layon or a late harvest Chenin, or a strong black coffee: acidity cuts the very rich yolk.
pairing.brennans: Domaine des Baumard ‘Clos Sainte Catherine’ Coteaux du Layon 2006: a sweet Loire Chenin Blanc from the Brennan's list, honeyed but fresh enough for a yolk and coconut custard.

variations: Quindão: bake the same mixture in one buttered and sugared 7 inch (18 cm) ring mould for 50 to 60 minutes and slice.
Lime quindim: add the finely grated zest of 1 lime to the yolks.
Muffin tin method: use a well buttered and sugared non-stick muffin tin for 12 smaller quindins, baked 25 to 30 minutes.
safety: The yolks are fully cooked when set; they reach well over 160°F (71°C).
Pour boiling water carefully into the tin in the oven, and lift the tin out with oven gloves.
Keep quindim refrigerated and eat within 3 days.

title: Chocoflan
summary: Cajeta in the bottom of a tin, a thin chocolate cake batter over it and a flan mixture poured gently on top, which then changes places with the cake in the oven so that, when turned out, flan sits on chocolate cake under a caramel glaze. It is in the course to teach density and the science of batters, with a water bath bake and a clean inversion.
skills: layers that swap places in the oven
equipment: Bundt tin of about 6 cups (1.5 litres), or an 8 inch (20 cm) round cake tin at least 3 inches (7.5 cm) deep
Roasting tin large enough to hold it with water halfway up
Two mixing bowls and a whisk
Blender for the flan
Fine sieve
Large spoon for pouring over
Foil
Kettle
Serving plate with a rim, wider than the tin

ingredients.item: Cajeta (goat's milk caramel) or thick dulce de leche

mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C) with a shelf in the middle. Boil a kettle.
Butter the tin heavily, into every crease if using a bundt.
Warm the cajeta for 10 to 15 seconds in the microwave until it just flows, then spoon it evenly over the base of the tin.
Brew the coffee and keep it hot; bring the egg and buttermilk to room temperature.
Have the roasting tin ready and a piece of foil large enough to cover the cake tin.

timeline.do: Oven on; butter the tin; spread the cajeta.
Mix the cake batter; blend and strain the flan.
Layer, cover and bake in the water bath 50 to 60 minutes.
Cool 30 minutes; chill at least 4 hours.
Loosen, warm the base, invert and serve.

steps.do: Cake batter: whisk the flour, cocoa, sugar, bicarbonate and salt in a bowl. Whisk in the egg, buttermilk and oil until smooth, then whisk in the hot coffee. The batter will be very thin.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, pourable chocolate batter, like double cream.
steps.mistake: Thinking the batter is too runny and adding flour; it must be thin for the layers to swap.
steps.fix: Leave it as it is: a thick batter cannot let the flan sink through it.

steps.do: Pour the cake batter over the cajeta in the tin from about 2 inches (5 cm) above it, moving round the tin so it settles in an even layer. It is fine if the cajeta swirls a little.
steps.look: Dark batter covering the caramel layer.
steps.mistake: Stirring the batter into the cajeta.
steps.fix: Pour gently from close to the surface; do not mix.

steps.do: Flan: blend the condensed milk, evaporated milk, eggs and vanilla for 15 seconds, then strain through the fine sieve. Pour it SLOWLY over the back of a large spoon held just above the batter, moving the spoon around so it spreads in a layer on top.
steps.look: A pale cream layer floating on top of the chocolate batter. It looks wrong; that is correct.
steps.mistake: Pouring the flan in a stream, so it plunges into the batter and mixes with it.
steps.fix: Go slowly over the spoon; a little mixing at the edges still works.

steps.do: Cover the tin tightly with buttered foil. Set it in the roasting tin in the oven and pour boiling water into the roasting tin to come halfway up the sides. Bake 50 to 60 minutes for a 6 cup (1.5 litre) tin.
steps.look: When you lift the foil at the end, the top looks like set chocolate cake; a skewer pushed into the middle comes out clean, and the flan underneath is set with a slight wobble.
steps.mistake: Leaving the foil off, so the cake top dries and domes and the flan overcooks.
steps.fix: Cover tightly; check at 50 minutes and give it 10 more if the skewer is wet with batter.

steps.do: Lift the tin out of the water and cool on a rack for 30 minutes, then refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight.
steps.look: The cake has firmed and pulled very slightly from the sides.
steps.mistake: Turning it out warm, when the flan is too soft and breaks.
steps.fix: Chill it fully: cold flan sets firm enough to stand.

steps.do: To unmould, run a thin knife around the edges (and the central tube of a bundt). Dip the base of the tin in hot water for 30 seconds. Put the plate upside down on the tin, hold them together and flip in one movement. Lift the tin away slowly; scrape any cajeta left inside over the top.
steps.look: A cream coloured flan layer on top of dark chocolate cake, with amber cajeta running down the sides.
steps.mistake: Lifting the tin before the cake has dropped onto the plate.
steps.fix: Tap the tin and wait a minute; if it still sticks, warm the base again.

steps.do: Sprinkle with toasted pecans if using, then cut into 6 wedges with a sharp knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between cuts.
steps.look: Two clean, distinct layers in each slice, caramel glistening on top.
steps.mistake: Cutting with a cold, dry knife, which drags the flan into the cake.
steps.fix: Dip and wipe the knife between every slice.

science: The flan mixture of condensed and evaporated milk with eggs is denser, at about 1.1 grams per millilitre, than the thin cake batter. As the oven heats the batter, the bicarbonate reacts with the acids in the natural cocoa and buttermilk, releasing carbon dioxide; the batter becomes full of bubbles and lighter still, so it rises up through the heavier flan, which sinks. The layers swap places before either has set. The water bath keeps the temperature around the tin close to 212°F (100°C), so the flan sets smoothly without curdling while the cake bakes through. Alkalised cocoa has no acid to react with the bicarbonate, so it gives poor rise and can leave a soapy taste. Cajeta is milk and sugar cooked to caramel.
plating: Cut a wedge with a hot knife and lay it on its side on a dessert plate so both layers show, flan on top. Spoon a little extra warm cajeta over the top so it drips down the cut face, and scatter a few pecans. A spoon of softly whipped cream or crème fraîche on the side cuts the sweetness.

pairing.drink: A coffee, or a tawny port or Pedro Ximénez sherry: dried fruit and caramel suit chocolate and cajeta.
pairing.brennans: Banane au Chocolat: the Brennan's dessert cocktail of crème de banane, crème de cacao and Pedro Ximénez sherry, whose chocolate and raisin notes suit a chocolate cake under caramel.

variations: Full size: double every quantity for a 10 to 12 cup (2.4 to 2.8 litre) bundt and bake 70 to 85 minutes.
Orange chocoflan: add the finely grated zest of 1 orange to the flan mixture.
Mocha: add 1 tsp (2 g) instant espresso to the cake batter and use a coffee liqueur in the flan instead of vanilla.
safety: The flan contains raw egg and must be fully set: the centre reaches about 170°F (77°C), past the 160°F (71°C) that cooks eggs.
Use oven gloves to lift the tin from the water bath; boiling water scalds.
Keep refrigerated and eat within 3 days.
