title: Japanese Cotton Cheesecake
summary: A cheesecake that is half soufflé: a smooth cream cheese and yolk base lightened with a meringue whipped only to soft peaks, folded gently, baked low in a water bath and cooled slowly so it stays tall, wobbly and crack free. A meringue taken one step too far splits the top, so it teaches judging peaks precisely.
skills: a meringue whipped to soft peaks only
equipment: 7 inch (18 cm) round cake tin, solid based (not springform), at least 3 inches (7.5 cm) deep
Baking paper for the base and a collar standing 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) above the rim
Heavy duty foil to wrap the outside of the tin
Roasting tin for the water bath
Heatproof bowl over a pan of barely simmering water
Stand mixer or hand mixer, with a clean, grease free bowl
Balloon whisk, sieve and a large flexible spatula
Kettle and an oven thermometer

ingredients.item: Full fat cream cheese, at room temperature

ingredients.note: yolks at room temperature, whites cold
or 1/4 tsp (1 g) cream of tartar

mise: Line the base of the tin with a circle of baking paper and the sides with a collar of paper rising 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) above the rim; a light grease helps it stick.
Wrap the outside of the tin in two layers of heavy foil so no water can get in.
Heat the oven to 320°F (160°C) with a shelf in the lower third, and check it with an oven thermometer. Boil a kettle.
Separate the eggs carefully; not a speck of yolk may go into the whites. Put the whites in the clean mixer bowl in the fridge.
Sift the flour and cornflour together twice.

timeline.do: Line and wrap the tin; oven on; separate the eggs.
Make the cheese base.
Whip the meringue to soft peaks; fold; fill the tin.
Bake 20 minutes at 320°F (160°C), then 50 minutes at 265°F (130°C).
Cool in the switched off oven, door ajar, 15 minutes; then on a rack.
Chill at least 3 hours, or serve warm and wobbly.

steps.do: Put the cream cheese, butter and milk in the heatproof bowl over barely simmering water and whisk for 5 to 7 minutes until completely melted and smooth. Take off the heat and whisk in the 6 yolks one at a time, then the salt.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, pourable cream with no lumps of cheese; it is warm, not hot.
steps.mistake: Overheating the base so the cream cheese splits or the yolks start to cook.
steps.fix: Keep the water at a bare simmer and take the bowl off as soon as it is smooth; let it cool 2 minutes before adding the yolks.

steps.do: Sift the flour and cornflour over the base and whisk until not one lump remains. Strain the whole mixture through the sieve into a large bowl.
steps.look: A thick, silky batter that falls from the whisk in a smooth ribbon.
steps.mistake: Leaving small lumps of flour, which bake as specks in the crumb.
steps.fix: Always strain; press any lumps through with the spatula.

steps.do: Whip the cold whites with the lemon juice on medium speed until foamy, then add the sugar in three parts, a minute apart, and continue whipping until the meringue forms SOFT peaks: when you lift the whisk, the peak bends over and folds back on itself like a soft hook.
steps.look: A glossy, smooth meringue with soft, drooping peaks; it slides slowly when the bowl is tilted.
steps.mistake: Whipping to stiff peaks, which makes the meringue too strong: the cake rises too fast in the oven and the top cracks.
steps.fix: Stop early and check often by lifting the whisk; if you go slightly too far, fold with extra care and accept a small crack: the cake will still taste right.

steps.do: Fold a third of the meringue into the cheese base with the whisk to loosen it. Add half the remaining meringue and fold with the spatula in large, gentle strokes, then the rest, stopping as soon as no white streaks remain.
steps.look: A pale, airy, even batter, thick and light, with no streaks of meringue.
steps.mistake: Stirring vigorously, which knocks out the air and gives a dense, flat cake.
steps.fix: Fold from the bottom up and turn the bowl as you go. A few tiny white flecks are fine.

steps.do: Pour the batter into the lined tin from a little height, to break large bubbles, and tap the tin twice on the worktop. Set it in the roasting tin and pour hot water into the roasting tin to a depth of about 1 inch (2.5 cm).
steps.look: A smooth, level surface without large bubbles.
steps.mistake: Using a springform tin without a good foil wrap, so water seeps in and the base turns soggy.
steps.fix: Use a solid based tin, or wrap a springform in two layers of foil.

steps.do: Bake at 320°F (160°C) for 20 minutes, then lower the oven to 265°F (130°C) and bake a further 50 to 55 minutes without opening the door. It is done when the top is pale golden, risen and springs back, and the whole cake wobbles as one mass when the tin is nudged.
steps.look: A tall, golden, smooth top that has risen above the tin edge, with no cracks.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven door to check during the first hour, which lets the cake sink.
steps.fix: Use the oven light. If the top cracks, it was too hot or the meringue too stiff: lower the first temperature by 10°F (5°C) next time.

steps.do: Turn off the oven and leave the cake inside with the door slightly ajar for 15 minutes. Then lift it out, remove the foil and let it cool on a rack for 30 minutes before removing it from the tin and peeling off the paper.
steps.look: The cake sinks only a little and stays tall and smooth.
steps.mistake: Taking it straight from the hot oven into cool air, so it collapses and wrinkles.
steps.fix: Cool it gradually; a little shrinkage is normal.

steps.do: Brush the top with the warm sieved apricot jam if you like, then serve warm and jiggly, or chill for at least 3 hours for a denser, creamier texture. Slice with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry.
steps.look: A shining golden top; a fine, cotton soft, moist crumb when cut.
steps.mistake: Slicing a warm cake with a dry knife, which squashes it.
steps.fix: Warm and wipe the knife between every cut.

science: This cake is held up by a meringue foam and set by egg and starch. Whites whipped only to soft peaks have air bubbles that can still expand gently in the oven; stiff peaks have bubbles with tighter, stronger walls that expand quickly and then burst, so the cake rises too fast and the surface tears. The cornflour and flour absorb water and swell, binding the egg proteins into a moist, flexible network rather than a dry crumb, so the cake can stretch as it rises. The water bath keeps the tin at about 212°F (100°C), so the outside does not set into a crust before the middle has finished rising. Cooling slowly lets the steam inside contract gently; sudden cold makes it collapse.
plating: Serve a tall slice standing upright on a small plate, the shining top facing the guest. Dust a thin line of icing sugar across one side, or spoon a little fresh berry coulis beside it. A few raspberries or slices of strawberry add colour and acidity. For the famous wobble, serve it warm on a board and cut at the table.

pairing.drink: A gently sweet sparkling wine, such as a demi sec Champagne or a Moscato d'Asti, or green tea: light sweetness and bubbles suit the airy, lightly tangy cake.
pairing.brennans: Laurent-Perrier ‘Harmony’ Demi Sec NV (375 ml): a half bottle of gently sweet Champagne from the Brennan's list, light enough for a cheesecake that is mostly air.

variations: Matcha cotton cheesecake: sift 1 tbsp (6 g) matcha with the flour.
Lemon: add the finely grated zest of 1 lemon to the cheese base.
Cupcake size: bake in paper lined ramekins in a water bath for 30 to 35 minutes at 300°F (150°C).
safety: The eggs are fully cooked; the centre reaches well over 160°F (71°C).
Pour the hot water into the roasting tin in the oven, and take the tin out with oven gloves.
Keep refrigerated and eat within 3 days.

title: Rasmalai
summary: Fresh cheese made at home by splitting boiled milk with lemon juice, drained, kneaded until perfectly smooth, shaped into discs, poached in a boiling syrup until they double in size, then soaked in a saffron and cardamom milk reduced on the side. It is Bengali sweet making at its finest: making cheese, and kneading it smooth enough to hold together in a syrup.
skills: splitting milk with acid for chhena
equipment: Two large heavy saucepans, one of at least 4 quarts (4 litres)
Wide pan of at least 10 inches (26 cm) with a lid, for poaching
Muslin or cheesecloth and a colander
Clean worktop or large plate for kneading
Slotted spoon
Wide shallow serving dish
Mortar and pestle for the cardamom

ingredients.note: not ultra high temperature (UHT) milk, which curdles poorly

ingredients.item: Lemon juice mixed with an equal amount of water
Whole milk, for the rabri (reduced milk)
Caster sugar, for the poaching syrup

ingredients.note: soaked in 1 tbsp (15 ml) warm milk

mise: Start this the day before, or at least 7 hours ahead: the discs need 4 hours in the milk.
Line the colander with a double layer of muslin over the sink.
Mix the lemon juice and water.
Crack the cardamom, discard the husks and grind the seeds; soak the saffron in warm milk.
Sliver the pistachios.

timeline.do: Make the chhena; drain and hang it 30 minutes.
Start reducing the milk for the rabri.
Knead the chhena; shape 12 discs.
Poach the discs in boiling syrup for 12 to 15 minutes.
Squeeze the discs and soak them in the warm saffron milk; chill at least 4 hours.
Garnish with pistachios and serve cold.

steps.do: Chhena: bring the 2 quarts (2 litres) milk to a full boil in the large pan, stirring so it does not catch. Take it off the heat, wait 1 minute, then add the diluted lemon juice a tablespoon at a time, stirring slowly, until the milk separates. Stop the moment the liquid (whey) turns clear and greenish yellow.
steps.look: Soft white curds clumping together and floating in a clear, pale green liquid; no milky whiteness left in the whey.
steps.mistake: Adding all the lemon at once or too much of it, which makes the chhena squeaky, rubbery and grainy.
steps.fix: Add slowly and stop as soon as the whey is clear. Keep the leftover lemon water for another use.

steps.do: Pour into the muslin lined colander. Run cold water over the curds for 30 seconds to wash off the lemon taste and stop the cooking. Gather the cloth, twist gently to squeeze out water, and hang it from the tap for 30 to 45 minutes.
steps.look: A soft, moist ball of crumbly cheese that holds together when pressed, damp but not dripping.
steps.mistake: Squeezing it bone dry or hanging it for hours, so the discs crack in the syrup; or leaving it too wet, so they dissolve.
steps.fix: Pinch a little: it should hold together and feel moist, like soft cookie dough. If too wet, hang 10 minutes more.

steps.do: Rabri: meanwhile, bring the 5 cups (1.2 litres) milk to a boil in the second pan, then simmer over medium low heat, stirring and scraping the base every few minutes, for 40 to 50 minutes until reduced by about a third. Stir in the 1/3 cup (70 g) sugar, the cardamom and the saffron with its milk. Keep it warm.
steps.look: A slightly thickened, pale golden milk, flecked with saffron, smelling of cardamom.
steps.mistake: Leaving it unstirred, so the milk scorches on the base.
steps.fix: Stir regularly, scraping the bottom; use a heavy pan.

steps.do: Knead the chhena on the worktop: push it away with the heel of your hand, gather it back and repeat for 6 to 8 minutes until the graininess has gone completely and the dough is smooth and slightly greasy.
steps.look: A smooth, soft, pliable dough that leaves a greasy film on your palm and shows no cracks when rolled.
steps.mistake: Kneading too little, so the discs have grains and fall apart in the syrup.
steps.fix: Keep going until a small ball rolled between your palms has no cracks at all.

steps.do: Divide into 12 equal pieces. Roll each into a smooth ball, then flatten gently into a disc about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) across and 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick. Smooth the edges so there are no cracks. Cover with a damp cloth.
steps.look: Twelve smooth, even, crack free discs.
steps.mistake: Leaving cracks at the edges, which split open in the syrup.
steps.fix: Roll and press again; a cracked disc can be re-rolled from the start.

steps.do: Poach: bring the 1 cup (200 g) sugar and 4 1/4 cups (1 litre) water to a full rolling boil in the wide pan. Slide in the discs, cover and keep the syrup at a hard, rolling boil for 12 to 15 minutes. After 8 minutes, gently turn them with a spoon.
steps.look: The discs swell to roughly double their size and float freely in the bubbling syrup; they look spongy.
steps.mistake: Using a small pan so the discs crowd and cannot expand, or simmering gently instead of boiling, so they stay dense.
steps.fix: Use a wide pan and keep the boil vigorous; add a splash of hot water if the syrup reduces too much.

steps.do: Lift out each disc with the slotted spoon, let it cool for a minute, then press it gently between your palms or two spoons to squeeze out the syrup. Drop it straight into the warm saffron milk.
steps.look: The discs shrink a little when squeezed, then drink up the milk like a sponge.
steps.mistake: Pressing so hard that the disc breaks.
steps.fix: Squeeze lightly; they only need the excess syrup out.

steps.do: Let the rasmalai cool to room temperature, then chill at least 4 hours or overnight. Stir in the rose water if using, and serve cold, scattered with pistachios.
steps.look: Soft, plump, pale gold discs swimming in saffron milk.
steps.mistake: Serving after a short soak, when the centres are still sweet with syrup rather than milky.
steps.fix: Give them their full 4 hours; they are better the next day.

science: Milk proteins called caseins are held in tiny bundles that stay dispersed at milk's normal acidity. Adding acid drops the pH towards about 4.6, where the caseins lose their charge and clump together into curds, separating from the whey. Boiling the milk first also brings whey proteins into the curd, giving a softer cheese. Too much acid makes the curd tighten into a rubbery texture. Kneading breaks the curd granules down and smears the milk fat through them, giving a smooth, elastic paste that holds together. In a thin, rapidly boiling syrup, steam forms inside the discs and makes them puff, while the thin syrup does not draw out much water. A heavy syrup would make them dense. Reducing milk concentrates its sugars and proteins, which thickens it slightly.
plating: Serve cold in a shallow glass bowl or small individual bowls: three discs per person, arranged in a triangle, with saffron milk poured around them to half cover. Scatter slivered pistachios and a few saffron threads over the top, and a dried rose petal or two if you have them. Spoon more milk over just before serving so the discs glisten.

pairing.drink: Masala chai or a cardamom coffee; with wine, a light, aromatic sweet white such as a late harvest Riesling suits the saffron and rose.
pairing.brennans: Brandy Milk Punch: the Brennan's brunch classic of brandy, cream, vanilla bean and nutmeg, a sweet spiced milk drink that echoes the cardamom and saffron milk here.

variations: Rasgulla: poach the same discs shaped into balls, and serve them in their syrup instead of the milk.
Mango rasmalai: stir 1/2 cup (120 g) mango pulp into the cooled reduced milk.
Quick version: soak shop bought rasgullas, squeezed, in the saffron milk for 4 hours.
safety: Keep the finished rasmalai refrigerated and eat within 2 days; it is a fresh dairy dessert.
Boiling syrup and milk can scald: use a deep pan and slide the discs in gently.

title: Kuih Talam Pandan
summary: A two layer steamed kuih: a bright green, sweet pandan layer of rice flour and tapioca starch, set by steaming, under a soft, salted coconut layer steamed on top until the two fuse. It teaches setting by steam in layers and the balance of salt against sweet.
equipment: Large steamer, or a wok or wide pot with a rack and a domed lid
Square tin, 8 inches (20 cm), at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep, or a round tin of the same size
Clean tea towel to wrap the lid
Blender
Muslin or a very fine sieve
Two mixing bowls, a whisk and a small saucepan
Fork
Sharp knife, lightly oiled, or a plastic knife

ingredients.note: or 1 tsp (5 ml) pandan extract with green colouring

ingredients.item: Rice flour, for the white layer
Mung bean flour (hoen kwe) or more rice flour
Neutral oil, for the tin and the knife

mise: Start this the day before or in the morning: the kuih needs at least 4 hours to cool before it can be cut.

Blend the pandan leaves with only 3/4 cup (200 ml) of the water until finely shredded. Strain through muslin, squeezing hard, then strain again. Make the juice back up to 2 1/3 cups (550 ml) with the rest of the water.
Oil the tin lightly.
Fill the steamer with water to about 2 inches (5 cm) below the rack and bring to a full boil. Wrap the lid in the tea towel, knotting it on top, away from the flame.

timeline.do: Make the pandan juice; heat the steamer; oil the tin.
Mix and steam the green layer for 25 minutes.
Cook the white layer just until it thickens; pour it on.
Steam 15 minutes more.
Cool completely, at least 4 hours.
Unmould and cut with an oiled knife.

steps.do: Green layer: whisk the 1 cup (120 g) rice flour, the tapioca starch and the sugar in a bowl, then whisk in the pandan juice until smooth and the sugar dissolves. Strain through a fine sieve into a jug.
steps.look: A thin, smooth, bright green liquid with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Leaving lumps of starch, which set as white specks.
steps.fix: Always strain; press through any lumps with a spoon.

steps.do: Set the empty tin in the steamer for 2 minutes to heat it. Stir the green mixture well, as the starch settles fast, and pour it into the hot tin. Cover with the cloth wrapped lid and steam over a full boil for 25 minutes.
steps.look: After 25 minutes, a glossy, firm, deep green surface that springs back when touched and is no longer liquid in the middle.
steps.mistake: Pouring the batter without stirring, so the starch has sunk and the layer sets unevenly, firm below and runny above.
steps.fix: Stir right before pouring. If the centre is still liquid at 25 minutes, steam 5 minutes more.

steps.do: White layer: whisk the 1/3 cup plus 1 tbsp (50 g) rice flour, mung bean flour and salt into the coconut milk until smooth, and strain into the small saucepan. Warm over low heat, stirring constantly, for 3 to 5 minutes until it thickens to the consistency of single cream. Take it off before it boils.
steps.look: A smooth, white, slightly thickened cream that coats the back of a spoon.
steps.mistake: Pouring raw coconut mixture onto the hot green layer, which can split and weep oil, or overcooking it into lumps.
steps.fix: Precook gently; if it starts to lump, whisk hard off the heat and strain.

steps.do: Lightly scratch the surface of the set green layer all over with a fork so the white layer will stick. Pour the white mixture on gently, cover and steam 15 minutes.
steps.look: A smooth, pure white top layer that has set but still has a soft wobble.
steps.mistake: Letting water drip from the lid onto the surface, which pits the top.
steps.fix: Keep the lid wrapped in the cloth; wipe the inside of the lid if needed.

steps.do: Lift the tin out carefully and cool at room temperature for at least 4 hours, uncovered, until completely cold and firm. Do not refrigerate, which hardens it.
steps.look: A firm, springy cake with two clean layers that no longer feels warm underneath.
steps.mistake: Cutting it warm, when it is sticky and the layers smear.
steps.fix: Wait until it is completely cool.

steps.do: Run an oiled knife round the edges and turn it out, or cut it in the tin. Cut into 16 pieces about 2 inches (5 cm) square, oiling and wiping the knife between cuts.
steps.look: Clean squares with a sharp line between a bright green base and a white top.
steps.mistake: Cutting with a dry, sharp metal knife, which drags and tears the layers.
steps.fix: Oil the knife or use a plastic knife, and wipe it clean after each cut.

science: Rice flour and tapioca starch are the structure. When heated in water, starch granules absorb water, swell and burst, thickening the mixture and then setting it into a gel as it cools. Rice flour gives a firm, short gel that cuts cleanly; tapioca adds stretch and shine but too much turns gummy. Steaming cooks the layer evenly at 212°F (100°C) without drying the surface. Precooking the coconut layer gently swells some starch around the fat droplets, so the coconut cream stays emulsified on the hot green layer rather than splitting into oil. Salt in the white layer sharpens and balances the sweetness of the green. Pandan's aroma comes from a compound also found in fragrant rice, which is why blending it in a small volume gives the strongest colour and flavour.
plating: Arrange the squares on a small plate or a banana leaf, two or three per person, set slightly apart and turned so the layers face the guest. They are served at room temperature, as an afternoon sweet with tea. For a party, arrange them in rows on a platter lined with banana leaf, alternating their direction.

pairing.drink: Hot jasmine or pandan tea, or a lightly sweet, floral white such as Moscato: the floral notes meet the pandan and the gentle sweetness matches the kuih.
pairing.brennans: Castello Banfi ‘Florus’ Moscadello di Montalcino 2011: a late harvest Moscato from the Brennan's list with floral sweetness that suits pandan and coconut.

variations: Kuih talam ubi: replace the green layer with grated cassava, sugar and coconut milk steamed until set.
Gula melaka: replace the sugar in the base layer with dark palm sugar for a brown layer under the coconut.
Seri muka: use a base of steamed glutinous rice pressed firm instead of the pandan starch layer.
safety: Steam burns: lift the lid away from you and use oven gloves to take the tin out.
Eat within 2 days at cool room temperature, covered.

title: Nigerian Coconut Candy
summary: Fresh coconut cracked and grated by hand, cooked in a nutmeg sugar syrup until the syrup is heavy, then stirred hard until the sugar crystallises into a dry, white, sandy coat around every strand. It teaches reading sugar stages by eye and by spoon, and the opposite of a brittle: here you stir to make sugar crystallise.
skills: cooking sugar to the right stage
equipment: Hammer or the back of a heavy cleaver, and a screwdriver or skewer
Butter knife or coconut tool for prising out the flesh
Vegetable peeler
Box grater (coarse side) or food processor with a grating disc
Wide, heavy frying pan or saucepan, about 11 inches (28 cm)
Wooden spoon or heatproof spatula
Baking tray lined with baking paper
Sugar thermometer (optional)

ingredients.note: shake it: you should hear water sloshing
or the coconut's own water made up with tap water

mise: Open the coconut: find the softest of the three eyes and pierce it with a screwdriver or skewer; drain the water into a glass and keep it.
Hold the coconut in a folded towel in one hand over a bowl and tap firmly all round its middle with the back of the cleaver or a hammer, turning it, until it cracks open into two halves.

Prise out the white flesh in pieces with the butter knife, sliding it between the flesh and the shell. Peel off the thin brown skin with the peeler for a white candy (leave it for a brown, rustic candy).
Grate the flesh on the coarse side of the grater or with a grating disc. You need about 4 cups (400 g).
Line the tray with baking paper.

timeline.do: Crack, prise, peel and grate the coconut.
Boil the syrup; add the coconut.
Reduce until the spoon leaves a clean track.
Stir constantly as the sugar crystallises.
Spread on the tray to cool and crisp.

steps.do: Put the sugar, water, salt and nutmeg in the wide pan over medium heat and stir until the sugar dissolves. Bring to a boil and boil 2 minutes without stirring.
steps.look: A clear syrup with even, small bubbles; no grains of sugar left at the bottom.
steps.mistake: Letting undissolved sugar cling to the pan sides, which can make the syrup crystallise early.
steps.fix: Wash the sides down with a wet pastry brush.

steps.do: Stir in the grated coconut until every strand is coated. Cook over medium heat for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring every minute or so, as the syrup bubbles and reduces.
steps.look: At first the coconut swims in thin syrup; gradually the bubbles become larger and slower and the syrup thickens.
steps.mistake: Turning the heat to high to speed it up, so the syrup caramelises and browns before the water has cooked off.
steps.fix: Keep medium heat; colour should stay white or barely cream.

steps.do: Test: draw the spoon across the base of the pan. When it leaves a clean track that stays open for 2 seconds and the syrup is heavy and glossy, at about 235 to 240°F (113 to 116°C), the syrup has reached the soft ball stage and is ready to crystallise.
steps.look: A sticky, glossy glaze that clings to the coconut; the track across the pan base stays clear.
steps.mistake: Stopping too early, when there is still too much water for the sugar to crystallise.
steps.fix: Keep cooking and test every minute. A drop of syrup in cold water should form a soft ball.

steps.do: Add the vanilla, then stir constantly and vigorously, scraping the pan, for 3 to 6 minutes. The syrup will turn cloudy, then dry, then break into white, sandy grains that coat the coconut.
steps.look: The shine disappears; the mixture turns opaque white and looks frosted, then becomes loose and crumbly with dry sugar crystals clinging to each strand.
steps.mistake: Giving up when it looks cloudy, or stopping stirring, so it sets into a sticky toffee.
steps.fix: Keep stirring hard; agitation is what makes the crystals form. If it stays glossy, cook 2 minutes more and stir again.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat while the grains still look faintly moist. Tip onto the lined tray and spread in a thin layer with the spoon. Leave 30 minutes to cool and crisp, breaking up any large clumps as it cools.
steps.look: White, frosted, crunchy clusters of coconut that break apart easily.
steps.mistake: Cooking on past this point, so the sugar melts again and caramelises into a brown, sticky mass.
steps.fix: Pull it off a little early; it dries further as it cools.

steps.do: Store in an airtight jar for up to 1 week, and serve in small handfuls.
steps.look: Crisp, dry, white candy that does not stick together.
steps.mistake: Storing it in a humid place uncovered, where it softens.
steps.fix: Keep it sealed; re-crisp in a 250°F (120°C) oven for 5 minutes if it softens.

science: As sugar syrup boils, water evaporates and the concentration of sugar rises, which raises the boiling point; temperature is therefore a measure of how much water remains. At about 235 to 240°F (113 to 116°C) the syrup is supersaturated: it holds more dissolved sugar than it can keep once it cools. A brittle or caramel is never stirred at this stage so the sugar cools into a smooth glass. Here, vigorous stirring creates seed crystals, and the extra sugar comes out of solution all at once as fine crystals, coating the coconut in a dry, white crust. That crystalline coat protects the coconut from humidity, which is why the candy stays crunchy. If you keep heating, the crystals melt again and the sugar begins to caramelise.
plating: Pile the candy loosely in a small bowl or on a plate lined with a square of banana leaf or paper, so the clusters stay crisp and do not compress. It is sold in small paper or plastic packets on Nigerian streets; for a dinner, serve a small heap beside coffee, or crumble it over vanilla ice cream.

pairing.drink: A milky coffee or a creamy liqueur: smooth, rich flavours soften the intense sweetness.
pairing.brennans: Floating in South Africa: the Brennan's dessert cocktail of Amarula, an African cream liqueur, with vanilla ice cream and root beer, a creamy partner for a West African sweet.

variations: Brown coconut candy: leave the brown skin on and cook the sugar a little further to a pale caramel before the coconut goes in; it will set as a toffee rather than crystallising.
Ginger coconut candy: add 1 tsp (5 g) finely grated ginger with the coconut.
Coloured candy: add a drop of food colouring to the syrup, as is often done for parties.
safety: Cracking a coconut takes force: hold it in a towel, keep your fingers clear of the strike and work over a bowl.
Boiling sugar syrup causes severe burns: keep children away, use a long spoon and do not taste it from the pan.

title: Suspiro a la Limeña
summary: Lima's sigh: a manjar blanco of condensed and evaporated milk reduced to the colour of wet sand and enriched with yolks, set in glasses under an Italian meringue made with a port syrup and dusted with cinnamon. It pairs a slow milk reduction with the cooked meringue you learnt in the semifreddo, this time flavoured with wine.
skills: a manjar blanco of reduced milks
an Italian meringue with port syrup
equipment: Heavy saucepan of about 3 quarts (3 litres)
Flat edged heatproof spatula
Small heavy saucepan for the port syrup
Sugar or digital probe thermometer
Stand mixer or hand mixer, with a clean, grease free bowl
Piping bag fitted with a large star nozzle, about 1/2 inch (1.2 cm)
Four glasses or small bowls of about 3/4 cup (180 ml)
Small bowl, whisk and a fine sieve

ingredients.item: Egg whites, large, at room temperature

mise: Separate the eggs; keep yolks and whites in separate bowls, the whites free of any yolk.
Wipe the mixer bowl and whisk with a little vinegar or lemon on paper to remove any grease.
Fit the piping bag with the star nozzle and stand it in a tall glass.
Set out the glasses on a tray.

timeline.do: Reduce the milks to manjar blanco, 30 to 40 minutes.
Temper in the yolks; fill the glasses; chill at least 3 hours.
Boil the port syrup to 240°F (116°C); whip the meringue.
Pipe the meringue onto the cold manjar; dust with cinnamon.
Serve.

steps.do: Pour the evaporated and condensed milk into the heavy saucepan and bring to a simmer over medium heat. Cook for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring and scraping the whole base with the flat spatula without stopping for more than 30 seconds, until it thickens and turns the colour of wet sand.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, light caramel coloured cream; when you draw the spatula across the base, the track stays open for a second before closing.
steps.mistake: Stopping stirring, so the milk sugars scorch on the base and leave brown flecks and a bitter taste.
steps.fix: Scrape edge to edge constantly. If it catches, pour into a clean pan without scraping the burnt layer and carry on over lower heat.

steps.do: Whisk the yolks and vanilla in the small bowl. Whisk in a ladle of the hot manjar, a little at a time, then pour the warmed yolks back into the pan, stirring. Cook over low heat for 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until it coats the spatula thickly. Do not let it boil.
steps.look: A smooth, thicker, glossy cream with no threads of egg.
steps.mistake: Adding yolks straight into the hot milk, so they scramble into threads.
steps.fix: Temper slowly; if threads form, pass the manjar through a sieve.

steps.do: Divide the hot manjar between the glasses, filling each about two thirds full. Tap the glasses on the worktop to level it, cool 20 minutes, then refrigerate at least 3 hours until cold and set.
steps.look: A smooth, level, set cream that barely moves when the glass is tilted.
steps.mistake: Topping warm manjar with meringue, which melts and slides.
steps.fix: Chill it fully first.

steps.do: Port syrup: put the port and sugar in the small saucepan, stir once to dissolve over medium heat, then boil without stirring until it reaches 240°F (116°C), about 5 to 7 minutes. When it reaches 230°F (110°C), start whipping the whites with the salt to soft peaks.
steps.look: Thick, dark red syrup with large, slow bubbles; a drop in cold water forms a soft ball. The whites hold soft peaks.
steps.mistake: Pulling the syrup below 235°F (113°C), which gives a weak meringue that weeps in the glass.
steps.fix: Use the thermometer; tilt the pan so the probe sits in the syrup in a small pan.

steps.do: With the mixer on medium, pour the hot syrup in a thin, steady stream down the side of the bowl, avoiding the whisk. Turn to high and whip 6 to 8 minutes until the meringue is glossy, holds stiff peaks and the bowl is only lukewarm.
steps.look: A shiny, pale pink, thick meringue that holds a stiff peak with a slight curl; it smells of port.
steps.mistake: Stopping while the meringue is still warm, so it is too soft to pipe.
steps.fix: Keep whipping until the bowl feels barely warm to the touch.

steps.do: Fill the piping bag with meringue. Pipe a swirl over each glass of cold manjar, starting at the outer edge and spiralling up to a peak about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) high. Dust lightly with cinnamon through a fine sieve.
steps.look: A tall, neat, glossy swirl of pink meringue with a light brown dust of cinnamon.
steps.mistake: Squeezing the bag from the middle, so the meringue comes out unevenly.
steps.fix: Twist the top of the bag closed and squeeze from the top with one hand, guiding the nozzle with the other.

steps.do: Serve within 2 hours of piping, or keep the finished glasses in the fridge, uncovered, for up to 4 hours before serving.
steps.look: The meringue holds its shape without weeping.
steps.mistake: Leaving it overnight, when the meringue can soften and weep.
steps.fix: Pipe the meringue close to serving; the manjar can be made 2 days ahead.

science: Manjar blanco is milk concentrated by evaporation. As water boils off, lactose and milk proteins become more concentrated and react through Maillard browning, turning the milk tan and giving it a caramel flavour. The pan base runs far hotter than the liquid above it, so constant scraping prevents scorching. Tempering the yolks raises their temperature gradually so they thicken the cream without curdling. In the meringue, the port syrup boiled to 240°F (116°C) holds so little water that, poured into the whipping whites, it partly cooks them and coats the air bubbles in a thick sugar film, creating a dense, stable, glossy foam. Below about 235°F (113°C) there is too much water, and the meringue weeps.
plating: Serve in clear glasses so the two layers show: a sandy gold base and a tall pink-white swirl. Set each glass on a small saucer with a teaspoon at the side. A single dusting of cinnamon is the traditional finish; for a dinner party, add a thin strip of orange zest leaning against the meringue.

pairing.drink: A tawny port, served lightly chilled, or a strong espresso: port echoes the meringue and its nuttiness suits the caramel milk.
pairing.brennans: Niepoort Colheita Port 1997 (375 ml): a tawny, single harvest port from the Brennan's list whose caramel and nut notes match manjar blanco and the port meringue.

variations: Suspiro de lúcuma: stir 1/2 cup (120 g) lúcuma pulp into the manjar after the yolks.
Torched meringue: brown the piped meringue lightly with a blowtorch.
Pisco meringue: use 2 tbsp (30 ml) pisco and 2 tbsp (30 ml) water in place of the port.
safety: The manjar yolks are cooked; the meringue whites are heated by the hot syrup but may not reach 160°F (71°C), so use pasteurised whites for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or unwell.
Boiling sugar syrup causes severe burns; pour carefully and keep children away.

title: Bread Pudding Soufflé with Whiskey Sauce
summary: A rich New Orleans bread pudding of French bread, custard, cinnamon and raisins, baked, then broken up and folded into a meringue and raised in ramekins into a soufflé, served with a hot whiskey sauce poured into its centre at the table. It teaches the soufflé rise on a familiar base, and it is the dessert family closest to the one on the Brennan's menu.
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) square baking dish for the bread pudding
Four ramekins of about 1 cup (240 ml), straight sided
Pastry brush
Stand mixer or hand mixer, with a clean, grease free bowl
Large mixing bowl and a whisk
Large flexible spatula
Small heavy saucepan for the sauce
Baking tray
Instant read thermometer

ingredients.item: Day old French bread, in 1 inch (2.5 cm) cubes
ingredients.note: a light, airy New Orleans style loaf is best

ingredients.item: Egg whites, large, at room temperature
Soft butter and sugar, for the ramekins
Double or heavy cream, for the sauce
Light brown sugar, for the sauce
Cornflour mixed with 1 tbsp (15 ml) water

mise: Make the bread pudding first; it can be made a day ahead and chilled. Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) and butter the square dish.
Soak the raisins in the bourbon.
Brush the ramekins with soft butter in upward strokes from base to rim, then coat with sugar, tipping out the excess. Chill them.
Separate the eggs for the soufflé, keeping the whites spotless; wipe the mixer bowl with vinegar on paper.
Mix the cornflour with the water for the sauce.

timeline.do: Soak the bread in custard 20 minutes; bake the pudding 35 to 40 minutes.
Cool the pudding; prepare the ramekins.
Make the whiskey sauce and keep it warm.
Raise the oven to 375°F (190°C); break up the pudding; whip and fold the meringue.
Bake the soufflés 20 to 25 minutes without opening the door.
Dust, carry to the table, pour the sauce into the centre.

steps.do: Bread pudding: whisk the milk, 1/2 cup (120 ml) cream, 2 eggs, 1/2 cup (100 g) sugar, melted butter, vanilla, cinnamon and nutmeg in the large bowl. Add the bread and soaked raisins with their bourbon, press down and soak 20 minutes, turning once.
steps.look: Bread that has drunk up the custard and is soft all the way through when squeezed; little liquid left in the bowl.
steps.mistake: Using fresh bread, which turns to mush, or soaking too briefly, leaving dry centres.
steps.fix: Use day old bread; if the bread is very dry, soak a little longer and press it under the custard.

steps.do: Pour into the buttered dish and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 35 to 40 minutes, until puffed, golden and set in the centre, a knife comes out clean and the centre reads 160°F (71°C) or more.
steps.look: Golden brown and crisp at the edges, firm in the middle, smelling of cinnamon and vanilla.
steps.mistake: Taking it out while the centre is still liquid custard.
steps.fix: Check with the thermometer; bake 5 minutes more if needed. Cool at least 30 minutes.

steps.do: Whiskey sauce: heat the 1 cup (240 ml) cream and the brown sugar in the small saucepan until simmering. Whisk in the cornflour slurry and simmer 1 minute, whisking, until lightly thickened. Off the heat, stir in the whiskey and butter. Keep warm.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, light caramel coloured sauce that coats a spoon; it smells of whiskey and vanilla.
steps.mistake: Boiling the sauce hard after adding the whiskey, which drives off its flavour, or adding cornflour without whisking, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Add the whiskey off the heat; strain the sauce if lumps form.

steps.do: Raise the oven to 375°F (190°C) and put the baking tray in to heat. Weigh out about 2 cups (300 g) of the cooled bread pudding into a bowl and break it up with a fork into a coarse, moist paste.
steps.look: A rough, soft mixture with no large lumps of bread.
steps.mistake: Using hot pudding, which melts the meringue.
steps.fix: Cool it to room temperature first; chill it if made ahead, then let it warm 20 minutes.

steps.do: Whip the 4 egg whites with the cream of tartar on medium speed until foamy, then add the 1/4 cup (50 g) sugar gradually and whip on high until the meringue holds firm, glossy peaks that stand straight with just the tip bending.
steps.look: A smooth, shiny meringue; the peaks hold their shape; the bowl can be tipped without the whites sliding.
steps.mistake: Over whipping until dry and grainy, which makes folding hard and the soufflé crack.
steps.fix: Stop at glossy firm peaks. Grainy whites can be partly rescued by whisking in a fresh white by hand.

steps.do: Stir a quarter of the meringue into the pudding to lighten it, then fold in the rest gently in two additions, stopping as soon as no white streaks remain. Spoon into the ramekins to the rim, level with a palette knife and run your thumb round the inside edge to make a shallow groove.
steps.look: Light, airy mixture filling the ramekins to the rim with a clean edge.
steps.mistake: Overfilling or leaving mixture on the rim, which stops the soufflé climbing straight.
steps.fix: Level flat and wipe the rims clean; the groove helps it rise straight like a hat.

steps.do: Set the ramekins on the hot tray and bake 20 to 25 minutes without opening the door, until risen about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) above the rim, golden on top and just set with a slight wobble.
steps.look: Tall, straight sided soufflés with golden tops that quiver when the tray is moved.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven door early, so the soufflés collapse.
steps.fix: Use the oven light. If one leans, the ramekin was unevenly buttered; brush upwards next time.

steps.do: Dust with icing sugar and serve immediately. At the table, break a hole in the centre of each soufflé with a spoon and pour in 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) of the warm whiskey sauce.
steps.look: A golden, airy soufflé that sighs as the sauce goes into its centre.
steps.mistake: Leaving them on the counter while you finish other things, so they sink.
steps.fix: A soufflé waits for nobody: have the guests seated before it comes out.

science: A soufflé rises because air beaten into egg whites expands in the oven heat, and the water in the mixture turns to steam and expands the bubbles further. The egg white proteins, unfolded by whipping, set around the bubbles as they heat, fixing the structure. Cream of tartar is an acid that stabilises the foam so it holds up to folding. The bread pudding base supplies flavour and body; folding gently keeps as many bubbles as possible. Buttered, sugared ramekins give the rising mixture something to grip and climb. Once out of the oven, the gases cool and contract, so a soufflé begins to fall within minutes. The whiskey sauce is thickened with cornflour, whose starch granules swell in the hot cream.
plating: Set each ramekin on a small plate lined with a folded napkin, which stops it sliding and protects the table from the heat. Dust the tops with icing sugar through a fine sieve. Bring the whiskey sauce in a small warm jug. At the table, the server breaks the top with a spoon and pours the sauce into the centre, as is done in New Orleans restaurants.

pairing.drink: A small glass of bourbon, a sweet Madeira or a late harvest white: caramel and spice for the whiskey sauce and cinnamon.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans Bread Pudding: the Brennan's dessert of warm bread pudding with whiskey caramel and buttermilk ice cream; after this soufflé you can explain to a guest how a bread pudding custard sets and why the whiskey sauce matters.

variations: Classic bread pudding: serve the baked pudding warm in squares with the whiskey sauce, without making the soufflé.
Praline: fold 1/4 cup (30 g) chopped toasted pecans into the pudding before baking.
Chocolate: melt 2 oz (55 g) dark chocolate into the custard for the bread pudding.
safety: The bread pudding custard must reach 160°F (71°C) in the centre; the soufflé whites are fully cooked in the oven.
The ramekins come out at about 375°F (190°C): serve them on plates with a napkin and warn guests.
Refrigerate leftover bread pudding within 2 hours and use within 3 days.

title: Tarte au Citron
summary: A pâte sucrée shell, blind baked to an even golden biscuit, filled with a sharp lemon cream cooked over water and finished with cold butter, then set until it slices clean with a mirror top. It demands a perfect sweet pastry and a smooth, sharp filling, and it is the French ancestor of the Lemon Tart on the Brennan's dessert list.
skills: blind baking to a golden shell
a lemon curd or baked lemon custard
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) tart ring or loose based tart tin, about 3/4 inch (2 cm) deep
Food processor or a mixing bowl and pastry scraper
Rolling pin and two sheets of baking paper
Baking beans or dried beans, and a sheet of baking paper
Pastry brush
Heatproof bowl over a pan of simmering water
Balloon whisk, fine sieve and microplane
Instant read thermometer
Stick blender (optional)
Long thin knife and a jug of hot water

ingredients.note: keep 1 tsp (5 ml) for sealing the shell
for zest; you need 1/2 cup (120 ml) juice, about 3 to 4 lemons

mise: Pâte sucrée: pulse the flour, icing sugar, almonds and salt in the processor; add the cold butter and pulse until it looks like fine breadcrumbs. Add the beaten egg, keeping back 1 tsp (5 ml), and pulse just until the dough clumps. Press into a flat disc, wrap and chill 1 hour.
Roll the dough between two sheets of baking paper to 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick and a circle about 11 inches (28 cm) across. Chill 10 minutes if soft.

Line the ring or tin: lift the pastry in, ease it into the corners without stretching, press it against the sides and trim the top with a knife, leaving it level with the rim. Prick the base with a fork and chill 30 minutes until firm.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a shelf in the middle.
Zest the lemons finely onto the sugar; juice them and strain the juice.

timeline.do: Make and chill the pastry dough.
Roll, line and chill the tin.
Blind bake 20 minutes with beans, 10 to 15 minutes without; seal with egg.
Make the lemon cream; blend in the butter.
Fill the cooled shell; chill at least 4 hours.
Slice with a hot knife and serve.

steps.do: Blind bake: line the chilled pastry with crumpled baking paper and fill to the top with baking beans, pushing them into the corners. Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 20 minutes. Lift out the paper and beans and bake 10 to 15 minutes more until the base is dry and evenly golden.
steps.look: An even, golden biscuit colour across the base and sides; the base looks dry and sandy, not shiny or pale.
steps.mistake: Pulling the shell when it is pale, so it softens under the filling and tastes raw.
steps.fix: Bake until golden all over; protect the rim with a strip of foil if it browns faster than the base.

steps.do: Brush the inside of the hot shell with the reserved 1 tsp (5 ml) beaten egg and return to the oven for 2 minutes to set it. Cool completely on a rack.
steps.look: A thin, shiny seal on the base that has set and is no longer wet.
steps.mistake: Skipping the seal, so the lemon cream slowly softens the pastry.
steps.fix: Brush thinly and bake 2 minutes; patch any small cracks with a scrap of raw dough pressed in, then bake 2 minutes more.

steps.do: Lemon cream: rub the zest into the sugar with your fingertips for 1 minute until damp and fragrant. Whisk in the lemon juice, eggs and yolk in the heatproof bowl. Set over barely simmering water and whisk constantly for 8 to 12 minutes until it reaches 180°F (82°C).
steps.look: The mixture thickens from a thin liquid to a cream that coats the whisk and leaves a trail on its surface; it smells intensely of lemon.
steps.mistake: Letting it get too hot, so the eggs scramble into lumps and the cream tastes eggy.
steps.fix: Keep the water at a bare simmer and whisk without stopping; strain immediately when it reaches 180°F (82°C).

steps.do: Strain the cream through the fine sieve into a clean bowl or jug, pressing the zest. Let it cool to about 140°F (60°C), 5 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally.
steps.look: A smooth, bright yellow cream, still warm.
steps.mistake: Adding the butter while the cream is too hot, so the butter melts into oil instead of emulsifying.
steps.fix: Wait until it reads 140°F (60°C), warm to the touch but no longer hot.

steps.do: Add the cold butter a few cubes at a time, blending with the stick blender (keeping the head submerged to avoid bubbles) or whisking hard, until all the butter is incorporated.
steps.look: A silky, pale, glossy, thick cream like soft mayonnaise; no visible butter or oil.
steps.mistake: Lifting the blender head out, which whips in air bubbles that spoil the smooth top.
steps.fix: Keep the blender at the bottom; tap the jug to bring bubbles to the surface and pop them with a pin.

steps.do: Pour the cream into the cooled shell, filling it to the rim. Tap the tin gently on the worktop to level it. Chill uncovered for at least 4 hours, until set.
steps.look: A mirror flat, glossy yellow surface level with the pastry rim.
steps.mistake: Covering the tart while warm, so condensation drips onto the surface.
steps.fix: Chill it uncovered; cover loosely only once it is cold and set.

steps.do: Remove the ring or tin. Cut with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between each slice, pressing straight down through the pastry rather than sawing.
steps.look: Clean slices with a sharp, glossy cut face and a crisp, unbroken pastry edge.
steps.mistake: Sawing through the pastry, which shatters it and drags the cream.
steps.fix: Press down firmly through the cream, then press through the base with one clean push.

science: Pâte sucrée is a short pastry: the butter coats the flour particles and limits gluten formation, and icing sugar dissolves easily and makes the texture fine and crumbly. Chilling firms the butter so the pastry holds its shape, and blind baking sets and dries the shell before a wet filling arrives. The lemon cream is a custard thickened by eggs; heated to 180°F (82°C), the proteins set into a smooth gel, and the sugar and acid both raise the setting temperature, giving more margin than a plain custard. Rubbing zest into sugar draws out its fragrant oils, which juice does not contain. Blending butter into the warm cream disperses the fat into tiny droplets, an emulsion that gives a silky texture and helps it set firm when cold.
plating: Lay a slice on a flat white plate, point towards the guest, the glossy top catching the light. Add a small quenelle of crème fraîche beside it and two or three raspberries, or a few strands of candied lemon zest on the tart. Dust a little icing sugar only over the pastry edge, never the cream. Serve it cool but not fridge cold, after 15 minutes out.

pairing.drink: A sweet wine with high acidity, such as a late harvest Riesling or a Sauternes, or a demi sec Champagne: the wine's acidity must match the lemon's.
pairing.brennans: Lemon Tart: the Brennan's dessert list builds its lemon tart from yuzu mousse, lemon jelly, sweet pastry crumb and toasted meringue; having made the classic French tart, you can explain each of its parts to a guest.

variations: Tarte au citron meringuée: pipe Italian meringue (as in the semifreddo) over the set tart and brown it with a blowtorch.
Lime tart: use lime zest and juice in place of lemon.
Baked lemon tart: whisk 3 eggs, 1/2 cup (100 g) sugar, 1/2 cup (120 ml) lemon juice and 1/2 cup (120 ml) cream and bake in the shell at 300°F (150°C) for 25 to 30 minutes until barely set.
safety: The lemon cream eggs are cooked to 180°F (82°C), past the 160°F (71°C) that makes them safe.
Keep the tart refrigerated and eat within 3 days.

title: Bakewell Tart
summary: A sweet shortcrust case, blind baked, spread with raspberry jam and filled with frangipane, the almond cream behind many French tarts, then scattered with flaked almonds and baked until risen and golden. It sets two doughs with opposite rules in one tin: cold, barely worked pastry and a soft butter batter creamed full of air.
skills: a feathered icing or flaked almonds
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) loose based fluted tart tin, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep
Mixing bowls, pastry scraper and a fork
Rolling pin and baking paper
Baking beans
Stand mixer or hand mixer, or a wooden spoon and strong arm
Offset palette knife or the back of a spoon
Baking tray
Wire rack

ingredients.item: Raspberry jam, good quality, with seeds
Eggs, large, at room temperature, beaten

mise: Pastry: rub the cold butter into the flour, icing sugar and salt with your fingertips (or pulse in a processor) until it looks like coarse breadcrumbs. Mix the yolk with 1 tbsp (15 ml) ice water, add it and bring together with a fork, adding more water a few drops at a time only if dry. Press into a disc, wrap and chill 1 hour.
Take the butter and eggs for the frangipane out of the fridge 1 hour ahead so they are at room temperature.
Roll the pastry between baking paper to 1/8 inch (3 mm) and line the tin, pressing into the flutes; leave a little overhang. Prick the base and chill 30 minutes.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a baking tray on the middle shelf.

timeline.do: Make and chill the pastry; bring frangipane ingredients to room temperature.
Roll, line and chill the tin; oven on.
Blind bake 15 minutes with beans, 8 to 10 minutes without.
Make the frangipane; spread jam; fill; bake 30 to 35 minutes at 340°F (170°C).
Cool at least 1 hour.
Dust with icing sugar and slice.

steps.do: Blind bake: line the chilled case with crumpled baking paper, fill with baking beans and bake on the hot tray at 375°F (190°C) for 15 minutes. Remove the paper and beans and bake 8 to 10 minutes more until the base is dry and pale biscuit coloured. Trim the overhang flush with a sharp knife while warm.
steps.look: A dry, sandy looking base with no shiny or raw patches; the edges lightly golden.
steps.mistake: Skipping the blind bake, so the jam and frangipane leave a soggy, raw base.
steps.fix: Always blind bake; if the base puffs up, press it down gently with a clean cloth while hot.

steps.do: Lower the oven to 340°F (170°C). Frangipane: beat the soft butter and caster sugar for 3 to 4 minutes until pale and fluffy. Add the beaten eggs a little at a time, beating well after each addition.
steps.look: A pale, light, smooth batter that holds soft peaks on the beaters, no curdled look.
steps.mistake: Using cold eggs or adding them too quickly, so the mixture curdles and splits.
steps.fix: If it starts to curdle, beat in a spoonful of the ground almonds with the next addition of egg.

steps.do: Fold in the ground almonds, the 2 1/2 tbsp (20 g) flour and the almond extract until just combined.
steps.look: A thick, spreadable, creamy batter.
steps.mistake: Beating hard after the almonds, which makes the frangipane greasy as the almond oils are released.
steps.fix: Fold gently and stop as soon as it is even.

steps.do: Spread the jam over the base of the cooled case in a thin, even layer, leaving a 1/2 inch (1 cm) border. Spoon the frangipane over it in dollops, then spread gently from the centre outwards with the palette knife so you do not drag the jam up. Level the top and scatter the flaked almonds.
steps.look: A smooth, level frangipane surface covering the jam completely, dotted with almonds.
steps.mistake: Spreading jam right to the edge, so it bubbles up and burns on the rim.
steps.fix: Leave a border; the frangipane seals the jam in.

steps.do: Bake at 340°F (170°C) for 30 to 35 minutes until risen, golden brown and springy in the centre, and a skewer comes out clean of raw batter (a little jam is fine).
steps.look: A domed, golden top with toasted almonds; the centre springs back when pressed lightly.
steps.mistake: Taking it out too soon, so the middle sinks and is wet.
steps.fix: If the top browns before the centre is set, lay a sheet of foil loosely over it and bake 5 to 10 minutes more.

steps.do: Cool in the tin on a rack for at least 1 hour, then remove the ring, dust lightly with icing sugar and cut into slices with a sharp knife.
steps.look: A sliced cross section showing crisp pastry, a ribbon of red jam and a moist, golden almond sponge.
steps.mistake: Slicing hot, so the frangipane crumbles and the jam runs.
steps.fix: Let it cool, or at least set for 30 minutes if serving warm.

science: Shortcrust stays tender because the cold butter coats the flour particles and keeps water from forming long gluten strands; very little working means very little gluten. Chilling firms the butter so the pastry holds its shape in the oven, and blind baking sets the base before a moist filling arrives. Frangipane works the other way: creaming soft butter with sugar traps millions of tiny air bubbles, which expand in the oven and lighten the almond cream. Eggs at room temperature emulsify into the creamed butter; cold eggs chill the butter so it cannot hold the water, and the batter splits, baking as a greasy layer. Ground almonds give moisture, fat and a fine crumb, while a little flour gives structure.
plating: Serve a slice slightly warm or at room temperature on a dessert plate, the pointed end towards the guest, the layers facing out. Add a spoon of clotted cream, crème fraîche or a small jug of warm custard, as is traditional in Britain. A few fresh raspberries on the side echo the jam.

pairing.drink: A sweet, fresh German Riesling or a cup of English tea: the acidity of Riesling lifts the almond and jam, and its sweetness matches the tart.
pairing.brennans: Hexamer ‘Meddersheimer Rheingrafenberg’ Riesling Spätlese 2010: a gently sweet, bright Riesling from the Brennan's list, fresh enough for raspberry jam and almond cream.

variations: Iced Bakewell: leave off the flaked almonds; once cool, cover with an icing of 1 cup (120 g) icing sugar mixed with 1 to 2 tbsp (15 to 30 ml) water and feather with lines of pink icing dragged through with a cocktail stick.
Cherry Bakewell: use cherry jam and top each slice with a glacé cherry on the icing.
Apricot Bakewell: use apricot jam and press a few halved ripe apricots, cut side up, into the frangipane before baking; add 5 to 10 minutes to the bake.
safety: The frangipane eggs are fully cooked once the centre is set and springs back.
Store at cool room temperature, covered, and eat within 3 days.

title: Boston Cream Pie
summary: A tender hot milk sponge split in two and filled with a thick vanilla crème pâtissière, cooked until it boils, then covered with a shining chocolate ganache that drips down the sides. It teaches the starch-thickened custard that every pastry kitchen runs on and the ganache, chocolate's own emulsion.
skills: a genoise or hot milk sponge
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) round cake tin, 2 inches (5 cm) deep
Stand mixer or hand mixer
Two medium saucepans and a whisk
Heatproof bowl and a fine sieve
Cling film
Long serrated knife
Cake board or serving plate, wire rack and a tray
Offset palette knife

ingredients.item: Whole milk, for the pastry cream
Vanilla pod, split, or vanilla extract
Caster sugar, for the pastry cream
Unsalted butter, for the pastry cream
Dark chocolate, 60 to 70 percent cocoa, chopped
Golden syrup or light corn syrup

mise: Make the pastry cream first; it needs at least 2 hours to chill.
Grease the cake tin and line the base with baking paper. Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
Sift the flour, baking powder and salt together for the sponge.
Chop the chocolate finely and put it in the heatproof bowl.

timeline.do: Make the pastry cream; chill it covered at least 2 hours.
Make and bake the hot milk sponge, 25 to 30 minutes.
Cool the sponge completely.
Split the sponge and fill with pastry cream.
Make the ganache; pour it over; chill 1 hour.
Slice with a hot knife and serve.

steps.do: Pastry cream: heat the milk with the vanilla pod (scraped) in a saucepan until steaming and small bubbles appear at the edge. Meanwhile whisk the yolks, sugar and cornflour in a bowl until smooth and pale.
steps.look: Hot milk just below a simmer; a thick, pale yellow yolk paste with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Letting the milk boil over while you whisk.
steps.fix: Heat it over medium heat and take it off as soon as it steams.

steps.do: Temper: pour a third of the hot milk onto the yolks in a thin stream, whisking constantly. Pour the warmed yolk mixture back into the saucepan with the rest of the milk.
steps.look: A smooth, warm, pale yellow liquid with no cooked bits of egg.
steps.mistake: Pouring the yolks into the hot milk, so they scramble.
steps.fix: Always add hot to cold slowly while whisking; strain if any threads appear.

steps.do: Cook over medium heat, whisking constantly and reaching into the corners, until the cream thickens and then BOILS. Keep it bubbling for a full 1 minute while whisking hard.
steps.look: First it thickens suddenly and looks lumpy, then it becomes smooth and glossy as you whisk; big, slow bubbles break the surface.
steps.mistake: Stopping as soon as it thickens, before it boils, so an enzyme in the yolk later thins the cream into a runny mess.
steps.fix: Make sure it boils for 1 minute; the starch protects the yolks from scrambling.

steps.do: Take off the heat, remove the vanilla pod and whisk in the butter (and vanilla extract if using). Pass through the sieve into a clean bowl, press cling film onto the surface and chill at least 2 hours.
steps.look: A thick, smooth, glossy custard that holds its shape on a spoon.
steps.mistake: Leaving it uncovered, so a rubbery skin forms on top.
steps.fix: Press the film directly onto the surface.

steps.do: Sponge: beat the eggs and sugar on high for 4 to 5 minutes until thick, pale and doubled. Meanwhile heat the milk and butter until the butter melts and the milk is hot, about 180°F (82°C). Fold the flour into the eggs in two additions, then pour in the hot milk and vanilla and fold gently until smooth.
steps.look: A thin, smooth, pourable batter.
steps.mistake: Beating hard after adding the flour, which knocks out the air and toughens the sponge.
steps.fix: Fold gently with a spatula, just until no flour shows.

steps.do: Pour into the tin and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 25 to 30 minutes until golden, springy and a skewer comes out clean. Cool 10 minutes in the tin, then turn out onto the rack and cool completely.
steps.look: An evenly golden, flat topped sponge that springs back when touched and has shrunk slightly from the sides.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven in the first 15 minutes, so the sponge sinks.
steps.fix: Wait until 20 minutes before checking.

steps.do: Split the cooled sponge horizontally into two even layers with the serrated knife, turning the cake as you cut. Put the bottom layer on the plate, whisk the cold pastry cream briefly until smooth and spread it 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick, stopping 1/2 inch (1 cm) from the edge. Set the top layer on, cut side down.
steps.look: Two even layers with a thick ribbon of custard between them that bulges just to the edge.
steps.mistake: Spreading warm or runny cream, which squeezes out under the top layer.
steps.fix: Use well chilled pastry cream; chill the filled cake 20 minutes before glazing.

steps.do: Ganache: heat the cream and syrup until just simmering and pour over the chopped chocolate. Leave 2 minutes, then stir slowly from the centre outwards until smooth and glossy. Cool 5 minutes, then pour over the top of the cake, nudging it to the edge with the palette knife so it drips down the sides. Chill 1 hour to set.
steps.look: A shining dark glaze that flows over the top and drips in neat drops down the sides.
steps.mistake: Stirring hot ganache vigorously, which beats in air and dulls it, or pouring it too hot, so it runs off completely.
steps.fix: Stir gently; if it is too thin, let it cool a few minutes more until it coats a spoon thickly.

science: Crème pâtissière is thickened by both egg and starch. The starch granules in the cornflour swell and burst as the mixture boils, thickening it and protecting the egg proteins from curdling, which is why, unlike a plain custard, it can and must boil. Egg yolks contain an enzyme, amylase, that breaks down starch; if the cream is not boiled long enough to destroy it, the custard thins out in the fridge. A hot milk sponge uses the heat of the milk to start dissolving the sugar and setting the batter quickly, giving a fine, tender, moist crumb with the air whipped into the eggs. Ganache is an emulsion of cocoa butter and water from the cream, stabilised by the chocolate's solids; stirring gently from the centre forms the emulsion without trapping air.
plating: Cut a wedge with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry, so the layers stay clean. Lay it on its side on a plate so the custard ribbon and the dark glaze show. Add a few fresh raspberries or a small spoon of softly whipped cream beside it. Serve chilled but not icy, after 10 minutes out of the fridge.

pairing.drink: Strong black coffee or a cold glass of milk; with wine, a tawny port or a sweet sherry suits chocolate and vanilla custard.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: the Brennan's coffee and chicory, bitter and roasted, cuts through chocolate glaze and custard.

variations: Genoise: replace the hot milk sponge with a genoise (as in the Black Forest gâteau) brushed with a little vanilla syrup.
Éclair cake: layer the pastry cream between sheets of baked choux or biscuits and glaze the top.
Coffee cream: dissolve 1 tsp (2 g) instant espresso in the milk for the pastry cream.
safety: The pastry cream boils, so its eggs are fully cooked; cool it quickly and keep it refrigerated.
Keep the finished cake refrigerated and eat within 3 days.

title: Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte
summary: A chocolate genoise split into three layers, each soaked in kirsch syrup and filled with sour cherries and whipped cream stabilised with gelatine, then covered in cream and finished with chocolate shavings and cherries. It teaches splitting a sponge, soaking with syrup and building and finishing a cream layer cake that stands up.
equipment: 7 inch (18 cm) round cake tin, 3 inches (7.5 cm) deep
Stand mixer with whisk
Heatproof bowl over a pan of simmering water
Sieve and a large flexible spatula
Long serrated knife and cocktail sticks for marking layers
Cake board and a turntable if you have one
Offset palette knife and a bench scraper
Piping bag with a large star nozzle
Small saucepan and a pastry brush
Vegetable peeler for the shavings

ingredients.item: Sour or morello cherries in syrup, drained, juice kept
ingredients.note: keep 8 whole cherries for the top
for the syrup and the cream

ingredients.item: Double or whipping cream, very cold
Dark chocolate bar, at room temperature

mise: Grease the tin, line the base with baking paper, and heat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
Sift the flour and cocoa together twice.
Drain the cherries over a bowl and keep the juice; set aside 8 of the best whole cherries for the top.
Kirsch syrup: warm 1/4 cup (60 ml) cherry juice with 2 tbsp (25 g) sugar until dissolved; cool and stir in 1/4 cup (60 ml) kirsch.
Sprinkle the gelatine over the 2 tbsp (30 ml) cold water and leave 5 minutes to swell.
Make chocolate shavings: draw the peeler firmly along the long edge of the bar onto a plate; chill them.

timeline.do: Bake the genoise; cool completely.
Make the cherry filling and kirsch syrup; cool.
Split the sponge into three; whip the stabilised cream.
Soak, fill and stack the layers; coat in cream; pipe and decorate.
Chill at least 4 hours or overnight.
Slice with a hot knife and serve.

steps.do: Genoise: whisk the eggs and 1/2 cup (100 g) sugar in the heatproof bowl over simmering water until warm to the touch, about 104°F (40°C). Transfer to the mixer and whip on high for 8 to 10 minutes until tripled, pale and very thick.
steps.look: The ribbon stage: when the whisk is lifted, the mixture falls in a thick ribbon that sits on the surface for 5 seconds before sinking.
steps.mistake: Under whipping, so the sponge is flat and dense.
steps.fix: Keep whipping until a figure of eight drawn with the ribbon stays visible for a few seconds.

steps.do: Sift the flour and cocoa over in three additions, folding gently with the spatula each time. Stir a large spoonful of the batter into the warm melted butter, then fold that mixture back into the batter.
steps.look: A glossy, airy, chocolate batter with no streaks of cocoa or pockets of butter.
steps.mistake: Pouring the butter straight in, which sinks to the bottom and deflates the batter.
steps.fix: Lighten the butter with some batter first, then fold it in quickly.

steps.do: Pour into the tin and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 25 to 30 minutes until risen, springy and a skewer comes out clean. Cool 10 minutes, turn out onto a rack, peel off the paper and cool completely, ideally for several hours or overnight wrapped in film.
steps.look: An evenly risen, flat sponge that springs back when touched and has pulled slightly from the sides.
steps.mistake: Splitting a warm sponge, which tears and crumbles.
steps.fix: A sponge made the day before cuts much more cleanly.

steps.do: Cherry filling: whisk the cornflour into 3/4 cup (180 ml) of the remaining cherry juice with the 2 tbsp (25 g) sugar in the small saucepan. Bring to a boil, whisking, and boil 1 minute until thick and clear. Stir in the drained cherries (minus the 8 for the top) and cool completely.
steps.look: Glossy, deep red cherries in a thick, translucent sauce.
steps.mistake: Using the filling warm, which melts the cream.
steps.fix: Spread it on a plate to cool quickly.

steps.do: Split the sponge into three even layers: mark the height with cocktail sticks around the side, then cut with the serrated knife, turning the cake as you saw gently.
steps.look: Three level discs of even thickness.
steps.mistake: Cutting straight through from one side, so the layers are wedge shaped.
steps.fix: Cut a shallow line all round first, then deepen it as you turn.

steps.do: Stabilised cream: warm the swollen gelatine for 10 to 15 seconds until just melted and clear, then let it cool slightly. Whip the cold cream with the icing sugar and the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) kirsch to soft peaks. With the mixer running, pour in the gelatine in a thin stream and whip to firm, smooth peaks.
steps.look: A smooth, thick cream that holds a firm peak and piped shapes.
steps.mistake: Adding hot gelatine to cold cream, which sets in rubbery strings.
steps.fix: Cool the gelatine until warm, not hot, and add it while whipping; if strings form, pass the cream through a sieve before it sets.

steps.do: Assemble: set the bottom layer on the board and brush generously with a third of the kirsch syrup. Pipe a ring of cream around the edge, spread the cherry filling inside it, then spread a thin layer of cream over the cherries. Add the second layer and repeat. Put the top layer on cut side down and brush with the last of the syrup.
steps.look: An even, straight stack; the cream ring holds the cherries in place without leaking.
steps.mistake: Under soaking, so the sponge is dry, or over soaking so it collapses.
steps.fix: Brush each layer until it is moist but not dripping; the soak should smell clearly of kirsch.

steps.do: Cover the top and sides with a thin layer of cream (the crumb coat), chill 15 minutes, then cover with a thicker final layer and smooth with the palette knife or bench scraper. Pipe 8 rosettes around the top edge, place a cherry on each and press chocolate shavings over the sides and the centre. Chill at least 4 hours.
steps.look: A smooth white cake with chocolate covered sides, rosettes and dark cherries around the top.
steps.mistake: Applying the final coat without a crumb coat, so cocoa crumbs streak the cream.
steps.fix: Always crumb coat and chill first.

science: A genoise gets its lift almost entirely from air whipped into whole eggs. Warming the eggs and sugar first helps the sugar dissolve and lets the proteins stretch more, giving a stronger, more voluminous foam. Folding preserves those bubbles; the butter adds tenderness but deflates foam if added carelessly. Splitting and soaking the sponge with syrup adds moisture and flavour, because a genoise is quite dry on its own. Whipped cream is a foam held by fat globules that partly break and join around air bubbles; over hours it slowly weeps. Gelatine sets into a gel as it cools, reinforcing the foam so the cream holds its shape in a tall cake for a day or more. Cornflour thickens the cherry juice so it does not soak the sponge.
plating: Cut a tall wedge with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped between slices, and lay it on its side on a dessert plate so the three layers of sponge, cream and cherries show. Make sure each slice has a rosette and a cherry at its outer edge. Scatter a few chocolate shavings on the plate. Serve chilled.

pairing.drink: A fortified red such as Banyuls or a ruby port, or a glass of kirsch for the brave: dark cherry fruit and sweetness to match chocolate and cherries.
pairing.brennans: Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva NV: a sweet fortified red from the Brennan's list whose dark cherry and cocoa notes mirror the cake.

variations: Without alcohol: soak the layers with cherry syrup alone, and leave the kirsch out of the cream.
Black Forest trifle: layer cubes of the sponge, cherry filling and cream in glasses.
Mascarpone cream: whip 1 cup (225 g) mascarpone into the cream in place of gelatine to stabilise it.
safety: The cake contains raw alcohol in the syrup and cream; label it for guests.
Keep the finished cake refrigerated and eat within 3 days.
