title: Profiteroles with Chocolate Sauce
summary: Pâte à choux cooked twice, first in the pan where the flour paste is dried and then beaten with eggs, and again in the oven where steam puffs it into hollow shells, filled with ice cream or crème pâtissière and finished with hot chocolate sauce at the table. The profiterole is the first full test of choux, the dough behind éclairs, gougères and the croquembouche.
skills: pâte à choux cooked and beaten
filling with ice cream or crème pâtissière
equipment: Medium heavy saucepan
Wooden spoon
Stand mixer with paddle, or a bowl and the wooden spoon
Piping bag with a plain 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) nozzle
Two baking trays lined with baking paper
Small bowl of water for wetting a finger
Small sharp knife or skewer
Wire rack
Small saucepan and a heatproof jug for the sauce
Ice cream scoop

ingredients.us: 2 to 3 (you may not need all of the third)

ingredients.item: Egg wash: 1 egg yolk with 1 tsp (5 ml) milk

ingredients.note: or 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) crème pâtissière, as in the Boston cream pie

mise: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with shelves in the upper and lower thirds.
Draw 16 circles of 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) on the baking paper, spaced 2 inches (5 cm) apart, then turn the paper over so the ink is underneath.
Beat the eggs in a jug.
Fit the piping bag with the nozzle and stand it in a tall glass.
Take the ice cream out of the freezer 10 minutes before filling, and scoop 16 small balls onto a chilled tray; refreeze.

timeline.do: Oven on; mark the trays; scoop and freeze the ice cream balls.
Make the panade and beat in the eggs.
Pipe and bake 25 minutes at 400°F (200°C), then 10 minutes at 340°F (170°C).
Pierce to release steam; cool completely.
Make the chocolate sauce; split and fill the puffs.
Pour the hot sauce over at the table.

steps.do: Panade: put the water, milk, butter, salt and sugar in the saucepan over medium heat until the butter melts and the liquid comes to a full, rolling boil. Take off the heat, tip in all the flour at once and stir vigorously with the wooden spoon until it forms a smooth ball.
steps.look: A smooth, shiny dough that comes away from the sides of the pan in one mass.
steps.mistake: Adding the flour before the liquid boils, or gradually, so lumps form.
steps.fix: Wait for a full boil, add the flour in one go and beat hard; lumps will smooth out as you beat.

steps.do: Return the pan to medium low heat and stir and press the dough against the base and sides for 2 to 3 minutes to dry it.
steps.look: A thin film forms on the base of the pan, the dough looks drier and less shiny, and it smells faintly of toasted flour.
steps.mistake: Skipping this step, so the dough holds too much water, takes fewer eggs and the puffs collapse.
steps.fix: Keep going until you see the film on the pan base; that is the sign.

steps.do: Tip the dough into the mixer bowl (or a bowl) and beat on low for 1 minute to release steam and cool it a little, to about 140°F (60°C). Add the beaten egg a little at a time, beating fully after each addition, until the dough is smooth and glossy.
steps.look: After each addition the dough first looks slippery and broken, then comes back together smooth.
steps.mistake: Adding all the egg at once, so the dough becomes soupy and can never firm up again.
steps.fix: Add gradually; once too much egg is in, you cannot take it out, so go slowly near the end.

steps.do: Test the consistency after most of the egg is in: lift the spoon or paddle. The dough is ready when it falls slowly and leaves a V-shaped point hanging from the spoon, and a finger drawn through it leaves a trench that closes slowly. Stop adding egg at that point, even if some is left.
steps.look: A glossy, smooth, pipeable paste that hangs from the paddle in a V.
steps.mistake: Adding egg by the count rather than the feel, giving a runny dough that spreads flat.
steps.fix: If the dough is still stiff and breaks off the spoon in clumps, add a little more egg; if too runny, pipe smaller puffs and bake a little longer.

steps.do: Fill the piping bag and pipe mounds 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) across and about 1 inch (2.5 cm) high, holding the bag upright with the nozzle just above the tray, squeezing, then stopping and flicking sideways. Dab the peaks flat with a wet finger and brush lightly with egg wash if using.
steps.look: Round, even domes without points.
steps.mistake: Leaving pointed tips, which burn.
steps.fix: Flatten each tip with a wet finger.

steps.do: Bake at 400°F (200°C) for 25 minutes WITHOUT opening the door, then lower to 340°F (170°C) and bake 10 minutes more, until deep golden brown, including in the cracks, and light when lifted.
steps.look: Puffed, well risen, golden shells that sound hollow when tapped underneath.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven early or taking them out pale, so they collapse as they cool.
steps.fix: Bake until the cracks are golden too; a pale puff is still wet inside.

steps.do: Take the trays out, pierce the side of each puff with a skewer to let steam escape, and return them to the switched off oven with the door ajar for 5 minutes. Cool completely on a rack.
steps.look: Crisp, dry, hollow shells that hold their shape when cool.
steps.mistake: Leaving the steam trapped, which softens the shells from inside.
steps.fix: Pierce each one; you can also scoop out any damp dough from inside.

steps.do: Chocolate sauce: heat the cream until simmering, pour over the chocolate, wait 2 minutes, then stir until smooth and add the milk to loosen. Split each puff horizontally with a serrated knife, fill with a ball of ice cream and replace the lid. Pile into bowls and pour the hot sauce over at the table.
steps.look: Crisp golden puffs, cold ice cream and a glossy, warm chocolate sauce running down them.
steps.mistake: Filling the puffs too early, so the shells go soft.
steps.fix: Fill just before serving; unfilled shells keep crisp for a day in a tin and can be crisped in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 5 minutes.

science: Choux is leavened almost entirely by steam. Cooking the flour in boiling water and butter gelatinises its starch into a thick paste, and drying it on the heat drives off excess water so it can absorb more egg. Eggs add protein for structure, fat for tenderness and more water to make steam. In a hot oven, that water turns to steam and expands rapidly, puffing the elastic paste into a hollow shell, while the egg proteins and starch set the walls in their risen shape. Opening the oven early lets the temperature fall before the walls are set, so the steam condenses and they collapse. The lower temperature at the end dries the walls so they stay crisp when cool. Piercing lets trapped steam escape.
plating: Put three or four filled profiteroles in a shallow bowl or on a plate, piled in a small pyramid. Bring the chocolate sauce to the table in a warm jug and pour it over the top so it runs down the sides and pools around them. A light dusting of icing sugar or a few toasted flaked almonds on top is optional.

pairing.drink: A late harvest dessert wine or a small cup of strong coffee: sweetness and acidity, or bitterness, to meet chocolate and cream.
pairing.brennans: Grgich Hills ‘Violetta’ Late Harvest Napa Valley 2012 (375 ml): a sweet, late harvest Californian white from the Brennan's list with the richness for chocolate sauce and vanilla cream.

variations: Éclairs: pipe 4 inch (10 cm) lengths, bake the same way, fill with crème pâtissière and dip in ganache.
Gougères: beat 3/4 cup (75 g) grated Gruyère and a pinch of pepper into the choux, pipe small rounds and bake as above.
Craquelin topping: lay thin discs of butter, sugar and flour dough on each puff before baking for a crackled crust.
safety: The choux eggs are fully cooked in the oven.
If filling with crème pâtissière, keep the filled puffs refrigerated and eat within a day.

title: Cannoli Siciliani
summary: A wine and vinegar dough rolled paper thin, wrapped around metal tubes and fried until blistered and bronzed, then filled at the last minute with sheep's milk ricotta drained overnight and beaten smooth with sugar, candied orange and chocolate. It teaches a blistered fried pastry and why cannoli are filled only moments before they are eaten.
equipment: Metal cannoli tubes, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) across and 5 to 6 inches (13 to 15 cm) long, at least 4
Fine sieve or colander lined with muslin, set over a bowl, for draining the ricotta
Rolling pin or a pasta machine
Round or oval cutter about 4 inches (10 cm)
Heavy pot or deep frying pan and a deep fry thermometer
Tongs and a spider
Wire rack lined with paper
Piping bag with a wide plain or star nozzle
Food processor or a bowl and spatula

ingredients.item: Sheep's milk ricotta (or whole cow's milk ricotta), pasteurised
Dark chocolate chips or chopped chocolate
Neutral oil or lard for frying

mise: The night before: put the ricotta in the muslin lined sieve over a bowl, cover and refrigerate overnight to drain. You should lose several tablespoons of liquid.

Shell dough: mix the flour, sugar, cocoa, cinnamon and salt; rub in the lard. Add the yolk, Marsala and vinegar and knead 5 minutes into a firm, smooth dough, adding a few drops of Marsala only if too dry. Wrap and rest 1 hour at room temperature.
Chop the candied peel, chocolate and pistachios.
Set up the frying station: oil 2 inches (5 cm) deep in the pot, no more than a third full, thermometer clipped on, rack and tongs beside it.

timeline.do: Drain the ricotta in the fridge.
Make the dough; rest 1 hour.
Make the filling; chill it in the piping bag.
Roll, cut, wrap and fry the shells in batches; cool.
Fill at the moment of serving; dip in pistachio and dust.

steps.do: Filling: press the drained ricotta through a fine sieve (or blend 30 seconds) until completely smooth. Beat in the icing sugar and cinnamon, then fold in the candied peel and chocolate. Taste and add sugar if needed. Spoon into the piping bag and chill.
steps.look: A thick, silky, smooth cream that holds its shape on a spoon, flecked with orange and chocolate.
steps.mistake: Using undrained ricotta, which makes a wet, grainy filling that soaks the shells.
steps.fix: If it is still loose, return it to the muslin for an hour or stir in 1 tbsp (8 g) more icing sugar.

steps.do: Roll the dough as thin as you can, to about 1/16 inch (1.5 mm), on a lightly floured surface or through a pasta machine to the second thinnest setting. Cut circles or ovals of about 4 inches (10 cm).
steps.look: A thin, smooth, slightly translucent sheet through which you can see the board.
steps.mistake: Rolling it too thick, which gives heavy, bready shells without blisters.
steps.fix: Roll thinner: the dough should almost show the colour of the worktop through it.

steps.do: Wrap each oval around a tube lengthwise, overlapping the edges by about 1/2 inch (1 cm). Brush a little egg white on the overlap and press firmly to seal, taking care not to get egg white on the tube itself. Flare the ends slightly outward.
steps.look: A neat cylinder sealed along one line, loose enough around the tube to slide off later.
steps.mistake: Getting egg white on the metal, which glues the shell to the tube.
steps.fix: Brush only the overlapping dough; wipe the tubes clean between batches.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 350°F (177°C). Lower 2 or 3 tubes at a time into the oil with tongs and fry 1 1/2 to 2 minutes, turning, until deep golden brown and covered in small blisters.
steps.look: The dough bubbles immediately, then blisters all over and turns a rich bronze.
steps.mistake: Frying too cool, so the shells soak up oil and stay pale and soft, or too hot, so they darken before they crisp.
steps.fix: Keep the oil at 340 to 360°F (171 to 182°C), adjusting the heat between batches.

steps.do: Lift the tubes out with tongs, draining the oil from inside, and stand them on the rack. When cool enough to hold, about 1 minute, grip the tube with a cloth and slide the shell off gently while still warm. Cool the tubes before reusing.
steps.look: A crisp, blistered, golden shell that slides off cleanly.
steps.mistake: Grabbing the hot tube with bare fingers, or letting the shell cool fully on the tube, so it sticks and cracks.
steps.fix: Use a folded cloth; slide off while warm. If a shell sticks, twist the tube gently.

steps.do: Shells keep crisp for up to 5 days in an airtight tin. At the moment of serving, pipe the filling into each shell from both ends, so it is filled through the middle.
steps.look: Shells filled evenly to both ends with smooth cream.
steps.mistake: Filling the cannoli an hour ahead, so the shells soak up moisture and turn soft.
steps.fix: Fill no more than 15 minutes before eating; for a party, set up the shells and piping bag and fill to order.

steps.do: Dip both ends in the chopped pistachios, dust with icing sugar through a sieve and serve at once, two per person.
steps.look: Bronze shells, white filling, green pistachio ends and a snowfall of sugar.
steps.mistake: Dusting with sugar long before serving, when it melts into the shell.
steps.fix: Dust at the last moment.

science: The wine and vinegar in the dough are acids that limit gluten development and keep the dough tender and easy to roll thin. Alcohol evaporates faster than water in the hot oil, creating tiny bubbles that blister the surface, the signature texture of a good shell. Fat in the dough makes the crisp shell short and flaky rather than tough. Thin dough loses its water quickly in oil at about 350°F (177°C), so it crisps through before it absorbs much oil. Ricotta is a soft cheese full of whey; draining it overnight removes that water, so the filling is thick and does not weep into the shell. A dry fried pastry absorbs moisture from a wet filling quickly, which is why cannoli are filled only at the last moment.
plating: Lay two cannoli side by side, or crossed, on a small plate, the pistachio ends facing out. Dust the plate and the shells with a little icing sugar and scatter a few pistachios and candied orange pieces beside them. Serve immediately, while the shells still crackle.

pairing.drink: A sweet Sicilian Marsala, a passito or a Recioto: dried fruit and honeyed sweetness suit ricotta, orange and chocolate.
pairing.brennans: Giuseppe Quintarelli Recioto della Valpolicella Classico 1997: a sweet Italian red from dried grapes on the Brennan's list, rich with dried cherry and chocolate notes for cannoli.

variations: Cannoli dip: serve the filling in a bowl with broken shells or fried dough strips for dipping.
Pistachio cannoli: beat 2 tbsp (30 g) pistachio paste into the filling.
Baked shells: brush thin dough on tubes with oil and bake at 400°F (200°C) for 12 to 15 minutes; less blistered, but no frying.
safety: Use pasteurised ricotta; keep the filling and filled cannoli refrigerated until serving.
The tubes come out of the oil at about 350°F (177°C): handle them only with tongs and a cloth.
Keep the oil no more than a third of the pot's depth; never leave it unattended.

title: Chebakia
summary: A spiced dough of flour, ground toasted sesame, almond, anise and saffron, rolled thin, cut and folded by hand into rosettes, fried until deep amber, soaked in warm orange blossom honey and showered with sesame. It is the Ramadan sweet of Morocco and a lesson in patient hand shaping and the hot pastry, warm honey rule.
equipment: Dry frying pan for toasting sesame
Spice grinder or food processor
Mortar and pestle for the saffron
Large mixing bowl
Rolling pin, or a pasta machine
Fluted pastry wheel or a sharp knife and a ruler
Heavy pot or deep frying pan and a deep fry thermometer
Wide saucepan for the honey
Two slotted spoons or spiders
Colander set over a bowl, and a tray lined with baking paper

ingredients.us: 2 tbsp, plus 1 tbsp for the honey

mise: Toast all the sesame (for the dough and the finish) in the dry pan over medium heat, stirring, 4 to 5 minutes until golden and fragrant. Cool; grind 50 g finely for the dough.
Steep the crushed saffron in 2 tbsp (30 ml) orange blossom water for 10 minutes until deep orange.
Cut a piece of baking paper to lay rosettes on as you shape them.
Line a tray with baking paper for the finished chebakia.

timeline.do: Toast and grind the sesame; steep the saffron.
Make and knead the dough; rest 1 hour.
Roll, cut and fold the rosettes.
Warm the honey to 120°F (50°C); heat the oil to 330°F (165°C).
Fry in batches, soak in honey, drain and sprinkle with sesame.
Cool and serve, or store in a tin.

steps.do: Mix the flour, ground sesame, almonds, yeast, anise, cinnamon and salt in the large bowl. Add the beaten egg, melted butter, olive oil and saffron water and rub together with your fingers. Add warm water a tablespoon at a time and knead for 10 minutes into a firm, smooth dough.
steps.look: A firm, smooth, golden dough flecked with sesame that springs back slowly when pressed.
steps.mistake: Making the dough too soft, so the rosettes lose their shape and absorb oil.
steps.fix: Add only enough water to bring it together; it should feel firmer than bread dough.

steps.do: Cover and rest the dough for 1 hour at room temperature. Divide it into 4 pieces and keep them covered.
steps.look: The dough has relaxed and is easier to roll, though it will not rise much.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rest, so the dough springs back and tears when rolled thin.
steps.fix: Give it the full hour; the yeast and rest relax the gluten.

steps.do: Roll one piece to 1/16 inch (2 mm) thick, or through a pasta machine to a middle setting. Cut rectangles of about 3 by 2 inches (8 by 5 cm). In each rectangle, make 4 parallel cuts lengthwise, leaving 1/2 inch (1 cm) uncut at each end, giving 5 strips joined at the ends.
steps.look: Even rectangles, each with four slits and intact ends.
steps.mistake: Cutting through the ends, so the rosette falls apart.
steps.fix: Stop each cut short of the edge.

steps.do: Shape: thread the middle finger of one hand through alternate strips (the first, third and fifth), lifting them up. With the other hand, pinch the two opposite corners of the rectangle together and turn the dough inside out over your finger to form a flower; pinch the corners firmly to seal. Lay on the paper and cover.
steps.look: A neat, compact rosette with strips twisted round a centre, like a closed flower.
steps.mistake: Shaping too loosely, so the rosettes open and lose their shape in the oil.
steps.fix: Pinch the corners firmly; practise on a few, then work quickly so the dough does not dry.

steps.do: Warm the honey with 1 tbsp (15 ml) orange blossom water in the wide saucepan to about 120°F (50°C), warm but not simmering. Heat the frying oil to 330°F (165°C).
steps.look: Runny, fragrant honey; oil gently shimmering.
steps.mistake: Boiling the honey, which darkens it and destroys its aroma.
steps.fix: Keep it warm, not hot; take it off the heat if it starts to bubble.

steps.do: Fry the rosettes 5 or 6 at a time for 5 to 7 minutes, turning once, until deep amber and the fierce bubbling around them has died down.
steps.look: Rich, deep golden brown rosettes; the bubbles slow to a gentle fizz, which means the water has cooked out and they will be crisp.
steps.mistake: Pulling them out pale, so they go soft and soggy in the honey.
steps.fix: Fry until deep amber and quiet; a pale chebakia turns limp.

steps.do: Lift them straight from the oil into the warm honey, pushing them under. Leave them 5 to 7 minutes, until they stop hissing and the honey has soaked in and they look glossy and dark.
steps.look: Shiny, mahogany rosettes, saturated with honey.
steps.mistake: Letting the honey cool and thicken, so it no longer soaks in.
steps.fix: Rewarm the honey gently between batches.

steps.do: Lift them into the colander to drain for 1 minute, then lay them on the lined tray and immediately sprinkle generously with the toasted sesame. Cool completely before storing.
steps.look: Glossy, dark rosettes covered in golden sesame; they become crisp and chewy as they cool.
steps.mistake: Waiting until the honey sets before adding sesame, so it will not stick.
steps.fix: Sprinkle while they are warm and sticky.

science: The yeast and the long rest are not for rising: fermentation and time relax the gluten network so a thin sheet can be cut and twisted without springing back or tearing. Ground toasted sesame and almonds are rich in oil, which coats the flour and shortens the gluten, making the fried pastry crisp and brittle rather than bready. Frying until the bubbling slows means most of the water has left the dough; a dry, porous structure absorbs honey without collapsing. Honey loses its delicate aroma when overheated, so it is kept warm. Warm, runny honey penetrates the hot pastry; as both cool, the honey thickens and sets into a glossy coating. Toasting sesame develops nutty flavours through the Maillard reaction.
plating: Pile the chebakia in a pyramid on a decorated plate or in a small bowl, as served with harira at the end of a Ramadan fast. Scatter a little more sesame around them. For a dessert plate, set three rosettes in a triangle with a few dates and a glass of mint tea beside them.

pairing.drink: Moroccan mint tea, very sweet; with wine, an aromatic sweet white such as late harvest Gewürztraminer, whose floral and spice notes meet orange blossom and anise.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives 2007: a late harvest Alsace Gewurztraminer from the Brennan's list, floral and honeyed, a natural partner for orange blossom honey and anise.

variations: Simpler shape: cut the dough into small diamonds or twisted strips instead of rosettes; the flavour is the same.
Without yeast: use 1/2 tsp (2 g) baking powder and rest the dough 1 hour covered.
Baked chebakia: brush rosettes with oil and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 15 to 20 minutes, then dip in warm honey; less crisp.
safety: Keep the frying oil no more than a third of the pot's depth and never leave it unattended.
Freshly fried pastry and warm honey are very hot: use slotted spoons and let them cool before eating.
Chebakia keep for 2 to 3 weeks in an airtight tin.

title: Yakgwa (Korean Honey Cookies)
summary: A sesame oil dough sweetened with honey and rice wine, stacked and folded for layers, fried first at a low heat so it opens and then at a higher heat to colour, and soaked in a ginger and honey syrup until glossy. It is a frying technique all its own: slow, then hot, then soaked.
skills: a sesame oil dough folded for layers
frying at low then higher heat
equipment: Medium saucepan for the syrup
Large mixing bowl and a sieve
Rolling pin and a bench scraper
Yakgwa mould, or a small round or flower cutter about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm), or a knife
Skewer or chopstick
Heavy pot or wok and a deep fry thermometer
Slotted spoon
Wire rack and a shallow dish for soaking

ingredients.item: Rice syrup (jocheong) or light corn syrup
Soju, rice wine or vodka mixed with water
Pine nuts or chopped pumpkin seeds

mise: Make the syrup first so it is cool: simmer the rice syrup, honey, water, ginger and cinnamon stick in the saucepan for 5 minutes. Take off the heat and cool to room temperature; remove the ginger and cinnamon.
Grate a thumb of ginger and squeeze it through a cloth to get 1 tbsp (15 ml) juice.
Mix the honey, soju and ginger juice in a small bowl.
Have the frying thermometer clipped to the pot with oil about 2 inches (5 cm) deep.

timeline.do: Make and cool the syrup.
Make, fold and cut the dough.
Fry slowly at 230 to 250°F (110 to 120°C), then at 300°F (150°C).
Soak in the syrup at least 6 hours, or overnight.
Drain, garnish and serve.

steps.do: Put the flour, salt, pepper and cinnamon in the bowl, drizzle in the sesame oil and rub it in with your fingers for 2 to 3 minutes until every particle is coated. Press the mixture through the sieve to make it even.
steps.look: A fine, sandy, slightly damp mixture that clumps when squeezed, smelling of sesame.
steps.mistake: Skipping the rubbing, so oil sits in patches and the layers are uneven.
steps.fix: Rub thoroughly and sieve; it should look like damp sand all through.

steps.do: Pour in the honey mixture and mix with a spatula, cutting and pressing, just until it comes together. Do not knead.
steps.look: A rough, crumbly dough that holds together when pressed.
steps.mistake: Kneading, which develops gluten and makes hard, dense cookies with no layers.
steps.fix: Press it together, never knead.

steps.do: Press the dough into a rectangle about 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) thick. Cut it in half with the bench scraper, stack one half on the other and press down. Repeat cutting, stacking and pressing 3 times.
steps.look: A compact block in which faint layers are visible at the cut edges.
steps.mistake: Overworking or rolling hard, which merges the layers.
steps.fix: Press gently with your palms or a light roll each time.

steps.do: Roll or press the dough to 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) thick and cut into 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) squares, or press into a yakgwa mould. Prick each piece through in two or three places with the skewer.
steps.look: Even pieces with layers visible on their sides and small holes through the centre.
steps.mistake: Forgetting to prick, so the centres stay raw and the cookies puff unevenly.
steps.fix: Prick each piece right through; the holes let heat reach the middle.

steps.do: Heat the oil to 230 to 250°F (110 to 120°C). Lower in the cookies and fry slowly, turning occasionally, for 10 to 15 minutes, until they float, swell and the layers open like pages.
steps.look: Pale, puffed cookies with visible separated layers; only small bubbles around them.
steps.mistake: Frying hot from the start, so the outside browns and seals before the layers can open, leaving a hard, raw centre.
steps.fix: Keep the oil low; use the thermometer and adjust the heat often.

steps.do: Raise the oil to 300°F (150°C) and fry 3 to 5 minutes more, turning, until evenly deep golden brown. Lift onto the rack to drain for 2 minutes.
steps.look: Deep golden brown cookies with open layers; they sound hollow when tapped.
steps.mistake: Letting the oil go above 320°F (160°C), which burns the honey in the dough.
steps.fix: Watch the colour closely in this stage; honey browns quickly.

steps.do: While still warm, put the cookies in the shallow dish and pour over the cool syrup to cover. Soak at least 6 hours, or overnight, turning once.
steps.look: The cookies absorb the syrup and become glossy, dark and soft through.
steps.mistake: Soaking for only a few minutes, so the centre stays dry.
steps.fix: Be patient; the long soak is what makes yakgwa.

steps.do: Lift them from the syrup, let excess drip off for 5 minutes, and top each with a pine nut or a few pumpkin seeds. Serve, or store in an airtight container for up to 1 week.
steps.look: Shiny, amber cookies, moist and chewy inside with visible layers.
steps.mistake: Serving them dripping wet with syrup.
steps.fix: Drain on a rack before serving.

science: Rubbing sesame oil into flour coats the particles with fat, which limits how much gluten can form when the liquid goes in; that, and not kneading, keeps the cookies tender. Stacking and pressing creates thin layers separated by oiled surfaces, a simple form of lamination. Frying at a low temperature lets heat penetrate slowly while the outside stays soft enough to stretch; the water in each layer turns to steam and pushes the layers apart before the crust sets. Raising the heat then browns the honey and flour through caramelisation and Maillard reactions. Pricking lets heat and steam reach the centre. Warm, porous cookies soak up cool syrup by capillary action, which is why they are soaked while still warm.
plating: Arrange the yakgwa on a small dark plate or a wooden tray, slightly overlapping, each crowned with a pine nut. Serve three or four per person with a cup of hot ginger or barley tea. For a celebration, stack them in a neat tower on a raised plate, as they are served at Korean holidays.

pairing.drink: Hot ginger tea or a sweet, aromatic Riesling: ginger echoes the syrup, and a sweet Riesling's acidity balances the honey.
pairing.brennans: Dr. Hermann ‘Ürziger Würzgarten in der Kranklei’ Riesling Spätlese Goldkapsel 2018: a sweet, spicy Mosel Riesling from the Brennan's list, bright enough to cut through honey syrup.

variations: Mini yakgwa: cut 1 inch (2.5 cm) pieces and fry 8 to 10 minutes at the low heat.
Cinnamon and ginger syrup: add 1 tbsp (15 ml) more ginger juice and a pinch of ground cinnamon to the syrup.
Yakgwa ice cream: crumble soaked yakgwa over vanilla ice cream, a modern Seoul café dessert.
safety: Keep the oil no more than a third of the pot's depth and never leave it unattended; adjust the heat gradually.
Honey cookies brown and burn quickly at higher heat; turn the burner down at once if they darken.

title: Knafeh Nabulseyeh
summary: Shredded kataifi pastry tossed in ghee and pressed around a layer of white Nabulsi or Akkawi cheese, desalted until mild, baked until crisp and golden, turned out and soaked with cool orange blossom syrup, served hot while the cheese stretches. It teaches desalting cheese and the syrup rule once more: cool syrup on hot pastry.
equipment: Round metal baking tin, about 9 inches (23 cm), shallow
Large bowl for soaking the cheese, kept in the fridge
Small saucepan for the syrup
Sharp knife or kitchen scissors for chopping the pastry
Large bowl for tossing the pastry
Flat, heatproof serving plate larger than the tin
Oven gloves
Pastry brush

ingredients.item: Nabulsi or Akkawi cheese, sliced 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick
ingredients.note: both are brined and salty and must be desalted

ingredients.item: Orange food colouring or a pinch of ground turmeric
ingredients.note: optional, for the traditional orange colour

mise: Desalt the cheese: put the slices in a large bowl of cold water in the fridge. Change the water every hour for 4 to 6 hours, until a nibble tastes mild and only lightly salty. Drain and pat dry with paper.
Make the syrup: boil the sugar and water for 5 minutes, stir in the lemon juice, cool, then add the orange blossom water. It must be completely cool before serving.
Pull the kataifi apart and chop it into short lengths of about 1 inch (2.5 cm) with scissors.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with a shelf in the lower third.
Grate the mozzarella; grind the pistachios.

timeline.do: Start desalting the cheese in the fridge; change the water hourly.
Make the syrup and cool it.
Toss the kataifi with ghee; build the knafeh in the tin.
Bake 25 to 35 minutes until the base is deep gold.
Turn out, pour over the cool syrup, add pistachio and serve hot.

steps.do: Brush the tin with 1 tbsp (14 g) of the ghee and, if using, a few drops of orange colouring mixed into it. Toss the chopped kataifi in the large bowl with the rest of the ghee, rubbing it through with your fingers until every strand is coated.
steps.look: Separated, shiny, evenly buttered strands with no dry clumps.
steps.mistake: Leaving dry patches of pastry, which burn and stay brittle and white.
steps.fix: Rub the ghee through thoroughly; the pastry should glisten all over.

steps.do: Press half the kataifi firmly into the tin in an even layer about 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) thick, packing it tight with the bottom of a glass.
steps.look: A compact, level base that covers the tin with no gaps.
steps.mistake: Leaving it loose, so it falls apart when turned out.
steps.fix: Press hard; a firmly packed layer holds as a crust.

steps.do: Lay the desalted cheese slices over the pastry to within 1/2 inch (1 cm) of the edge and scatter the mozzarella over them. Cover with the remaining kataifi and press down firmly again.
steps.look: Cheese sealed in completely with no white showing at the edges.
steps.mistake: Taking the cheese right to the edge, so it leaks, burns on the tin and sticks.
steps.fix: Leave a border of pastry to seal it in.

steps.do: Bake on the lower shelf at 400°F (200°C) for 25 to 35 minutes, until the edges are deep golden and you can see the base is browned when you tilt the tin or lift an edge with a knife.
steps.look: Bubbling ghee at the edges, a smell of toasted butter, and a crisp, deep golden base.
steps.mistake: Taking it out pale, so the pastry is soft and the knafeh breaks when turned.
steps.fix: Bake until the base is deep gold; the base becomes the top.

steps.do: Run a knife round the edge. Put the serving plate upside down on the tin and, wearing oven gloves, flip it over in one quick movement. Lift the tin away.
steps.look: A golden, crisp, round knafeh on the plate, the orange coloured base now facing up.
steps.mistake: Hesitating, so it slides and breaks.
steps.fix: Flip decisively over a sink or tray in case ghee drips.

steps.do: Immediately pour the cool syrup over the hot knafeh, starting from the centre, until absorbed; use about two thirds and serve the rest on the side. Scatter the ground pistachios in a ring or all over. Serve hot, cutting wedges so the cheese stretches.
steps.look: The syrup hisses as it soaks in; the knafeh glistens, and when cut the cheese pulls in long strings.
steps.mistake: Using hot syrup on hot pastry, which makes it soggy, or letting the knafeh cool before serving, so the cheese sets.
steps.fix: Syrup cool, pastry hot, and serve within minutes.

science: Nabulsi and Akkawi are brined cheeses: salt was added to preserve them. Soaking in fresh water lets salt diffuse out of the cheese, and changing the water keeps the concentration difference high so it keeps moving out. Desalted, the cheese tastes sweet and milky and melts into stretchy strings because its proteins form long strands when heated. Ghee is butter with the water and milk solids removed, so it crisps the pastry without steaming it and does not burn at high heat. Cool syrup poured on hot pastry soaks in while the steam leaving the hot pastry keeps the strands crisp; hot syrup on hot pastry adds water that cannot escape, and the pastry turns soggy.
plating: Serve the whole knafeh at the table on its round plate, glistening with syrup, the ground pistachios in a bright green ring around the centre. Cut generous wedges with a sharp knife and lift them with a cake slice so the cheese stretches between knife and plate. Put the extra syrup in a small jug for those who want it sweeter.

pairing.drink: Strong Arabic coffee or a sweet Chenin Blanc: bitterness or bright acidity to balance the rich cheese and syrup.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Huet ‘Le Mont’ Vouvray Moelleux 2009: a sweet, honeyed Loire Chenin Blanc from the Brennan's list with the acidity to cut a hot cheese pastry soaked in syrup.

variations: Knafeh na'ameh: use fine semolina dough crumbs tossed in ghee instead of kataifi for the soft, smooth version.
Ricotta and mozzarella: replace the brined cheese with a mix of drained ricotta and mozzarella, no desalting needed.
Individual knafeh: bake in four small tins for 20 to 25 minutes.
safety: Desalt the cheese in the fridge, not on the counter, and change the water regularly.
Inverting a tin of hot ghee and pastry can splash: use oven gloves and work over a tray.
Eat knafeh fresh; refrigerate leftovers and reheat in the oven.

title: Galaktoboureko
summary: A semolina custard flavoured with vanilla and lemon, enriched with eggs below the temperature at which they would set into threads, baked between buttered sheets of phyllo until golden and puffed, and soaked in cold lemon syrup. It joins a starch-thickened custard with phyllo work and the two temperature rules that decide the dish.
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) square baking dish, at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep
Heavy saucepan of about 3 quarts (3 litres)
Whisk and a wooden spoon
Instant read thermometer
Small saucepan for the syrup and one for clarifying butter
Pastry brush
Damp tea towel and cling film for keeping phyllo moist
Sharp knife

ingredients.item: Lemon peel strip and lemon juice
Vanilla pod, split, or vanilla extract
Unsalted butter, to clarify for the phyllo
ingredients.note: gives about 1/3 cup (80 ml) clarified butter

mise: Syrup first: boil the 1 cup (200 g) sugar, the water and lemon peel for 5 minutes, then add the lemon juice and cool completely, ideally in the fridge.
Clarify the butter: melt it over low heat, skim off the foam and pour the clear yellow fat away from the milky water at the bottom.
Unroll the phyllo, trim the sheets to about 10 by 14 inches (25 by 36 cm) if needed so they overhang the dish, and keep them under cling film and a damp towel.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a shelf in the middle.
Brush the dish with clarified butter.

timeline.do: Make the syrup and chill it; clarify the butter.
Cook the semolina custard; cool to 140°F (60°C); add the eggs.
Layer the phyllo, add the custard, fold and top; score.
Bake 40 to 45 minutes until deep golden.
Pour the cold syrup over the hot pastry; leave at least 3 to 4 hours.
Cut and serve at room temperature.

steps.do: Custard: heat the milk with the vanilla and lemon zest in the heavy saucepan until simmering. Rain in the semolina in a thin stream while whisking constantly, then cook over medium low heat for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring with the wooden spoon, until thick enough that a spoon leaves a trail that slowly closes.
steps.look: A thick, smooth, pale porridge that plops and bubbles slowly, smelling of vanilla and lemon.
steps.mistake: Adding the semolina too fast, so it forms lumps.
steps.fix: Pour slowly while whisking; whisk hard or press lumps out through a sieve if they appear.

steps.do: Take off the heat, remove the vanilla pod and beat in the 3 1/2 tbsp (50 g) butter and the 1/2 cup (100 g) sugar until melted. Let the custard cool, stirring occasionally, until it reads 140°F (60°C).
steps.look: A glossy, thick custard that has stopped steaming heavily.
steps.mistake: Adding the eggs while the custard is still above 150°F (65°C), so they set on contact into threads.
steps.fix: Wait for the thermometer; stir to speed cooling or set the pan in cold water.

steps.do: Whisk the 2 eggs into the custard one at a time, whisking hard for about 30 seconds after each, until fully incorporated and smooth.
steps.look: A smooth, loose, glossy custard with no streaks or threads of egg.
steps.mistake: Adding both eggs at once without whisking, which can leave streaks.
steps.fix: Whisk vigorously after each egg.

steps.do: Lay a phyllo sheet in the dish, letting it overhang the edges, and brush it all over with clarified butter. Repeat with 5 more sheets, turning each slightly so the overhang covers all sides. Pour in the custard and level it.
steps.look: A buttered phyllo nest holding a smooth, level custard.
steps.mistake: Letting the phyllo dry out while you work, so it cracks and crumbles.
steps.fix: Keep the stack covered with film and a damp towel; work quickly; a cracked sheet can be patched with the next.

steps.do: Fold the overhanging sheets back over the custard, brushing each with butter. Layer the remaining 4 sheets on top, folding or trimming them to fit and brushing each with butter. Brush the top generously. Score the top layers into 4 to 6 squares with a sharp knife, cutting through the pastry but not into the custard.
steps.look: A neat, golden buttered top with clean score lines.
steps.mistake: Cutting deep into the custard, so it bubbles up through the cuts.
steps.fix: Score only the top few sheets.

steps.do: Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 40 to 45 minutes until the top is deep golden brown and puffed and the custard is set (it wobbles only slightly in the middle).
steps.look: Puffed, crisp, golden phyllo; the custard has risen and set.
steps.mistake: Taking it out pale, so the pastry goes soggy under the syrup.
steps.fix: Bake until deeply golden; the colour is crispness.

steps.do: As soon as it comes out of the oven, ladle the cold syrup slowly and evenly over the hot pastry. Leave it to soak at room temperature for at least 3 to 4 hours before cutting.
steps.look: The syrup hisses and is absorbed; the top stays crisp and glossy.
steps.mistake: Pouring warm syrup on hot pastry, or waiting until the pastry has cooled, which makes it soggy.
steps.fix: Always cold syrup on hot pastry, straight from the oven.

science: Semolina is coarse durum wheat flour; its starch granules absorb hot milk, swell and burst, thickening the custard. Because the starch already holds the structure, the eggs mainly enrich it and help it set and puff in the oven. Egg proteins set quickly at around 150°F (65°C); added to a custard hotter than that, they cook on contact into visible threads, so the custard is cooled first. Clarified butter has no water, so the phyllo sheets fry crisp rather than steaming. Pouring cold syrup over hot pastry means the steam still escaping from the phyllo pushes outward while the cool syrup soaks in slowly, so the layers stay crisp. Two hot liquids or two cold ones give a soggy pastry.
plating: Cut squares with a sharp knife along the scored lines and lift them with a spatula. Serve one square per person on a small plate, the crisp, glossy top up, with a spoon of the syrup that has pooled in the dish drizzled around it. A light dusting of cinnamon is traditional in some homes.

pairing.drink: A honeyed sweet white such as Sauternes, Barsac or a Greek Muscat: honey and citrus notes to match lemon syrup and vanilla custard.
pairing.brennans: Château Climens Barsac Premier Cru Classé 2010: a sweet Bordeaux from the Brennan's list with honey, citrus and acidity for a lemon syrup custard pie.

variations: Bougatsa: use the same custard without syrup, bake, and dust with icing sugar and cinnamon.
Orange: replace the lemon zest and peel with orange, and add 1 tsp (5 ml) orange blossom water to the syrup.
Individual rolls: wrap spoonfuls of cooled custard in buttered phyllo strips and bake 20 to 25 minutes.
safety: The custard eggs are fully cooked in the oven; keep leftovers refrigerated and eat within 3 days.
Boiling syrup can burn: cool it fully before use.

title: Apfelstrudel
summary: A strudel dough kneaded until smooth and elastic, rested warm, then stretched over the backs of the hands on a floured tablecloth until you can read through it, spread with butter toasted crumbs and spiced apples and rolled using the cloth. Stretching strudel dough to transparency is one of the great hand skills in pastry.
skills: stretching over the backs of the hands until you can read through it
equipment: Large table that you can walk around, at least 3 by 2 feet (90 by 60 cm)
Clean, smooth cotton tablecloth or a large sheet, larger than the table top
Warm bowl to cover the dough while it rests
Rolling pin
Large frying pan for the crumbs
Large bowl for the apples
Pastry brush
Large baking tray lined with baking paper
Sharp serrated knife

ingredients.item: White wine vinegar or lemon juice
Tart apples (Bramley, Granny Smith or Braeburn), peeled, cored and thinly sliced
ingredients.note: about 4 large; slices 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick

ingredients.item: Raisins, soaked in 2 tbsp (30 ml) rum or warm water

mise: Dough: mix the flour and salt, add the warm water, 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil and vinegar and knead for 8 to 10 minutes, slapping the dough on the worktop, until very smooth, silky and elastic.
Shape into a ball, coat lightly with oil, put it on a plate and cover with a bowl warmed with hot water and dried. Rest 1 hour in a warm place.
Crumbs: melt the 4 tbsp (56 g) butter in the frying pan and toast the breadcrumbs over medium heat, stirring, 4 to 6 minutes until golden. Cool.
Apples: toss the slices with the lemon juice, sugar, cinnamon and drained raisins just before stretching the dough, so they do not release too much juice.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Spread the cloth over the table and rub flour evenly into it.

timeline.do: Knead the dough; rest it warm for 1 hour.
Toast the crumbs; prepare the apples; flour the cloth; oven on.
Roll, then stretch the dough over the backs of your hands.
Fill, roll with the cloth and lift onto the tray.
Bake 35 to 40 minutes, brushing with butter twice.
Cool at least 20 minutes; dust and slice.

steps.do: Put the rested dough in the centre of the floured cloth and roll it with the rolling pin into a rectangle about 12 by 8 inches (30 by 20 cm). Brush it lightly with melted butter.
steps.look: A smooth, soft rectangle that rolls out easily without springing back.
steps.mistake: Working with cold or unrested dough, which springs back and tears.
steps.fix: Rest it longer under a warm bowl until it relaxes.

steps.do: Remove any rings. Slide your hands, palms down and fists loosely closed, under the centre of the dough. Gently lift and move your hands apart, stretching the dough over the backs of your hands, working outward from the centre and moving round the table.
steps.look: The dough thins evenly and becomes translucent in the centre.
steps.mistake: Using your fingertips, which poke holes in the dough.
steps.fix: Use the backs of your hands and knuckles, never the fingertips.

steps.do: Lay the dough down and, working round the table, pull the thicker edges gently outward with your fingers until the whole sheet is paper thin and about 30 by 24 inches (75 by 60 cm). Trim off the thick outer border with scissors.
steps.look: A sheet so thin you can read the pattern of the cloth (or a newspaper) through it.
steps.mistake: Panicking at small holes and starting again.
steps.fix: A few small holes do not matter; they are hidden when the strudel is rolled. Patch large tears with a trimmed scrap.

steps.do: Let the dough dry for 2 to 3 minutes, then brush it all over with melted butter. Scatter the toasted crumbs over the third of the dough nearest you, leaving a 2 inch (5 cm) border at the sides. Spread the apple mixture over the crumbs, leaving any juice in the bowl.
steps.look: A thin buttered sheet with a band of crumbs and apples along one long edge.
steps.mistake: Pouring the apple juices onto the dough, which makes it soggy and tear.
steps.fix: Lift the apples out with your hands and leave the juice behind.

steps.do: Fold the side borders in over the filling. Lift the edge of the cloth nearest you and use it to roll the strudel away from you, letting it roll itself over and over, until all the dough is wrapped round the filling in many layers.
steps.look: A neat, tight, long roll with the seam underneath.
steps.mistake: Rolling by hand, which tears the dough.
steps.fix: Let the cloth do the work: lift it and the strudel rolls by its own weight.

steps.do: Roll the strudel off the cloth onto the lined tray, seam side down, curving it into a horseshoe if it is longer than the tray. Brush generously with melted butter.
steps.look: A plump, curved roll, buttery on top.
steps.mistake: Lifting it with your hands, which can split it.
steps.fix: Lift the cloth and tip the strudel onto the tray in one movement.

steps.do: Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 35 to 40 minutes, brushing with more butter after 15 and 30 minutes, until deep golden and crisp and the apples are soft when tested with a skewer.
steps.look: A deep golden, flaky, crackling crust, with juices bubbling at the ends.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, so the inner layers are pale and doughy.
steps.fix: Bake until deep golden; tent loosely with foil if it browns too fast.

steps.do: Cool on the tray for at least 20 minutes, dust heavily with icing sugar and slice with the serrated knife into slices 2 inches (5 cm) wide. Serve warm with vanilla sauce or whipped cream.
steps.look: Slices that show many thin, crisp layers spiralling round soft, spiced apple.
steps.mistake: Slicing straight from the oven, so the filling runs out.
steps.fix: Let it rest; the apple juices thicken as it cools slightly.

science: Strudel dough uses strong flour, high in protein, kneaded hard to develop a long, elastic gluten network that can stretch to transparency without tearing. Resting is essential: the gluten relaxes so the dough stops springing back, and warmth keeps it supple. A little acid helps the gluten stretch. Oil in the dough adds extensibility. When baked, each paper thin layer brushed with butter crisps separately as the water in the dough evaporates, giving dozens of flaky leaves. Toasted buttered crumbs absorb the apple juices so they do not soak the pastry, while adding flavour. Tart apples hold their shape better and balance the sugar.
plating: Serve a warm slice on its side, slightly tilted so the spiral of layers shows, on a plate pooled with warm vanilla sauce. Dust the top with icing sugar through a fine sieve just before serving. A spoon of whipped cream beside it is the Viennese café way.

pairing.drink: An Austrian sweet wine or a strong coffee with cream: honeyed acidity matches spiced apple, as in a Viennese café.
pairing.brennans: Kracher ‘Cuvée’ Auslese Burgenland 2017: a sweet Austrian wine from the Brennan's list, from the same country as the strudel, with the acidity for baked apple.

variations: Topfenstrudel: fill with quark or curd cheese beaten with eggs, sugar, lemon zest and raisins.
Shop phyllo: brush 6 sheets of phyllo with butter, stack, fill and roll the same way; less authentic, much quicker.
Pear and walnut: replace half the apples with pears and add 1/2 cup (50 g) toasted walnuts.
safety: Remove rings and watches before stretching: they tear the dough and catch the cloth.
Hot apple filling stays very hot: let the strudel rest before slicing and serving.

title: Cantonese Mooncakes
summary: A thin golden crust made from golden syrup, lye water and oil, wrapped evenly around lotus seed paste and a salted duck egg yolk, pressed in a carved mould, baked and egg washed, then rested for days until the crust softens and shines. The Mid-Autumn mooncake teaches a thin, even crust around a heavy filling and a sharp print from the mould.
skills: a golden syrup and lye water dough
lotus seed paste and salted yolk
equipment: Mooncake press or wooden mould for 3.5 oz (100 g) cakes
Digital kitchen scale that reads to 1 g
Mixing bowl and a spatula
Baking tray lined with baking paper
Small fine brush for egg wash
Small bowl and a fine sieve for the egg wash
Spray bottle with water
Cling film
Airtight container for resting the cakes

ingredients.item: Golden syrup or invert sugar syrup
Lye water (kansui, food grade alkaline water)
ingredients.note: weigh it; Asian grocers sell it
vacuum packed, or from whole salted duck eggs

ingredients.item: Shaoxing wine or a little vodka

ingredients.note: [or red bean paste; you need 330 g, a little is spare]

mise: At least 3 hours ahead (or the day before), make the crust dough: stir the golden syrup, lye water and oil together until fully blended and glossy. Add the sifted flour and fold until just combined into a soft, smooth dough. Do not knead. Wrap in film and rest at room temperature for 2 to 4 hours.
Prepare the yolks: rinse, pat dry, brush with Shaoxing wine and bake on a lined tray at 350°F (175°C) for 6 to 8 minutes until they just begin to bubble. Cool.
Weigh the filling: divide the lotus paste into 6 portions of 55 g. Flatten each, put a yolk in the centre and wrap the paste around it, rolling into a smooth ball. Cover.
Divide the rested crust dough into 6 portions of about 30 g for a 100 g mould (crust about 30 percent of the weight, filling and yolk the rest); roll into balls and cover.
Mix the egg wash: yolk, white and water, then pass through a fine sieve. Heat the oven to 350°F (180°C).

timeline.do: Make and rest the crust dough; prepare the yolks and filling balls.
Wrap, press and unmould the mooncakes.
Bake 5 minutes; cool 10 minutes; egg wash; bake 12 to 15 minutes more.
Cool completely, then rest in an airtight container 1 to 3 days.
Cut into wedges and serve with tea.

steps.do: Flatten a crust ball between two sheets of film into a thin, even round about 4 inches (10 cm) across, slightly thicker in the centre than at the edges.
steps.look: An even, soft disc with no cracks.
steps.mistake: Making the edges as thick as the centre, so the crust gathers into a thick lump at the top.
steps.fix: Press the edges thinner; they will bunch together as you wrap.

steps.do: Peel off the top film, set a filling ball in the centre, then cup the disc in your hand and gently push the crust up around the filling with your thumb and fingers, rotating as you go, until it is completely covered. Pinch the top closed and roll into a smooth ball.
steps.look: A smooth ball with a thin, even crust all round and no filling showing.
steps.mistake: Stretching the crust too hard, so it tears and the filling peeks through.
steps.fix: Ease it up slowly; patch a thin spot with a pinch of extra dough and roll smooth.

steps.do: Dust the ball very lightly with flour and tap off the excess. Dust the mould lightly too. Put the ball in the mould, seam side up, set the mould on the tray and press down firmly and evenly for 3 seconds, then lift the press to release the cake.
steps.look: A neat cake with a crisp, sharp pattern on top and straight sides.
steps.mistake: Too much flour, which blurs the pattern and leaves white patches; or too little, so it sticks in the mould.
steps.fix: A whisper of flour is enough; brush off any excess with a dry brush.

steps.do: Mist the cakes lightly with water from the spray bottle to prevent cracking. Bake at 350°F (180°C) for 5 minutes to set the pattern.
steps.look: The crust sets and turns pale cream; the pattern is fixed.
steps.mistake: Egg washing before the first bake, which blurs the pattern.
steps.fix: Bake briefly first; wash afterwards.

steps.do: Take the tray out and cool for 10 minutes. Brush the tops with a very thin coat of egg wash, dabbing gently so it does not pool in the pattern.
steps.look: A thin, even sheen with the pattern still crisp.
steps.mistake: Brushing on too much egg wash, which fills the pattern and makes it blurry and dark.
steps.fix: Wipe most of the wash off the brush first; use a very soft brush and dab.

steps.do: Return to the oven and bake 12 to 15 minutes until golden brown, egg washing once more halfway through if you want a deeper colour.
steps.look: Shiny, even, golden brown cakes with a sharp pattern; the sides are pale gold.
steps.mistake: Overbaking, so the crust turns dark and dry.
steps.fix: Take them out as soon as they are golden; they darken a little as they rest.

steps.do: Cool completely on the tray, then store in an airtight container at room temperature for 1 to 3 days before serving. The crust will soften and become glossy.
steps.look: After resting, the crust is soft, shiny and slightly oily, the classic look of a finished mooncake.
steps.mistake: Eating them the same day, when the crust is hard and dry.
steps.fix: Wait at least 1 day; this resting is part of the recipe.

steps.do: To serve, cut each mooncake into 4 wedges with a sharp knife, so the yolk shows in the centre of each piece.
steps.look: Clean wedges: a thin golden crust, smooth lotus paste and an orange yolk at the centre like a moon.
steps.mistake: Sawing with a dull knife, which drags the yolk.
steps.fix: Press down cleanly with a sharp knife wiped between cuts.

science: Golden syrup is an invert sugar syrup: its sugar has been split into glucose and fructose, which attract water and keep the crust soft and pliable, and brown readily for a deep colour. Lye water is alkaline; it neutralises the acidity of the syrup, which helps the crust brown more deeply and evenly, and makes it softer. The oil coats the flour so little gluten forms, which is why the dough is folded, not kneaded. Resting lets the flour absorb the syrup evenly so the dough becomes smooth and stretchy enough to wrap thinly. After baking, moisture and oil migrate from the dense filling into the dry crust over a day or more, softening it and giving the glossy finish called returning oil.
plating: Present whole mooncakes on a small plate first so the pattern is admired, then cut each into four wedges and arrange them in a fan, the yolk side facing the guest. Serve with small cups of hot oolong or jasmine tea, as they are rich and sweet. They are traditionally shared at the Mid-Autumn Festival under the full moon.

pairing.drink: Hot oolong, pu'er or jasmine tea: the tannin and warmth cut the rich lotus paste and salted yolk, as they are served in Hong Kong.

variations: Red bean mooncakes: use sweetened red bean paste instead of lotus seed paste.
Without yolk: use 70 g of lotus paste per cake and add a few toasted melon seeds.
Snow skin mooncakes: a no bake version with a glutinous rice flour skin, kept chilled.
safety: Lye water is strongly alkaline: use food grade only, measure it exactly, avoid skin and eye contact, and store it out of children's reach.
Use commercially salted duck egg yolks and bake them as described; store finished mooncakes airtight and eat within a week.

title: Semla
summary: Soft cardamom buns, freshly ground spice in an enriched dough, baked golden, hollowed out and filled with homemade almond paste mixed with the scooped crumb and a little milk, then crowned with whipped cream and dusted with icing sugar. The Swedish Lenten bun joins an enriched dough with almond paste made by hand and piped cream.
skills: scooping and making almond paste filling
equipment: Stand mixer with dough hook, or a large bowl
Mortar and pestle
Food processor for the almond paste
Baking tray lined with baking paper
Pastry brush
Serrated knife and a teaspoon
Piping bag with a large open star nozzle
Whisk or mixer for the cream
Fine sieve for dusting

ingredients.item: Caster sugar, for the almond paste
Double or heavy cream, very cold

mise: Crack the cardamom pods in the mortar, pick out and discard the papery husks and grind the black seeds to a fine powder. Do this just before mixing; the aroma fades quickly.
Warm the milk to 99°F (37°C), blood warm.

Almond paste: grind the almonds and sugar in the processor for 2 to 3 minutes until fine and starting to clump; add 1 tsp (5 ml) water and the almond extract and pulse into a firm paste. Wrap and set aside.
Line the tray with baking paper.

timeline.do: Grind the cardamom; make the dough; first rise 1 hour.
Shape 6 buns; second rise 30 to 45 minutes; make the almond paste.
Egg wash; bake 10 to 12 minutes at 425°F (220°C).
Cool completely, at least 1 hour.
Cut lids, scoop, fill with almond paste, pipe cream, dust.

steps.do: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar, salt and ground cardamom. Add the warm milk and the beaten half egg and knead for 8 to 10 minutes (5 to 6 in a mixer on medium low) until smooth and elastic. Add the soft butter in pieces and knead 4 to 5 minutes more until it is fully absorbed.
steps.look: A soft, smooth, slightly tacky dough that pulls cleanly from the bowl; a small piece stretched thin goes translucent without tearing (the windowpane test).
steps.mistake: Adding the butter at the start, which slows gluten development and gives a heavy bun.
steps.fix: Knead first, butter last; keep kneading until the windowpane test works.

steps.do: Shape into a ball, cover and leave to rise in a warm place for 45 minutes to 1 hour until doubled.
steps.look: A dough doubled in size that holds a dent when gently poked with a floured finger.
steps.mistake: Rising it in a hot place, so it over proofs and tastes yeasty.
steps.fix: Warm, not hot: about 75 to 80°F (24 to 27°C).

steps.do: Divide into 6 pieces of about 80 g. Roll each into a tight ball by cupping your hand over it on an unfloured worktop and moving in small circles. Space them 2 inches (5 cm) apart on the tray, cover and rise 30 to 45 minutes. Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
steps.look: Smooth, round, taut balls that puff up by about half and spring back slowly when poked.
steps.mistake: Shaping loosely, so the buns spread flat.
steps.fix: Roll tightly to build surface tension; a little friction from an unfloured surface helps.

steps.do: Brush with the remaining beaten egg and bake 10 to 12 minutes until deep golden and hollow sounding when tapped underneath. Cool completely on a rack.
steps.look: Glossy, deep golden buns, soft inside and smelling strongly of cardamom.
steps.mistake: Filling warm buns, so the cream melts and slides off.
steps.fix: Cool them fully, at least 1 hour.

steps.do: With the serrated knife, cut a lid about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick off the top of each bun, angled slightly. Scoop out a heaped teaspoon of crumb from each, leaving a wall about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick.
steps.look: Six hollowed buns with neat lids and a bowl of soft crumb.
steps.mistake: Scooping too deep, so the bun breaks.
steps.fix: Leave a sturdy base and walls.

steps.do: Grate or crumble the almond paste into the bowl of scooped crumb, add 3 tbsp (45 ml) milk and mash into a thick, spoonable filling, adding more milk only if needed. Spoon it back into the buns, mounding slightly.
steps.look: A moist, thick, fragrant almond filling that holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Making it runny, so it soaks the bun and the cream slides.
steps.fix: Add milk a spoonful at a time; it should hold on a spoon turned sideways.

steps.do: Whip the cold cream to firm peaks, spoon into the piping bag and pipe a tall swirl about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) high on each bun. Set the lid on top and dust heavily with icing sugar through the sieve.
steps.look: A golden bun, a tall white swirl of cream peeking out under its lid, and a snowy dusting.
steps.mistake: Over whipping the cream until grainy, which looks rough when piped.
steps.fix: Stop at firm, smooth peaks; if grainy, fold in a little liquid cream by hand.

science: Cardamom's aroma comes from volatile oils inside the seeds, mainly cineole and terpinyl acetate, which begin to evaporate within hours of grinding; grinding fresh, and only the seeds, gives a much stronger, cleaner flavour than pre ground powder, which often includes the woody husk. Kneading develops gluten, an elastic network that traps the gas made by the yeast, so the buns rise light. Butter added after the gluten has formed enriches the dough without weakening it as much. Almond paste is ground almonds and sugar; the almonds release oil as they are ground, binding the paste. Whipping cream traps air in a network of partially joined fat globules, which is why cold cream whips best.
plating: Serve each semla on a small plate with a fork and spoon, as the Swedes do, or in a shallow bowl of warm milk (hetvägg, the old way). Dust the lid generously with icing sugar just before serving. Set them in pairs on a platter for coffee, the cream swirls facing the guest.

pairing.drink: Strong filter coffee, the Swedish fika way, or a glass of cold milk; a sweet sparkling wine for a party.
pairing.brennans: Congregation Single-Origin Coffee: the single origin coffee on the Brennan's list is the natural partner for a cardamom bun, the way Swedes take semla at fika.

variations: Semmelwrap: roll the bun flat, fill with almond paste and cream and wrap like a tortilla, a recent Stockholm bakery trend.
Shop almond paste: use 7 oz (200 g) good almond paste (at least half almonds) in place of homemade.
Hetvägg: serve the filled bun in a bowl of hot milk with cinnamon, the original way.
safety: Keep filled semlor refrigerated and eat the same day; the cream and almond filling are perishable.
Unfilled buns freeze well for up to a month.

title: Dan Tat (Hong Kong Egg Tarts)
summary: A water dough and a butter dough laminated together into a flaky Chinese puff pastry, pressed into small fluted tins and filled with a smooth, lightly sweet egg custard baked only until it is just set, flat and glossy. It teaches laminating two doughs and baking a custard that must not puff.
skills: a water dough and butter dough laminated
a smooth egg custard baked just set
equipment: 12 fluted egg tart tins, about 2 3/4 inches (7 cm) across, or a 12 hole muffin tin
Mixing bowls and a bench scraper
Rolling pin
Round cutter about 3 1/4 inches (8 cm), fluted if possible
Cling film
Whisk, jug and a fine sieve
Baking tray
Ruler

ingredients.item: Plain flour, for the water dough
Unsalted butter or lard, soft, for the water dough
Egg, beaten, for the water dough
Plain flour, for the butter dough
Cold unsalted butter, for the butter dough
ingredients.note: or half butter and half lard

mise: Water dough: mix the 100 g flour and salt, rub in the soft butter, add the beaten egg and enough cold water to make a soft, smooth dough. Knead 2 minutes, wrap and chill 30 minutes.

Butter dough: rub or press the cold butter into the 60 g flour until it forms a smooth paste. Shape into a square about 4 by 4 inches (10 by 10 cm) between film and chill 30 minutes until firm but pliable.
Custard syrup: dissolve the sugar in the hot water and let it cool to lukewarm.
Have the tart tins ready on a baking tray; you do not need to grease them if using pastry with this much butter.

timeline.do: Make the water dough and butter dough; chill both 30 minutes; make the syrup.
Enclose the butter dough; give three letter folds, chilling between.
Roll, cut and line the tins; chill 20 minutes.
Mix and strain the custard; oven to 400°F (200°C).
Fill and bake 15 minutes at 400°F (200°C), then 10 to 12 minutes at 350°F (175°C).
Cool 10 minutes; unmould and serve warm.

steps.do: Roll the chilled water dough into a square about 7 by 7 inches (18 by 18 cm). Set the butter dough square on it at an angle, like a diamond, and fold the four corners of the water dough over it to enclose it completely, pinching the seams.
steps.look: A neat, sealed parcel with no butter dough showing.
steps.mistake: Using butter dough that is much firmer or softer than the water dough, so it breaks or squeezes out when rolled.
steps.fix: Both doughs should feel about equally firm; let the colder one warm for a few minutes.

steps.do: Roll the parcel into a rectangle about 12 by 6 inches (30 by 15 cm), rolling from the centre outwards. Fold it in three like a letter. Turn it 90 degrees. Wrap and chill 20 minutes. Repeat the roll and fold twice more, chilling between, for three folds in all.
steps.look: A smooth block; at each cut edge you can see faint layers.
steps.mistake: Rolling while the dough is warm, so butter smears through and the layers are lost.
steps.fix: Chill whenever the dough feels soft or butter shows through; flour lightly to prevent sticking.

steps.do: Roll the dough to 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick. Cut 12 rounds with the cutter. Press each into a tin, easing it in with your thumbs from the base up the sides, so the wall is even and stands just above the rim. Chill 20 minutes. Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C).
steps.look: Twelve neat cases with even walls rising slightly above the tins.
steps.mistake: Stretching the dough into the tins, so it shrinks in the oven.
steps.fix: Ease it in rather than pulling; chill before baking.

steps.do: Custard: whisk the eggs gently with the lukewarm sugar syrup, the evaporated milk and vanilla, without creating foam. Strain twice through the fine sieve into a jug, then skim any bubbles from the surface.
steps.look: A smooth, pale yellow, bubble free liquid.
steps.mistake: Whisking hard, which makes bubbles that bake into pits on the custard.
steps.fix: Stir rather than whisk; strain twice and skim; let it rest a few minutes.

steps.do: Set the tins on the baking tray and fill each case to about 1/8 inch (3 mm) below the rim. Bake on the lower middle shelf at 400°F (200°C) for 15 minutes, then lower the oven to 350°F (175°C) and bake 10 to 12 minutes more.
steps.look: The pastry puffs and turns golden; the custard sets from the edge inwards and stays flat and glossy.
steps.mistake: Leaving the oven hot, so the custard puffs up like a soufflé and then sinks into a cratered, pitted surface.
steps.fix: Drop the heat on time; if the custard starts to dome, open the oven door 2 inches (5 cm) for 30 seconds.

steps.do: Take the tarts out when a gentle nudge of the tray sends one slow wobble across the centre of the custard and the surface is still flat and shiny. Cool 10 minutes in the tins, then ease them out with a small knife.
steps.look: Flaky golden pastry and a smooth, glossy, pale yellow custard that has set without puffing.
steps.mistake: Baking until the custard is completely firm, so it weeps and cracks as it cools.
steps.fix: Pull them while the centre still wobbles; carryover heat finishes the set.

steps.do: Serve the tarts warm, within 2 hours of baking, two or three per person, on a plate or a square of greaseproof paper.
steps.look: Pastry that shatters when bitten, custard that is silky and just set.
steps.mistake: Refrigerating them before serving, which softens the pastry.
steps.fix: Eat them warm; reheat leftovers at 325°F (160°C) for 5 minutes to recrisp.

science: Chinese puff pastry laminates a water dough, which contains gluten and stretches, with a butter dough, which is mostly fat. Rolling and folding creates many alternating thin layers of each; in the oven, water in the water dough turns to steam and lifts the layers apart, while the fat keeps them separate, giving flaky leaves. Keeping both doughs cool and of the same firmness stops the fat smearing into the dough. Egg custard sets at about 176 to 185°F (80 to 85°C). Sugar raises that temperature and buys margin. Past it, the protein network contracts and squeezes out water, so an overbaked custard weeps, pits and cracks, and if heated too fast the water in it boils and puffs it up before it sinks. Starting hot and then lowering the heat bakes the pastry and protects the custard.
plating: Serve the tarts on a small plate or a square of greaseproof paper, two or three together, still warm. In Hong Kong they come in a paper bag or on a saucer beside a cup of milk tea. For a dessert plate, set two tarts slightly apart with a few slices of fresh mango.

pairing.drink: Hong Kong milk tea or a gently sweet Chenin Blanc: tannic tea with milk, or a demi sec wine's acidity, balances the rich custard and pastry.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Huet ‘Le Mont’ Vouvray Demi-Sec 2023 (375 ml): a gently sweet Loire Chenin Blanc from the Brennan's list with the acidity for buttery pastry and egg custard.

variations: Shortcrust dan tat: use a sweet, cookie-like shortcrust (as in the library recipe) instead of puff; quicker and also traditional in Hong Kong.
Ginger milk custard: steep 1 tbsp (10 g) grated ginger in the hot syrup, then strain.
Bird's nest or almond tarts: add 1/4 tsp (1 ml) almond extract to the custard for a variation sold in Macau bakeries.
safety: The custard eggs are set when the centre has a single slow wobble; they reach a safe temperature as they finish setting.
Eat within 1 day, or refrigerate leftovers and reheat.

title: Pastéis de Nata
summary: All butter puff pastry rolled into a tight log, sliced into coins and pressed up the sides of a muffin tin with wet thumbs so the layers spiral, filled with a cooked custard of milk, cinnamon and lemon syrup and yolks, and baked in the hottest oven you have until the tops blister black in spots. It asks for laminated dough and an oven hot enough to scorch the custard.
skills: pressing pastry up the tin with wet thumbs
the hottest oven for blistered tops
equipment: 12 hole standard muffin tin, metal (not silicone)
Small bowl of cold water
Two small saucepans
Whisk and a sugar or probe thermometer
Fine sieve and a jug
Sharp knife and a ruler
Rolling pin and cling film
Fine sieve for dusting

ingredients.note: or the rough puff from the mille-feuille

mise: Roll the pastry sheet into a tight log from the short end, like a Swiss roll, so the layers spiral. Wrap in film and chill 30 minutes.
Syrup: boil the sugar, water, cinnamon stick and lemon peel to 220°F (104°C), about 3 minutes. Take off the heat and leave to infuse.
Whisk the flour into 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the cold milk until smooth.
Separate the eggs; keep the whites for another recipe.
Heat the oven to its maximum, ideally 500 to 550°F (260 to 290°C), with a shelf in the upper third, for at least 30 minutes.

timeline.do: Roll the pastry log and chill; make the syrup; oven on to its maximum.
Slice and press the pastry into the tin; chill.
Cook the milk base; add syrup and yolks; strain.
Fill and bake 10 to 12 minutes at maximum heat.
Cool 10 to 15 minutes; dust and serve warm.

steps.do: Trim the ends of the log and cut it into 12 coins about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick. Set a coin, spiral side up, in each muffin cup.
steps.look: Twelve neat coins, each showing a tight spiral of layers.
steps.mistake: Slicing a warm, soft log, which squashes the spiral.
steps.fix: Chill the log until firm and use a sharp knife.

steps.do: Dip your thumbs in cold water and press the centre of each coin down to the base, then push the pastry outward and up the sides of the cup with your thumbs, turning the tin, until the pastry is thin at the base, slightly thicker at the rim and rises just above the top of the cup. Chill the tin 15 minutes.
steps.look: Thin, even cases with the spiral layers running up the sides; a lip just above the rim.
steps.mistake: Leaving the base thick, so it stays doughy under the custard.
steps.fix: Press the base thinnest of all; wet thumbs stop the pastry sticking.

steps.do: Heat the remaining 3/4 cup (180 ml) milk until simmering, then whisk it into the flour and milk paste. Return to the pan and cook over medium heat, whisking, for 1 to 2 minutes until it thickens to a smooth, thin white sauce. Take off the heat.
steps.look: A smooth, slightly thick white sauce that coats a spoon.
steps.mistake: Adding the flour straight to hot milk, which makes lumps.
steps.fix: Always slake the flour in cold milk first; strain if lumpy.

steps.do: Remove the cinnamon stick and lemon peel from the syrup and pour the warm syrup into the milk base in a thin stream, whisking. Let it cool for 5 minutes to about 140°F (60°C), then whisk in the yolks and vanilla. Strain into a jug.
steps.look: A thin, smooth, pale yellow custard, warm but not hot.
steps.mistake: Adding yolks to a hot base, so they scramble.
steps.fix: Cool it to 140°F (60°C) first; strain out any threads.

steps.do: Fill each pastry case three quarters full with the custard. Bake on the upper shelf at the oven's maximum for 10 to 12 minutes, until the pastry is deep golden and crisp and the custard has puffed and blistered with dark brown and black spots.
steps.look: Leopard spotted tops of black and dark brown on a golden custard; the pastry crackles.
steps.mistake: Baking at a moderate heat, which gives a pale, flat top and soggy pastry.
steps.fix: Use the hottest setting your oven has; if the tops do not blister, finish 1 to 2 minutes under a hot overhead grill (broiler), watching closely.

steps.do: Cool the tarts in the tin for 5 minutes, then lift them out with a small knife onto a rack. Serve warm, after 10 to 15 minutes, dusted with cinnamon and icing sugar.
steps.look: Shattering pastry and a custard that trembles; the spots look caramelised, not burnt through.
steps.mistake: Taking them out of the tin immediately, when the custard is too soft and the pastry may break.
steps.fix: Wait 5 minutes; they firm up enough to lift.

science: Rolling the puff pastry into a log and pressing the slices up the tin turns the horizontal layers so they spiral up the sides; in the hot oven the water in the butter layers turns to steam and pushes them apart, so the walls are flaky and crisp. Very high heat sets and dries the pastry before the wet custard can soak it. The custard is thickened partly by flour, which gelatinises in the milk base and protects the yolks so they can withstand fierce heat without curdling. The syrup's sugar raises the setting temperature further. At over 500°F (260°C), the sugar and milk proteins on the surface caramelise and undergo Maillard browning in seconds, creating the dark, blistered spots while the custard beneath stays creamy.
plating: Serve on a small plate or a paper napkin, two per person, still warm. Put shakers of cinnamon and icing sugar on the table so each person dusts their own, as in the Lisbon cafés. A small strong coffee alongside is traditional.

pairing.drink: An espresso, or a sweet fortified Portuguese wine such as Madeira or tawny port: caramel and acidity for a scorched custard tart.
pairing.brennans: Broadbent ‘Single Cask’ Malvasia Madeira 500 ml 2009: a rich Portuguese Madeira from the Brennan's list, caramel and acid together, made for a Lisbon custard tart.

variations: Homemade pastry: use the rough puff from the mille-feuille, rolled thin, spread with soft butter and rolled into the log.
Orange: use orange peel in the syrup instead of lemon.
Mini tarts: use a mini muffin tin, coins 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) thick, and bake 7 to 9 minutes.
safety: An oven at 500 to 550°F (260 to 290°C) is extremely hot: use long oven gloves, open the door carefully and keep your face back from the heat.
The yolks cook fully in the very hot oven; eat the tarts the same day, or refrigerate and reheat.
